The hadith of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, collected in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs, is the one to weigh when considering the background of the verse. When ʿUmar was informed that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had divorced his wives, he left his house for the Masjid and found the people at its doorsteps already talking about the news. He said to himself that this was something which must first be investigated, went in to the Prophet ﷺ and asked him whether he had divorced his wives. He said: no. Having found out the truth, ʿUmar returned and, standing at the door of the Masjid, made an announcement in the loudest voice that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had not divorced his wives, and that whatever the people were saying was wrong. Thereupon the verse was revealed.

### Qiyās and ijtihād in new problems

From this verse comes the rule for problems not specifically mentioned in the authoritative texts, the nass, of the Qur'an or Sunnah. Their rulings are deduced in the light of the Qur'an through ijtihād and qiyās, because the verse commands turning to the Prophet ﷺ for the resolution of new problems when he is present, and, when he is not, to the scholars and jurists of the community, who have the ability to extract and formulate injunctions from the texts. Points of guidance follow. In the absence of explicit textual authority, the course is to turn to the jurists and scholars. The injunctions given by Allah are of two kinds, some explicit textual imperatives, others carrying meanings hidden in the depths of the verses as Allah willed in His infinite wisdom. It is the duty of the scholars to extract and formulate those meanings through the established methodology of ijtihād and qiyās. And for the great masses of Muslims, it is necessary to follow the guidance the scholars give in such problems, as the Aḥkām al-Qur'ān sets out. If anyone suspects that the verse has no relation with deducing injunctions, and only instructs people not to indulge in rumour-mongering in situations of peace and fear before an enemy, the answer is that the verse makes no mention of an enemy. The state of peace and fear is universal, and the way it relates to the enemy, so it relates to day-to-day problems, for a new problem throws the commoner into a fix where both sides hold probability of gain and loss, and the smartest way out devised by the Sharīʿah is to turn to those capable of extracting injunctions. The outcome of ijtihād, lastly, stays humble. A ruling extracted through investigation cannot categorically be declared the absolute truth in the sight of Allah, and the probability always exists that it might turn out otherwise. What one gains from it is the positive, overwhelming and weightier opinion of its being true, and that is the thing to act upon.

### The inner reading

Istinbāṭ, precise extraction, is the mining of the jewels of meanings. The heedless have no confidant for their secrets, so they pour them out to one another. The believers have the opposite estate: the One who knows their secrets is also their Friend and Protector. Whatever reaches them, they raise it in speech with Him, needing no created being to broadcast it to. Allah hears their whispered confidence, and Allah knows their hidden affairs. Had such people carried their secrets to the respected ones, the people of the story, the doubts would have been dispelled and the light of guidance and spiritual instruction would have carried them through. And were it not for Allah's bounty toward His friends, they would stray down every valley of parting that the moment opens, exactly as their outward look-alikes do.

### In short

- News of security or fear is not to be broadcast before verification, for repeating all one hears is enough to make a liar.
- The reference runs to the Prophet ﷺ and the authorities, which covers rulers and, by trust and wājib obedience, the scholars and jurists.
- ʿUmar's handling of the divorce rumour, ask first, then announce the truth from the Masjid door, is the pattern the verse demands.
- Where the texts are silent, the qualified investigate and deduce through ijtihād and qiyās, and the masses follow, for following Satan needs no help from anyone but a few.

84.text:
The command and its setting: "So fight in the cause of Allah ˹O Prophet˺. You are accountable for none but yourself. And motivate the believers ˹to fight˺, so perhaps Allah will curb the disbelievers' might" (4:84). The battle of Uḥud had passed in the month of Shawwāl, and in keeping with the date the disbelievers had set, the Prophet ﷺ prepared to meet them at Badr in the month of Dhū al-Qaʿdah, the engagement the historians call the minor Badr. Some people betrayed a little hesitation about going along, some from recent wounds and some because of rumours, so the verse came down telling him to ignore the infirm and the scared among the Muslims and march to jihād without hesitation, even alone, for Allah is his helper. With that guidance he went ahead to the lesser Badr with seventy Companions, as promised to Abū Sufyān after Uḥud. Allah put awe and fear into the hearts of Abū Sufyān and his accomplices of the tribe of Quraysh, and not one of the unbelievers of Makkah showed up, so they proved false to their solemn promise. Allah prevented the mischief of the disbelievers, and the Prophet ﷺ returned safely with his companions, as al-Qurṭubī and al-Mazharī relate the event, the same encounter the Qur'ān had already told in sūrat Āl ʿImrān.

### Phrase by phrase

**"So fight in the cause of Allah ˹O Prophet˺"** addresses the Prophet ﷺ alone, and the implication is that he should fight irrespective of whether anyone is ready to go with him. The word for perhaps, when used in relation to Allah, means that He has taken the thing upon Himself. He has been promised victory, so the fight goes on even if he stands single, and the report has him saying:

> By Him in Whose Hand is my soul, I shall sally forth to fight even if I go alone.

**"You are accountable for none but yourself"** cuts the responsibility down to one man. He is not tasked with the staying behind of others. The verse about self-destruction was once read against such a fighter. Abu Isḥāq asked al-Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib whether a man who meets a hundred enemies and still fights them belongs among those meant by the words "And do not throw yourselves into destruction (by not spending your wealth in the cause of Allah)" (2:195). He said no, because Allah said this to His Prophet, and the destruction verse is about spending in His cause. Imām Aḥmad recorded the parallel question, whether a man who attacks the lines of the idolaters is throwing himself to destruction, and received the same answer for the same reason.

**"And motivate the believers ˹to fight˺"** keeps the mission of persuasion alive. He is to incite them by encouraging them and strengthening their resolve, and if they stay unresponsive even after the effort, his prophetic work is done, and from that point he is not responsible for what they do. At the battle of Badr, while organising the lines, he said to the believers:

> Stand up and march forth to a Paradise, as wide as the heavens and Earth.

Many hadiths encourage jihād. Al-Bukhārī recorded from Abū Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> Whoever believes in Allah and His Messenger, offers prayer, pays the zakāh and fasts the month of Ramaḍān, will rightfully be granted Paradise by Allah, no matter whether he migrates in Allah's cause or remains in the land where he is born.

Asked whether the people should acquaint others with this good news, he spoke instead of the hundred grades:

> Paradise has one hundred grades which Allah has reserved for the mujāhidīn who fight in His cause, the distance between each two grades being like the distance between heaven and Earth. So, when you ask Allah, ask for al-Firdaws, the best and highest part of Paradise, above which is the Throne of the Most Beneficent, and from which originate the rivers of Paradise.

The hadith also has narrations from ʿUbādah, from Muʿādh and from Abū ad-Dardāʾ. Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī heard his own version addressed to him by name:

> O Abū Saʿīd, whoever accepts Allah as his Lord, Islam as his religion and Muḥammad as the Prophet, he would rightfully acquire Paradise.

He liked the words so much that he asked for them to be repeated, and the Prophet ﷺ repeated them, then mentioned another deed, one by which Allah raises a servant a hundred grades in Paradise, the distance between two grades being as between heaven and Earth. Asked what it was, he said: jihād in Allah's cause. Muslim collected it.

**"so perhaps Allah will curb the disbelievers' might"** explains what the motivating achieves. Their resolve is strengthened to meet the enemy, to defend Islam and its people, and to endure the enemy patiently. Perhaps awe enters their hearts and they fold, and the lone fighter wins through alone.

**"And Allah is far superior in might and in punishment"** gives the reason such success is certain. He is able over them in this life and the Hereafter: "But if it had been Allah's will" (47:4), He could have had His way with them outright. The punishment may fall on the Day of Judgement, or right here in this mortal world, as some hold. Whichever it is, He is the strongest in war and the mightiest in punishing.

### The two kinds of religion

One form religiosity takes is the public observance of outward rites, with no change made in one's life, and such religion is resented by no one, since nobody needs to oppose it. Another form calls for sacrifice and disturbs the pattern of a life. When that kind is invoked, people divide. One group of opponents is made of people whose leadership in the religious field stands on rites that cost their worldly interests nothing. They work by the maxim that speaking in defence of truth damages those interests, while silence or opposition brings benefit, so they oppose the religion of sacrifice to protect their positions. The other group is made of people with a live conscience who judge above gain and expediency, accepting without hesitation a reality that argument has proved. True Muslims are told not to let such differences constrain their social relationships and not to adopt a discourteous attitude, for a Muslim's manner is free of reactionary impulse. It is for Allah to judge and requite as He wishes.

### In short

- After Uḥud the appointment was kept at the lesser Badr with seventy men, and Allah filled Abū Sufyān and the Quraysh with awe, so the enemy never showed and the promise of the disbelievers proved false.
- The Prophet ﷺ is charged with his own fight and with urging the rest, no more. The lone charge answered a question about whether fighting against odds is self-destruction, which it is not, for that verse concerns spending.
- The urging rests on the hundred grades and al-Firdaws, the highest of them, and on the deed that raises a servant a hundred degrees, which is jihād in Allah's cause.
- Success belongs to Allah, whose might and punishment exceed the disbelievers', in this world and the next.

85.text:
The law of the helping word: "Whoever intercedes for a good cause will have a share in the reward, and whoever intercedes for an evil cause will have a share in the burden. And Allah is Watchful over all things" (4:85). The verse takes the common human act of putting in a word for someone and sorts it by what the word serves.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Whoever intercedes for a good cause will have a share in the reward"** means that whoever intercedes in a matter producing good results acquires a share in that good. The word for intercession, shafāʿah, means literally to meet or to join, or to cause a meeting or joining, which is why shaf, its root word, names an even number, a pair, the opposite of witr, the odd. Taken literally, it is the yoking of your strength to a weak seeker of justice so the appeal grows stronger, or the standing beside a helpless solitary person so that he has the strength of a pair. In the reading of one school it names whoever helps to unite or reconcile two parties, and the reward of that good deed reaches him, the person of the good intercession being Abū Bakr. Mujāhid ibn Jabr read the verse as sent down about people recommending on one another's behalf.

**"and whoever intercedes for an evil cause will have a share in the burden"** means he carries a burden from what resulted and from the intention. In the same school reading, the evil intercession covers the ascribing of partners to Allah and the work of the tale-bearer, and its face among the opponents of the faith was Abū Jahl. Directing another person to some good in a manner containing no sin or oppression earns a share of the reward of the outcome, while a bad intercession, one containing sin or oppression, earns a share of the sin. Become a means of goodness and a share of the good is yours. Become a means of evil and you are guilty of a part of it.

**"And Allah is Watchful over all things"** turns on the word muqīṭ. Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿAṭāʾ, ʿAṭiyyah, Qatādah and Matar al-Warrāq said it means Watcher. Mujāhid said it means Witness, and in another narration, Able to do. Lexically the word carries power, observation and the dispensation of sustenance, and all three meanings stand here. Taken as power, rewarding and punishing the maker of a recommendation and its executor is nothing difficult for Him. Taken as observation, He is ever present, knowing best who recommends with what intention, whether sincerely to help a brother-in-faith for Allah's pleasure, or to make him a target of self-interest and extract an advantage as a bribe. Taken as sustenance, what He has written for someone reaches that one without fail. No recommendation corners Him into giving. He bestows as He wills and on whom He wills, while the good recommender is rewarded for free, since a helping hand went out from him to the helpless.

### The rules of a fair recommendation

For a recommendation to be fair and permissible, the claim of the person recommended must be true and permissible, and in the second place the person may be unable to carry his claim to those in authority because of weakness or lack of resource, which is what another may do for him. Recommending what is not true and rightful, or forcibly influencing its acceptance, falls under bad recommendation, and so does pressure exerted through one's connections and influence, for that is an act of injustice. Whoever recommends in the permissible way for a permissible claim or job gets a share in its reward, and whoever recommends something impermissible, or uses an impermissible method, gets a share in its punishment. The share does not depend on the recommendation succeeding. Should the official do the needful for the one wronged, the recommender is rewarded much like the official who removed the injustice. Should he recommend the impermissible, he becomes a sinner either way.

The Prophet ﷺ said that whoever talks another into a good deed earns a reward like the doer's own, and the reverse holds with matching weight. A hadith from Abū Hurairah appearing in Ibn Mājah reports the warning:

> Whoever helps in the killing of a Muslim, even by part of a word, will face Allah with a sign written between his eyes: this man is deprived of the mercy of Allah.

The limit of the act is set in the hadith of Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī:

> Intercede and you will gain a reward of it. Yet Allah shall decide whatever He wills by the words of His Prophet.

Where a weak person cannot carry his problem up to a higher authority, or cannot set out correctly what he needs, carry it for him. Past that point the affair leaves your hands. Acceptance or rejection is not yours to manage, no interference in the deciding is allowed, and disgust at an outcome that goes against you has no place. Read as a word of cause, the verse carries the same hint, and al-Mazharī reports from the great exegete Mujāhid that the maker of a recommendation earns its reward even when nobody accepts it. This is not special to the Prophet ﷺ. Any recommendation made to any human being is bound by the principle: make it and be done with it. He illustrated it himself. He recommended to Barīrah, a bondwoman freed by ʿĀʾishah, that she consider remarrying her husband Mughīth, from whom she had dissolved her marriage, for the man was emotionally disturbed out of his love for her. She answered that if it was a command she was all for it, but if it was a recommendation, she did not feel like accepting it at all. He said that it was a recommendation and not a command, and she, knowing he would take nothing amiss that went against the set rule, said in all frankness that she did not accept it. He took it gracefully and let her stay as she was.

In the present day the whole thing has been mutilated. What passes for recommendation is a pushy exercise of cashing in on connections, acquaintance and VIP influence, with relentless pressure, which is why people grow angry when their recommendation is rejected, and some stoop to open hostility. Yet compelling a person to do something against his conscience and good discretion is compulsion and coercion, a grave sin, like depriving a free person of his freedom of action, or like stealing from someone in order to give to a destitute. And a recommendation against which anything is taken in return is a bribe, declared by hadith to be ill-gotten and ḥarām, whether the bribe is money or a job-related favour, such as harnessing someone to a personal chore in return. Al-Kashshāf draws the full outline. The good recommendation aims at fulfilling the right of a Muslim, bringing him a permissible benefit, or shielding him from harm and loss. It is made for no worldly expediency, but to help a weak person with the pleasure of Allah as the only seek. No bribe is taken against it, financial or physical. It concerns nothing impermissible, and it does not seek pardon for a proven crime whose punishment stands fixed in the Qur'ān. Praying to Allah that the need of some Muslim be fulfilled also counts, as al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ and al-Mazharī note, as good recommendation, its reward reaching the one who prays. When a prayer goes up for a brother-in-faith's good, the angel answers: may Allah fulfil your need as well.

### The inner reading

Intercession sets free the state of the one interceded for, and by it the intercessor wins a weighty rank from Allah. Whoever rushes instead to corrupt what concerns the command carries the responsibility and the weight of the sin on his own back.

### In short

- Intercession couples strength with weakness. Its claim must be true, its method free of force, and its seeker unable to carry the matter alone.
- The share in reward or burden is earned by the act itself, not by its success, so the recommender neither pressures the decision nor rages at a refusal.
- Barīrah's refusal of the Prophet's ﷺ own recommendation, accepted gracefully, is the standing pattern of the limit.
- Payment for a recommendation is a bribe and ḥarām, and a prayer for a brother's need is itself a good intercession.

86.text:
The etiquette of the greeting: "And when you are greeted, respond with a better greeting or at least similarly. Surely Allah is a ˹vigilant˺ Reckoner of all things" (4:86). The verse opens the Islamic teaching on the salām, the greeting Muslims exchange, and it was revealed, one report holds, about a group of people who refrained from returning greetings.

### The greeting Islam gave

Lexically, taḥiyyah belongs to the sayings of ḥayyākallāh, may Allah keep you alive. In pre-Islam Arabia people greeted each other with ḥayyākallāh, or with asks for blessing on the morning, or other expressions of that nature. Islam changed the style and fixed a standard form, As-Salāmu ʿAlaykum, commonly though incompletely translated as peace be on you, for the words mean: may you remain safe from every pain, sorrow and distress. Ibn al-ʿArabī notes in the Aḥkām al-Qur'ān that Salam is one of the good names of Allah, so that the greeting declares Allah the guardian and caretaker of the one greeted.

The Islamic greeting stands alone among the customs of the world. All civilised people say something to express familiarity or affection at meeting, but compared broadly, this form stands out for comprehensiveness. It does not stop at affection. It joins to it the fulfilment of the demands of love, a prayer that the other be kept safe from all calamities and sorrows. It is no bland prayer for long life, as with the pre-Islam Arabs, but a prayer for a good life. It expresses the reality of the relation with Allah, that greeter and greeted are both dependent on Him, needing Him all the time, with no one bringing benefit to anyone without His will. Taken that way, the greeting is an act of worship in its own right and a medium for the remembrance of Allah, reminding a brother-in-faith of the object of his obedience and love. It also carries a promise, that the person greeted is safe from the greeter's own hands and tongue, so that the greeter stands as guardian of the other's life, property and honour. Ibn ʿUyaynah, in the report quoted by Ibn al-ʿArabī, asked whether one knows what the salām is, and answered that the greeter is saying: you are safe from me. The hadith of at-Tirmidhī, in the Book of Faith, runs:

> A Muslim is the one from whom all Muslims remain safe, safe from his tongue and safe from his hands.

One may wish Muslims would not utter these words as a habitual custom like the greetings of other peoples. Offered out of a full understanding of its reality, the greeting might be enough for the reform of a whole community, which is why the Prophet ﷺ laid such emphasis on popularising it.

### The merits of the greeting

Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim carries from Abū Hurairah the report that the Prophet ﷺ said:

> You cannot enter Paradise until you are a believer, and your belief, your īmān, cannot be complete until you love each other. I tell you something which, if you put it in practice, will establish bonds of love among you all: make the salām a common practice among you, including every Muslim, whether an acquaintance or a stranger.

ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar relates that someone asked the Prophet ﷺ which practice of Islam is the worthiest. The answer was to feed people and to spread the salām, known face or stranger, in a report the two collections of al-Bukhārī and Muslim carry. The Musnad of Aḥmad, at-Tirmidhī and Abū Dāwūd report from Abū Umāmah that the person nearest to Allah is the one who greets first. A hadith of ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd, in the Musnad of al-Bazzār and the al-Mu'jim al-Kabīr of aṭ-Ṭabarānī, teaches that the salām is one of the names of Allah with which He has blessed the people of the earth, so it must be made common. A Muslim who offers his salām in a gathering is blessed with a station of distinction, having reminded everyone of Allah. Should the gathering not return it, others better than they will respond, the angels of Allah. And in another hadith from Abū Hurairah, the big miser is the man who scrimps on the greeting, as aṭ-Ṭabarānī records in the al-Mu'jim al-Kabīr. The effect on the Companions can be gauged from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar, who would go to the bazaar for the single purpose of meeting any Muslim there in the hope of offering the salām and earning the reward of an act of worship, never intending to buy or sell, a narration of Tufayl ibn ʿUbayy ibn Kaʿb that appears in the Muʾatta of Imām Mālik.

### Phrase by phrase

**"And when you are greeted, respond with a better greeting"** means that if a Muslim greets with the salām, the greeting is returned with what is better, and the better return is recommended. The Prophet ﷺ taught it by action. ʿImrān ibn Ḥuṣayn, in the record of Imām Aḥmad, watched three men come in turn. The first said As-Salāmu ʿAlaykum, the Prophet ﷺ returned it, and after the man sat he said: ten. The second added the mercy of Allah, and heard: twenty. The third added the blessings of Allah, and heard: thirty. Abu Dāwūd recorded this narration, and at-Tirmidhī, an-Nasāʾī and al-Bazzār recorded it also, at-Tirmidhī calling it ḥasan gharīb, with further hadiths on the subject from Abū Saʿīd, ʿAlī and Sahl ibn Ḥanīf. The fuller teaching report has its own detail. One man greeted, and the return added a word of mercy. A second greeted with the mercy included, and the return added the blessings. The third combined all three in his initial greeting, and the Prophet ﷺ answered with a single word, and upon you. Asked why the prayers had shrunk, he said that the man had left nothing to add, for he had used up all the words in his salām, so the return on the principle of like for like was sufficient, in accordance with the teaching of the Qur'ān. Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported it with different chains.

Three rules emerge. The salām offered is returned by adding words to it, mercy upon peace, blessings upon mercy. The addition is restricted to three words as a sunnah-conforming act, for Ibn ʿAbbās, in the report al-Mazharī cites from al-Baghawī, explained that the salām ends at the word barakah, and saying anything beyond that was not the practice of the Prophet ﷺ. The logic is plain, since the occasion requires brevity, and excess that interferes with ongoing business or weighs on the listener is not appropriate. And if someone packs all three words into his initial salām, returning it with one word is correct, like for like, sufficient in obedience to the command of returning the same.

**"or at least similarly"** states the obligation. Returning the equal salām is a duty on every Muslim greeted with the full form, and failing it without an excuse the Sharīʿah admits makes a person a sinner, though the mode is his to choose, better words or identical ones. The passive voice of the verse, when you are greeted, without naming the greeter, hints that the salām was already the habitual common practice of the Muslims. The initial salām itself is a sunnah mu'akkadah, an emphasised practice, as the majority of the ʿulamā hold in the reading of al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ, and Ḥasan al-Baṣrī said that the initial salām is voluntary while returning it is an obligation.

**"Surely Allah is a ˹vigilant˺ Reckoner of all things"** closes the account. Everything is reckoned with Allah, and the reckoning includes all human and Islamic rights. The salām and its answer stand among them, and they too will be accounted for before Him.

### The wider rules of the greeting

The riding person greets the walking person, the walking person greets the one sitting, and a small group walking near a larger group is first to greet, as a hadith in al-Bukhārī and Muslim directs. On entering his house, a person should offer the salām to his family, an act of grace bringing blessings for him and them, as at-Tirmidhī has it. Meeting a Muslim more than once, the salām is offered every time, and it belongs to the practice at leave-taking as well, a rule that appears in at-Tirmidhī and Abū Dāwūd on the narration of Qatādah and Abū Hurairah. With the people of the covenant, the ahl adh-dhimmah, the salām is not initiated, nor is anything added when their greeting is returned, for the Two Ṣaḥīḥs direct that their greeting is returned equally. Ibn ʿUmar narrated the reason in the words of the Prophet ﷺ:

> When the Jews greet you, one of them would say: death be unto you. Therefore say: and the same to you.

In his Ṣaḥīḥ, Muslim recorded from Abū Hurayrah the further instruction not to initiate the greeting with the Jews and the Christians, and when meeting them on a road, to force them to its narrowest path. The schools add further notes. The Sunnah specifies leaving unanswered the greeting of the open disbeliever, the innovator and the wicked person. The same holds for one relieving himself, one in the bath and one eating, the disapproval being relaxed only in that last case. And to the disbeliever who says peace upon you, the answer is simply: and upon you. The exceptions to the obligation run the other way too. No answer is owed to a salām said to a person performing ṣalāh, for it spoils the prayer, and the same holds for one delivering a sermon, reciting the Qur'ān, calling the adhān or the iqāmah, teaching religious texts, or busy with the compulsions of human need, where even offering the initial salām is not permissible.

### The inner reading

In this verse the lovingly kind Beautiful-doer teaches His servants the courteous acts of companionship. Whoever wears no courtesy is unfit for company. Companionship has three sorts to it: courtesy in conforming to the Real, courtesy of sincerity with people, and courtesy in opposing the soul. A person not nurtured on these three has no part in the path of Muṣṭafā, and counts for nothing in the world of no god but God. The Lord first adorned Muṣṭafā himself with this quality, in his own words:

> My Lord taught me courtesy, so how beautifully I have been made courteous.

On the night of the miʿrāj, standing in the most tremendous station, he kept the courtesy of the Presence, of whom the verse says: "The eyesight did not swerve, nor did it transgress" (53:17). With people he kept the courtesy of company, of whom the verse says: "Surely you have a tremendous character" (68:4).

The courteous acts toward the Real run by principles. Work knowledge into every dealing. Reverence the Sharīʿah, and refuse to enact what your own wishes command. Honour the Sunnah and its folk, and keep clear of innovation and its folk. Lay suspicion and supposition aside. Stay far from disquieting thoughts, from eye-service, from ignorance and from laziness in worship. Do not dress yourself as the worshipful servant of anything outside the Sunnah, and keep the supererogatory acts hidden. Do not take the name of Allah in heedlessness, nor mix levity with seriousness, nor play with the Sharīʿah and the religion. Carry scrupulousness into speech, action, sight, food, sleep, movement and rest.

Even the one whose days pass in truthfulness and limpidity never approves of himself. Displeasure with self stays, and repentance binds him in every state, on the word of the Messenger:

> My heart becomes clouded, so I ask forgiveness from Allah one hundred times a day.

Abū Yazīd Basṭāmī carried displeasure with his own limpidness and self-purification so far that his glorification at times was a finger pointed at himself and the words: you are the miserable man of the time.

### In short

- Islam replaced the greetings of the age with one standard prayer for safety. That prayer carries a name of Allah, a reminder of Him, and a pledge of safety from the greeter's own hand and tongue.
- The merits are many: love and īmān, the worthiest deed after feeding people, nearness to Allah for greeting first, and a station of distinction in every gathering.
- The return is obligatory, and the better return is recommended. The addition is capped at barakah, and like for like suffices when the greeter spends all the words at once.
- The salām is not initiated with the people of the covenant, whose twisted greeting is answered with a plain and the same to you, and obligations pause where prayer, sermon, recitation, adhān, iqāmah, teaching and need hold a person.
- The greeting is a school of courtesy whose courtyard runs from the miʿrāj to the market, and its graduates never approve of themselves.

87.text:
The seal of the passage: "Allah, there is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him. He will certainly gather ˹all of˺ you together on the Day of Judgment" (4:87). After the commands about fighting, intercession and greeting, the verses close with the foundation everything rests on.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Allah, there is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him"** declares His Oneness, informing that He alone is God of all creation. The address works by negation and affirmation together. The negation takes in everything other than Allah, to whom divinity is impossible. What He affirms of Himself through His divinity admits no denial. The exhortation follows: believe in Him as the only object of worship, and let whatever you do be done as an act of worship before Him.

**"He will certainly gather ˺all of˺ you together on the Day of Judgment, about which there is no doubt"** is an oath that He will gather the earlier and the latter generations in one area, raising them from their graves, to reward or punish each person according to his or her actions. The Day of Qiyāmah, the fateful Day of Doom, is certain, and with it the promise of reward and punishment.

**"And whose word is more truthful than Allah's"** needs no answer, for no one utters more truthful statements than Allah, in His promise and His warning, in the stories of the past and the information of what is to come. The news of what will happen is true because Allah is its giver, and whose word can be more true than that of Allah.

### In short

- The verse declares the Oneness of Allah, negating every other object of worship and affirming what He has affirmed of Himself.
- The gathering on the Day of Qiyāmah is sworn and certain, and every soul meets its own return there.
- His word is the measure of truth, in promise, warning, history and news of the unseen alike.

88.text:
The censure of a divided community: "Why are you ˹believers˺ divided into two groups regarding the hypocrites while Allah allowed them to regress ˹to disbelief˺ because of their misdeeds?" (4:88). The verse answers a real argument that broke out among the Companions, and it settles the status of people whose Islam had come undone.

### The occasion reports

Imām Aḥmad recorded from Zayd ibn Thābit that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ marched towards Uḥud, and some who set out with him went back to al-Madinah. The Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ divided into two groups over them, one saying they should be killed and the other objecting, and the verse came down. al-Bukhārī and Muslim both carry the report, Ghundar and Ibn Muʿādh's father relating it from Shuʿbah on the authority of ʿAbdullāh ibn Yazīd ibn Thābit. The same occasion carries the Prophet's words about the city:

> She is Ṭaybah, and she expels filth, just as the bellows expels rust from iron.

A second report, carried by ʿAbdur-Raḥmān ibn Ḥamdān, tells of a group of Arabs who came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and embraced Islam, then contracted the illness and fever going round in Madinah, renounced Islam and left. Met by a group of Companions and asked why they had left, they answered that they had caught the illness of Madinah and disliked remaining there, whereupon the Companions asked whether they had no good example in the person of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Some judged them hypocrites and others still Muslims, and because of the difference of opinion the verse was revealed.

A third report comes from Mujāhid, relayed by ʿAbdullāh ibn Ḥāmid. Some disbelievers of Makkah came to Madinah pretending to have become Muslims, claiming to have arrived as emigrants, then turned apostates. They told the Prophet ﷺ of a plan to go to Makkah for merchandise, made their false excuse, departed and never returned. The Muslims of Madinah differed over them, some calling them believers, until the verse declared them disbelievers whose killing was due. Mawlānā Ashraf ʿAlī Thānāvī explains the word munāfiq here. Killing was not the lot of the hypocrites as such, since their disbelief stayed hidden within. These people stood elsewhere, for their apostasy had come out into the open. Those who took them for Muslims had perhaps taken a benign view under some interpretation, but that interpretation rested on sheer opinion, unsupported by any proof of the Sharīʿah, so no reliance was placed on it.

Al-ʿAwfī reported from Ibn ʿAbbās a Makkan version. Some people in Makkah said they embraced Islam yet gave their support to the idolaters. Going out of Makkah one day to fulfil some needs, they said to each other that if they met the Companions of Muḥammad, no harm would come to them from that side. When the believers learned of their outing, one group said to march against these cowards and kill them, for they supported the enemy against the Muslims. The other group said: glory be to Allah, will you kill a people who say what you say, only because they did not perform the emigration or leave their land? Is their blood then lawful and their money to be confiscated? So the believers split into two groups while the Messenger ﷺ was present among them, and he did not prohibit either group from pressing its argument, until the verse came down. Ibn Abī Ḥātim recorded this hadith. One gloss counts the people concerned as ten hypocrites who left Islam and Madinah for Makkah, the two parties disputing whether their wealth and blood had become lawful.

Ibn Abī Shaybah narrated from Ḥasan a different occasion. Suraqah ibn Mālik al-Mudlajī visited the Prophet ﷺ after the events of Badr and Uḥud and requested peace for his tribe, Banū Mudlaj, whereupon he sent Khālid to conclude the treaty on the terms:

> We will not support anyone against the Prophet ﷺ. If the Quraysh become Muslims, we too shall become Muslims. All tribes who enter into alliance with us shall become party with us in this treaty.

A further narration from Ibn ʿAbbās identifies the people of the fourth verse in this passage as the tribes of Asad and Ghaṭafān, while aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk ascribes the like conduct to the tribe of ʿAbd ad-Dār. The first two narrations appear in Rūḥ al-Maʿānī and the third in Maʿālim.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Why are you ˹believers˺ divided into two groups regarding the hypocrites"** asks in the tone of disapproval, and the question returns later in the verse in the same tone. The believers had split over the status of the returners, one party for the sword and the other for sparing them, over people who had not performed the hijrah, the emigration.

**"while Allah allowed them to regress ˹to disbelief˺ because of their misdeeds"** settles the matter from the divine side. The word of the verse means cast them back, as Ibn ʿAbbās glosses it, and what they earned was their defiance and disobedience to the Messenger ﷺ, their following of falsehood, their hypocrisy and their evil intentions.

**"Do you wish to guide those left by Allah to stray?"** exposes the futility of the sparing party's hope, for the question means: will you count them among the guided? Of him whom Allah has sent astray from His religion, no religion or argument can be found in favour.

**"And whoever Allah leaves to stray, you will never find for them a way"** states the rule outright. No path to guidance opens for the one He has left astray.

### The three groups and the two injunctions

The passage as a whole describes three groups of people under two injunctions. The first are the open apostates, whose case follows the ruling on disbelievers in general. The second are those who enter a no-war pact with the Muslims themselves, or who join hands with people holding such a pact. The third make peace only to buy time, and join the enemy camp at the first occasion of war, throwing the treaty obligations to the winds. The first group is fought in the absence of peace, the second is exempted from arrest and killing, and the third receives the same punishment as the first. The mapping runs through the following verses: the second verse carries the arrest and killing, the third gives the exemption in the event of peace, and the fourth returns to those who refuse peace, from which it follows that no fighting is due to them if they make peace, as the Bayān al-Qur'ān sets out.

The inward hearing of the verse is sterner still. Hold to the covenant regarding them, for they are My enemies. Neither in this world nor the next will they receive My good pleasure. No anxiety felt for them can rescue them from what the decree has fixed, and the decrees do not circle around the worries of people.

### In short

- The Companions split over the returners from Uḥud and over pretending emigrants who turned apostates, and Allah censured the division itself.
- The reports vary in setting: the Uḥud withdrawal, the fever that drove Arabs from Madinah, the merchandise excuse, the Banū Mudlaj treaty, and the Asad and Ghaṭafān peace-seekers.
- Allah had cast them back for what they earned, and no way exists to guide those He has left astray.
- Three groups stand in the passage, open apostates, pact-holders and double dealers, under two rules: fight in the absence of peace, and stand down in the event of peace.

89.text:
The wish and the command: "They wish you would disbelieve as they have disbelieved, so you may all be alike. So do not take them as allies unless they emigrate in the cause of Allah" (4:89). The verse exposes what the deserters want, then draws the line of association.

### Phrase by phrase

**"They wish you would disbelieve as they have disbelieved, so you may all be alike"** means they wish the believers to fall into misguidance, so that both stand equal in it, and the wish comes of their extreme enmity and hatred. They want company in unbelief, a level field with no side standing higher.

**"So do not take them as allies unless they emigrate in the cause of Allah"** forbids taking friends from among them in religion or for assistance and backing, even if they outwardly manifest belief, until the hijrah, the migration in the way of Allah, confirms it, an emigration in obedience to Allah. If they abandon it, as al-ʿAwfī reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, the alliance stays closed, and as-Suddī read the turning away as making their disbelief public.

### The emigration that ended and the emigration that continues

The emigration here has its own history. In the early period, migration from the homeland of disbelief, the dār al-kufr, was enjoined on all Muslims, which is why whoever failed to carry out the hijrah was not treated as a Muslim. When Makkah was conquered, the Prophet ﷺ declared that there is no emigration after the Victory, for the Conquest had made Makkah an abode of Islam, and the duty lapsed. The later rule, as Muḥammad Taqī ʿUthmānī notes, is that a Muslim living in a non-Muslim country where he cannot fulfil his religious obligations must emigrate if he has the means.

Another emigration continues. The abandonment of sins lasts as long as the time to repent remains, in the report of Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī. Al-ʿAynī, who wrote the commentary on al-Bukhārī, glossed it exactly so, and a hadith of the Prophet ﷺ teaches that the muhājir, the emigrant, is one who leaves everything Allah has prohibited, a saying recorded in al-Mirqāt.

The word therefore carries a dual sense. One leaves one's homeland to save one's faith, as the Companions did in moving from Makkah to Madinah and Ethiopia. The other leaves one's sins.

**"But if they turn away, then seize them and kill them wherever you find them"** gives the penalty for the turning back, meaning capture as prisoners and death in the Sacred Precinct or anywhere else.

**"and do not take any of them as allies or helpers"** closes the door a second time. From this the rule is drawn that seeking help from disbelievers is forbidden, ḥarām. When the Anṣār of Madinah sought the Prophet's permission to seek help from the Jews to offset the disbelievers, he answered:

> The bad ones! We do not need them.

So al-Mazharī relates the instruction.

### In short

- Their wish is equality in unbelief, born of pure enmity, and it is not granted.
- Alliance waits on a true emigration in the way of Allah, the kind that confirms belief, while open desertion forfeits protection.
- Emigration as a precondition of faith ended with the Conquest of Makkah, though the emigration from sin continues, and the duty stands for anyone who cannot practise his religion where he is.
- Seizing and killing follow the turn away, and help from disbelievers is ḥarām, as the Prophet's answer to the Anṣār shows.

90.text:
The exemption: "except those who are allies of a people you are bound with in a treaty or those wholeheartedly opposed to fighting either you or their own people. If Allah had willed, He would have empowered them to fight you" (4:90). Between the apostate and the double dealer stands a middle kind, and the verse protects them.

### Phrase by phrase

**"except those who are allies of a people you are bound with in a treaty"** excepts those who join and take refuge with a people with whom the Muslims hold a pact of peace, or with people of covenant status, and they are treated as the pact people are treated. So read as-Suddī, Ibn Zayd and Ibn Jarīr together. The story of the treaty of al-Ḥudaybiyyah, recorded in al-Bukhārī's Ṣaḥīḥ, set the pattern: whoever wished for peace with Quraysh could conclude a pact with them, and whoever wished for peace with Muḥammad ﷺ and his Companions could enter a pact on that side. Ibn ʿAbbās held that this verse was later abrogated by the words "Then when the Sacred Months have passed, kill the idolators wherever you find them" (9:5).

**"or those wholeheartedly opposed to fighting either you or their own people"** covers a second type under the exclusion. These approach the Muslims with hesitation in their breasts, having no heart to fight the Muslims, and no heart to fight their own people on the Muslim side, so that they stand neither with nor against. One reading names them the people of Ḥilāl ibn ʿUwaymir al-Aslamī. The Prophet ﷺ held a covenant with them, a pledge of security covering whoever attached himself to them, and they were annoyed at the great cost the pact exacted and held back from war by the ties of kinship. Among the ten who fled to Makkah, whoever reached the refuge of this covenant was excepted.

**"If Allah had willed, He would have empowered them to fight you"** names the restraint for what it is, a mercy. Had He willed to give them sway, He would have strengthened their hearts, and they would assuredly have fought, but He did not will it, and He cast terror into their hearts instead.

**"So if they refrain from fighting you and offer you peace, then Allah does not permit you to harm them"** states the limit plainly. No way stands open against them, no excuse for killing, no means of taking them captive or slaying them, as long as they hold this position. The schools note that this statement and what follows were abrogated by the verse of the sword. The position itself was lived by Banū Hāshim, the tribe of the Prophet ﷺ, at Badr, where al-ʿAbbās accompanied the idolaters into battle with great hesitation, and the Prophet ﷺ commanded that he not be killed, but only captured.

### The test of the hard demands

The deeper lesson runs beneath the law. After a person accepts the religion of Allah, life keeps presenting situations that test the sincerity of the decision, and migration is one such test. When worldly gains and convenience stand as obstacles in the path of religion, they are to be thrust aside. The movement then goes forward towards Allah, abandoning relatives and home if the situation demands. Whoever moves ahead in the path of truth in the moment of trial, ignoring personal gain and expediency, consolidates the attachment to truth and grows more sensitive to it. Whoever does not, diminishes in receptiveness. The hard demands of religion divide people into simple people, opponents and hypocrites, and Muslims must deal with each kind accordingly. They stay firm in eradicating evil through peaceful means, lenient in the discharge of moral responsibilities, and considerate to the weak. They busy themselves influencing others rather than being swayed, and they never challenge a group that wants to make peace with them.

### In short

- Refuge under a valid treaty shields a person, and covenant status extends to whoever joins the covenant people, as in the pact with Ḥilāl ibn ʿUwaymir al-Aslamī.
- The hesitant, who cannot fight either side, stand protected, for their restraint is a mercy Allah placed in their hearts.
- Withdrawal plus peace closes every avenue of harm, and al-ʿAbbās at Badr, captured rather than killed, is the pattern of the exemption.
- Migration remains the standing test of sincerity, and peace-seekers are never to be challenged.

91.text:
The last group: "You will find others who wish to be safe from you and their own people. Yet they cannot resist the temptation ˹of disbelief or hostility˺" (4:91). On the surface these resemble the hesitant of the previous verse, but the intention of each type differs. These are the hypocrites of both camps.

### Phrase by phrase

**"You will find others who wish to be safe from you and their own people"** describes people who pretend Islam before the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions, so that their blood, property and families stay safe with the Muslims. In secret they support the idolaters and worship what they worship, so as to be at peace with that side too. The tribes of Asad and Ghaṭafān are named in the reports. Ibn ʿAbbās tells that they professed Islam outwardly on coming to Madinah. To their own people they confided that they had really believed in monkeys and scorpions, while before the Muslims they piously declared themselves followers of the faith. Their condition is the one the Qur'ān had already drawn: "But when they are alone with their devils, they say: truly, we are with you" (2:14).

**"Yet they cannot resist the temptation ˹of disbelief or hostility˺"** means that every time they are sent back to fitnah, they yield to it, dwelling in it, and whenever they are summoned to idolatry they are overwhelmed, falling into it in the worst of ways. As-Suddī said the fitnah here is shirk. Ibn Jarīr recorded from Mujāhid that the verse was revealed about a group from Makkah who used to come to the Prophet ﷺ in al-Madinah pretending to be Muslims, then go back to Quraysh and revert to worshipping idols, wanting peace with both sides, so Allah commanded that they be fought unless they withdrew from combat and resorted to peace.

**"If they do not keep away, offer you peace, or refrain from attacking you, then seize them and kill them wherever you find them"** is the command of the last resort. Withdrawal means reverting to peaceful and complacent behaviour, restraining the hands means refraining from fighting, and only failing these does the seizing come, capture and death wherever they are come upon, the word of the verse, Thaqiftumūhum, meaning wherever you find them, in the Sacred Precinct or anywhere else.

**"We have given you full permission over such people"** closes the file. The warrant is unequivocal and plain, a clear and manifest proof to slay them and capture them, on account of their treachery.

### The inner reading

Whoever sets out to combine two opposites finds the effort ruined and the resolve stunted. An individual cannot be at once a hypocrite and one who submits wholeheartedly. Equally, no one can long for the Real while living by the precepts of the people of habit, since spiritual desire and habit stand opposed. Abandon whatever stance contradicts its fellow, and keep apart from what has no relation to you.

### In short

- The last group plays both camps, Muslim by day before the Muslims, idolater at home among idolaters, safe with everyone and true to no one.
- Every recall to fitnah, which is shirk, sweeps them back in, so the verse names them unable to resist.
- Only withdrawal, peace or restraint protects them. Failing all three, the warrant against them is full, plain and earned by treachery.
- Two opposites cannot be combined, in religion or in the life of the spirit, and the double-hearted ruin their own resolve.

92.text:
The law of the unintended death: "It is not lawful for a believer to kill another except by mistake. And whoever kills a believer unintentionally must free a believing slave and pay blood-money to the victim's family" (4:92). The verse opens the section of the surah that deals with killing, and it holds two obligations, an expiation owed to Allah and a compensation owed to people.

### Phrase by phrase

**"It is not lawful for a believer to kill another except by mistake"** states that a believer may not kill his believing brother under any circumstances, the mistake excepted. The Two Ṣaḥīḥs record from Ibn Masʿūd the boundary set by the Messenger of Allah ﷺ:

> The blood of a Muslim who testifies that there is no deity worthy of worship except Allah and that I am the Messenger of Allah is sacred, except in three instances: life for life, the married adulterer, and whoever reverts from the religion and abandons the community of the faithful.

Even for these three, the killing is not the business of ordinary citizens, for it belongs to the Muslim leader or his deputy.

The occasion of the exception is told in several reports. ʿAyyāsh ibn Abī Rabīʿah al-Makhzūmī, the half brother of Abū Jahl through his mother Asmāʾ bint Makhrabah, had embraced Islam and fled to Madinah, taking refuge in one of its fortresses, for he feared coming out in the open about his faith. His mother, greatly distressed, swore by Allah to stay out in the sun, neither eating nor drinking, until her sons brought him back. Abū Jahl and al-Ḥārith ibn Hishām, his half brothers on the mother's side, went looking for him in the company of al-Ḥārith ibn Zayd ibn Abī Anīsah. They found ʿAyyāsh in his fortress and told him that his mother had not entered a house since he left. She had sworn to touch no food until he returned. They gave him their assurance that they would coerce him into nothing and come between him and nothing of his religion. When they spoke of his mother's distress and gave their pledge, he came down. Once outside Madinah they bound him with strings and gave him a hundred lashes apiece, then delivered him to his mother. She refused to untie the fetters until he renounced his faith, and he lay bound in the sun until he yielded them part of what they wanted. Al-Ḥārith ibn Yazīd went to him and said that if what he had followed was guidance, he had now left it, and if it was error, he had been in error already. This is al-Kalbī's account, carried by Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq on the authority of ʿAbd ar-Raḥmān ibn al-Qāsim's father. The wound between the two men stayed open. ʿAyyāsh killed al-Ḥārith, whom other reports call al-Ḥārith ibn Yazīd al-ʿĀmirī or al-Ḥārith ibn Shadīd, out of revenge for the torture he and his brother had suffered for their Islam. The man had later embraced Islam and performed the hijrah, but ʿAyyāsh did not know it. On the day of the Makkan Conquest he saw him, took him for a disbeliever still, attacked him and killed him, and Allah sent down this verse. ʿAbdur-Raḥmān ibn Zayd ibn Aslam told a version in which the verse came down about Abū ad-Dardāʾ, who killed a man just as he embraced the faith, holding the sword above him. Told of it, Abū ad-Dardāʾ said the man had only pronounced the faith to avert death, and the Prophet ﷺ asked him whether he had opened his heart. The basis of that story stands in the Ṣaḥīḥ, though not about Abū ad-Dardāʾ.

**"must free a believing slave"** is the first obligation, the expiation for the great sin committed, even though it was a mistake. The slave freed must be one who believes in the divine Oneness of Allah, not a non-Muslim. Imām Aḥmad recorded the story of a man of the Anṣār who brought a slave-girl. He said that he had to free a believing slave, so if the Prophet ﷺ saw faith in her, he would free her. He asked her whether she testified that there is no deity worthy of worship except Allah, and she said yes. He asked whether she testified that he was the Messenger of Allah, and she said yes. He asked whether she believed in resurrection after death, and she said yes. He said: then free her. The chain is authentic, and the unknown name of the Anṣārī Companion takes nothing from that authenticity.

**"and pay blood-money to the victim's family"** is the second obligation, involving the killer and the family of the deceased, who receive the diyah as compensation for their loss. Imām Aḥmad and the compilers of the Sunan recorded from Ibn Masʿūd that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ determined the diyah for unintentional killing as camels of different year-classes, twenty of each class, and that is the wording of an-Nasāʾī. The jurists then count the kinds. Qatl al-ʿamad, the intentional killing, carries its own rule, while the quasi-intentional killing carries one hundred camels of four kinds, 25 of each, and qatl al-khaṭaʾ, the accidental killing, one hundred camels of five kinds, 20 of each, while payment in cash runs to ten thousand dirhams or one thousand dīnārs for both, as in the Hidāyah. The Two Ṣaḥīḥs record from Abū Hurayrah the case of the two women of Hudhayl who quarreled, whereupon one threw a stone at the other and killed her together with her unborn child. The Prophet ﷺ decided that the diyah of the child was the freeing of a male or female slave, and that the diyah of the woman was owed by the elders of the killer's tribe. The report shows that in what appears intentional, the diyah follows the pattern of the accidental.

**"unless they waive it charitably"** means the diyah must be delivered to the family unless they forfeit their right, remitting it as a charity to the killer. The diyah is distributed as inheritance under the Sharīʿah, an heir who forgives his share forgives that much of it, and if all the heirs forgive, the whole diyah stands forgiven. A victim with no legal heir has his diyah retired to the Bayt al-Māl, the state treasury, for diyah is inheritance and inheritance follows this rule.

**"But if the victim is a believer from a hostile people, then a believing slave must be freed"** narrows the case. If the murdered person was a believer whose family were combatant disbelievers, they receive no diyah, and the killer owes only the freeing of a believing slave as a redemption.

**"And if the victim is from a people bound with you in a treaty, then blood-money must be paid to the family along with freeing a believing slave"** covers the people of covenant status, the ahl adh-dhimmah, or those with whom a peace treaty runs. They deserve the diyah, the full diyah if the deceased was a believer, together with the freeing. The Sunna fixes the shares of this diyah: a third of a believer's diyah where the slain was a Jew or a Christian, and two thirds of a tenth where he was a Magian. The diyah of a Muslim and of a Dhimmi is equal, in the report of the Marāsil of Abū Dāwūd as the Hidāyah quotes it, and the covenant is general, covering the Dhimmi, the permanent protected resident, and the Musta'min, the holder of a temporary guarantee of peace. The diyah of such people is valid only when people of their kind exist to receive it. If they have none, or those people are Muslims, the diyah is deemed non-existent, for a Muslim does not inherit from a disbeliever, and the diyah of an heirless Dhimmi is retired into the Bayt al-Māl, as al-Durr al-Mukhtār rules.

**"Those who are unable, let them fast two consecutive months"** gives the substitute for one who cannot find or afford a slave to free: two months of fasting kept continuous. If the fast is broken without a cause such as illness, the count starts over, though for a woman her menstruation does not break the continuity. The verse names no substitute of feeding the needy for this fasting, as it does in the case of ẓihār, though al-Shāfī, in the more correct of two opinions of his, allows that transition here. For one who lacks the strength to fast even so, the course is to keep repenting until strength returns.

**"as a means of repentance to Allah"** names the purpose of it all, the repentance of the one who killed by mistake, and Allah is Ever All-Knowing of him and All-Wise in what he must do.

### The eight cases and the three kinds

Linked with the earlier verses on fighting and killing, the ruling takes in every case, for the person killed falls under one of four conditions: a Muslim, a Dhimmi, a beneficiary of a peace pact assured of life, property, honour and religion, or a belligerent disbeliever. Killing is of two types, intentional and accidental, so eight forms stand in all. The intentional killing of a Muslim carries the duty of even retaliation, qiṣāṣ, set out in sūrat al-Baqarah, with the ruling of the Hereafter following in verse 93. The accidental killing of a Muslim is the case of verse 92 itself. A Muslim was once subjected to qiṣāṣ for the intentional killing of a Dhimmi, in the report of Dāraquṭnī. The treaty case appears in this verse, and the fifth case appeared earlier at verse 90, where Allah declared no permission against the peace-seeker. The sixth goes with the fourth, since the covenant covers both the Dhimmi and the Musta'min, as al-Durr al-Mukhtār sets out. The seventh and eighth, the killing of belligerent disbelievers, stand justified by the legalisation of jihād itself, as the Bayān al-Qur'ān concludes.

The jurists divide the act itself into three kinds. Intentional killing is done with a weapon of iron or the like of it in cutting power, a sharp-edged bamboo or a sharp rock. Quasi-intentional killing is intended, but done with what does not cut off parts. Accidental killing, qatl al-khaṭaʾ, happens under misapprehension, when someone aims at a man taking him for game or a belligerent, or aims at game and strikes a man down. The second and third kinds both oblige the diyah and both carry sin, differing in weight, for the second is the more sinful through the presence of intention, and the third carries the lesser sin of heedlessness, as in the Hidāyah. The reality of these kinds belongs to the law of this world, while their being sinful turns on the volition of the heart and the intention behind the act, which Allah alone knows, so that by His knowledge the first may count non-intentional and the second intentional. Further rulings follow. The stated diyah applies to a male victim, and a woman's is half of it. The expiation, the freeing or the fasting, must come from the killer himself, while the diyah is the responsibility of his caretakers, named al-ʿāqilah in the terminology of the Sharīʿah. The transfer of the burden to them has its justice. The guardians are not wholly faultless, having failed to stop his gross heedlessness against human life. The fear of paying will make them careful in the future. In the freeing, a bondman and a bondwoman are equal, the Qur'anic word for a slave being general, though the physique freed must be sound, without deformity. And in intentional killing there is no expiation of this kind at all. There the duty is repentance alone.

### The weight the many carry

The inward teaching sees the same mercy at work. Allah mitigated the matter of the one who kills by mistake by giving the burden of restitution to the larger group, the ʿāqila. The elite are responsible for the blood-money of the weak and oppressed in the community, the people of deeper knowledge for the aspirants, and the shaykhs for the poor. Their way is to bear the burdens that afflict the weak.

A leader's mistake runs on the same principle. Al-Bukhārī recorded from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent Khālid ibn al-Walīd to Banū Jaḥshimah, who called them to Islam. Not knowing how to say we have become Muslims, they kept saying the word for Sabians instead, at which Khālid began killing them. The news reached the Prophet ﷺ, and he raised his hands and said:

> O Allah! I declare my innocence before You of what Khālid did.

He sent ʿAlī to pay the diyah of those killed and to compensate the property destroyed, down to replacing the dog's bowl. The report shows that the mistake of the leader or his deputy is paid from the treasury of the Muslims. Killing is a heinous and irreversible crime in every case, and the accidental form is dealt with more leniently. One who kills unintentionally, then fully realises the gravity of it, sincerely seeks forgiveness and pays the due compensation may hope for clemency, and the desire for self-reform that grows from facing the enormity is itself a gain. To that end the directives are given, and the self-punishment of a continuous fast is the starting point.

### In short

- A believer's blood is sacred, and only three causes lift the protection, each judged by the authority, not the crowd.
- The verse came down over ʿAyyāsh's revenge-killing of a man who had secretly entered Islam, a mistake in the eyes of the law and a wound of Makkah underneath it.
- Two obligations follow the accidental killing: the freeing of a believing slave, tested for faith as the Anṣārī's slave-girl was, and the diyah, camels by year-classes or its cash value, borne by the ʿāqila.
- Hostile families receive nothing, treaty people their full due, and inability turns the penance into two continuous months of fasting.
- Eight cases and three kinds of killing cover the field, the leader's error is paid from the treasury, and the strong carry the burdens of the weak.

93.text:
The warning: "And whoever kills a believer intentionally, their reward will be Hell" (4:93). After the ruling on the accidental killing comes the ruling on the deliberate, a sin so grave that the Qur'ān names it alongside shirk.

### Phrase by phrase

**"And whoever kills a believer intentionally"** means killing deliberately, with something lethal, aware that the slain is a believer. The verse came down over a calculated crime. Ibn ʿAbbās, in the report of al-Kalbī from Abū Ṣāliḥ, tells that Miqyās ibn Ṣabābah, a Muslim, found his brother Hishām murdered among Banū an-Najjār. He went to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who sent with him an emissary of Banū Fihr. The emissary was to greet the clan with the greeting of peace. His demand was twofold: hand over the killer for his brother's retaliation, if they knew him, or else pay the blood-money. They answered that they heard and obeyed, that they did not know the killer, and paid one hundred camels. Close to Madinah the devil whispered to Miqyās that accepting his brother's blood-money would be a slur on him. Killing his companion, the whisper ran, would avenge his brother in surplus of it. He fractured the skull of the man of Fihr with a rock, rode off with the camels to Makkah as a disbeliever, and boasted in verse:

> Through him I avenged Fihr and charged his blood-wit to the chiefs of Banū an-Najjār, the lords of Fari castle. By killing him I gave vent to my vengeance and eased my tension, and I was the first to return to the idols.

The verse was revealed, and a sentence of death was fixed for him. At the Conquest of Makkah he was chased down in the marketplace, captured and executed.

**"their reward will be Hell"** is the promise, abiding therein for the one who earns it. The gravity of the sin stands in the company it keeps, for the Qur'ān joins it to shirk in sūrat al-Furqān: "And those who invoke not any other god along with Allah, nor kill such person as Allah has forbidden, except for just cause" (25:68). The command returns in the prohibitions recited to the people: "Say: Come, I will recite what your Lord has prohibited you from: Join not anything in worship with Him" (6:151). Many verses and hadiths forbid murder. The Two Ṣaḥīḥs carry the word of Ibn Masʿūd that blood offences come first on the Day of Resurrection. No dispute between the people is judged before them. A hadith of Abū Dāwūd from ʿUbādah ibn aṣ-Ṣāmit states that the believer carries no burden while he sheds no prohibited blood. The shedding of forbidden blood is what burdens him. Another hadith weighs the world itself in the balance. The ruin of this earthly life matters less before Allah than the killing of one Muslim man or woman. For this life, the ruling stands in sūrat al-Baqarah, printed al-Baqara in one record: even retaliation, the deliberate killer killed in return, or pardoned against the blood-money. The Sunna then marks out a middle kind between the intentional and the unintentional, the quasi-deliberate, struck with what is not usually lethal. It carries no retaliation but the diyah instead. It is described as intentional, yet treated as unintentional in how the payment date is fixed and in how the killer's clan shares the weight. In this case and in the intentional one, redemption is the more urgent.

**"Allah will be displeased with them, condemn them, and will prepare for them a tremendous punishment"** adds the wrath and the curse, which is removal from mercy, to the prepared chastisement. The warning may be read of the person who deems such killing lawful, or as the requital if he were requited. Nor would it be anything new for the threat to be forgone, since He forgives whatever He wills other than the setting of partners with Him.

### Will his repentance be accepted

Ibn ʿAbbās held that the repentance of one who deliberately murders a believer is not accepted. Al-Bukhārī recorded that Ibn Jubayr, finding the people of knowledge of al-Kūfah divided on the question, travelled to Ibn ʿAbbās to ask him. The answer was that this verse was the last to be revealed on the subject, and nothing abrogated it. Muslim and an-Nasāʾī also recorded it. The majority of the scholars of the earlier and later generations, however, said the killer's repentance can be accepted. Should he repent and return to Allah in humility and submission, doing righteous deeds, then his evil deeds are changed into good ones. The deceased is compensated for his loss by reward for his suffering: "Except those who repent and believe, and do righteous deeds" (25:70). That verse is not to be considered abrogated, nor restricted to disbelievers who become Muslims. Such restriction contradicts its general, encompassing indications and would need evidence to support it. And the word goes wider still: "Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves! Despair not of the mercy of Allah" (39:53). This verse is general, and its list of sins runs from kufr and shirk through doubt and hypocrisy to murder. Everyone who turns back sincerely from any of these errors finds forgiveness, for Allah forgives not that partners be set up with Him in worship, but He forgives anything else to whom He wills, a word placed in this surah both before and after this verse to encourage hope. The Two Ṣaḥīḥs carry the story of a man of the Children of Israel who killed one hundred people. He then asked a scholar whether repentance was possible for him. The scholar asked what could prevent his repentance and told him to go to another land where Allah was worshipped. The man set out for that land and died on the road, where the angel of mercy was the one to take him. Though the report concerns an Israeli, it fits the Muslim community even more. Allah relieved the Muslims of the burdens and restrictions placed on the Jews, and He sent the Prophet ﷺ with the easy way of ḥanīfiyyah, the pure monotheism.

Abū Hurayrah and several among the Salaf read the verse as naming his punishment if Allah decides to punish him. Every threat issued for a sin works this way, and good deeds already done may hold the punishment back. Even if the murderer enters the Fire, as Ibn ʿAbbās stated for the one whose repentance was not accepted or who lacked saving good deeds, his stay is not eternal. It lasts a long time. The mutawātir hadiths state it plainly:

> Whoever has the least speck of faith in his heart shall ultimately depart the Fire.

The belief of the Ahl as-Sunnah wa'l-Jamāʿah is settled on this. The killer who is a believing Muslim will not remain in Hell eternally. He is punished in it for a long period, then removed from it through Allah's grace.

### The inner reading

As slaying another is forbidden, so is slaying yourself, since the follower of his own whims is already on the road to shedding his own blood. And whoever offers an aspirant no counsel and no admonition, no help in his resolve, is working to shed that aspirant's blood. Such a person sits captive to his own state. An unpleasant consequence fits him, for the states he barred others from should bring him no enjoyment. The command given of old still runs:

> O David, when you see someone seeking Me, become a servant to him.

### In short

- The verse answered the crime of Miqyās ibn Ṣubābah, who took the blood-money, killed his escort and fled to the idols, and was executed after the Conquest of Makkah.
- Deliberate murder keeps company with shirk in the Book, heads the judgement list of the Day of Resurrection, and outweighs the ruin of the whole world.
- Ibn ʿAbbās held its repentance barred and the majority held it open, while the verses of hope, and the man of the one hundred killings, weigh for mercy.
- The threat is conditional like every threat. The believing killer, punished long, leaves the Fire at last with the least speck of faith, as the Ahl as-Sunnah wa'l-Jamāʿah hold.

94.text:
The caution of the fighter: "O believers! When you struggle in the cause of Allah, be sure of who you fight. And do not say to those who offer you ˹greetings of˺ peace, “You are no believer!”" (4:94). The verse came down over killings that should never have happened, and it fixed a rule of the Sharīʿah that holds wherever Islam is professed.

### The occasions of the verse

Imām Aḥmad recorded, through ʿIkrimah from Ibn ʿAbbās, the case of a man of Banū Sulaym who was tending a flock of sheep and passed by some of the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ. He said the salām to them. They said to each other that he had only said it to protect himself from them, then they attacked him and killed him, and brought his sheep to the Prophet ﷺ, and the verse was revealed to its end. At-Tirmidhī recorded it in his chapter on tafsīr, calling it ḥasan, and noting that it is also reported from Usāmah ibn Zayd. Al-Ḥākim recorded it as well, judging its chain sound though the compilers did not collect it. Al-Bukhārī has the shorter form: a man was tending his sheep, the Muslims caught up with him, he said As-Salāmu ʿAlaykum, and they killed him and took his sheep. Ibn ʿAbbās said that the goods of this world were those sheep, and he recited the word: peace.

Imām Aḥmad also recorded the expedition to Idam, from al-Qaʿqāʿ ibn ʿAbdullāh ibn Abī Ḥadrad, on the authority of his father ʿAbdullāh ibn Abī Ḥadrad. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent them out, and ʿAbdullāh rode in a group that counted Abū Qatādah, al-Ḥārith ibn Rabʿī and Muhallam ibn Juthāmah ibn Qays among its men. At Idam a man passed them on his camel, ʿAmr ibn al-Aḍbaṭ al-Ashjaʿī, and he greeted them with the salām as he went by. The group did not attack him, but Muhallam ibn Juthāmah, because of some previous problem with him, killed him and took his camel. When they returned and told the Messenger of Allah ﷺ what had happened, a part of the Qur'ān came down about them. Only Aḥmad recorded this hadith.

A third report, in one school's record, concerns Usāmah ibn Zayd. His victim was Mirdās ibn Nuhayk al-Farārī, a fellow believer. And al-Bukhārī recorded from Ibn ʿAbbās the word the Prophet ﷺ spoke to al-Miqdād:

> You killed a believing man who hid his faith with disbelieving people, after he had announced his faith to you. Remember that you used to hide your faith in Makkah before.

That is the shorter version, without a complete chain. A longer version with a connected chain stands in the record of al-Bazzār. There, an expedition went out under the authority of al-Miqdād ibn al-Aswad by the Prophet's ﷺ command. At the designated place everyone had dispersed save one man of much wealth, who pronounced his witness that there is no deity worthy of worship except Allah. Al-Miqdād killed him regardless. One of the group rebuked him: the man had just testified that there is no god but Allah, and the rebuker swore to carry the story to the Prophet ﷺ. Back in Madinah, the report was made, and the Prophet ﷺ said:

> Summon al-Miqdād before me. O Miqdād! Did you kill a man who proclaimed: there is no deity worthy of worship except Allah? What would you do when you face: there is no deity worthy of worship except Allah, tomorrow?

The verse was revealed, and he said to al-Miqdād that the man had been a believer who hid his faith among disbelieving people and announced it to them, yet was killed by men who had themselves once hidden their faith in Makkah. Other incidents are reported with reference to this verse, and the respected scholars of tafsīr admit no contradiction among the narrations, since the whole set of events could stand behind the revelation.

### Phrase by phrase

**"O believers! When you struggle in the cause of Allah, be sure of who you fight"** carries a general rule for all Muslims: nothing is to be done summarily on guess alone, for acting on conjecture lands a person in trouble. The restriction to going out in the way of Allah is there because the events occurred in travel, or because doubts crop up in places never visited before, unlike the city of residence where people and things are familiar. Otherwise the rule is general, in travel and at home alike. The word of the verse is read two ways, discriminate and ascertain, and the sense is to tell the believer from the unbeliever before the blow falls. The Prophet ﷺ set the balance in a hadith:

> To act sensibly is from Allah, and to rush through is from Shayṭān.

So al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ cites it.

**"And do not say to those who offer you ˹greetings of˺ peace, “You are no believer!”"** lays down what the greeting establishes. Taken as the technical salām, the Muslim greeting, the words fit the first event most suitably. Taken as submission and surrender in the literal sense, they fit both events equally, and the reading of the word then covers the one who declares the profession of faith, the shahādah, which is an indication of being a Muslim. Either way, the instruction holds. In the case of one who professes Islam, no Muslim may interpret the declaration as hypocrisy without certain knowledge and proof, and no one may dig into his inward state on suspicion, waiting for a definite proof of certitude before the law applies to him. In the battles, some Companions could not hold this fine line. People presented themselves as Muslims, and some Companions took the profession for a lie, killed them and collected their belongings as spoils. Allah condemned the practice, though an admonition was counted sufficient for them, since the Companions did not know the rule clearly until that time.

**"seeking a fleeting worldly gain"** diagnoses the weakness behind the false step, the desire to acquire wealth through spoils. They looked at the man, saw the flock or the camel or the wealth, and read his words as a trick to save his life and property.

**"Instead, Allah has infinite bounties ˹in store˺"** turns the eyes away from the spoil. With Allah are plenteous spoils, which render a person free of any need to kill for property. The pure wealth with Allah is far better than what was acquired, and He has a tremendous reward for whoever stays his hand from a fellow believer.

**"You were initially like them then Allah blessed you ˹with Islam˺"** closes the argument with memory. They used to be in the same situation, hiding the faith from their people, just as the shepherd hid his, as Saʿīd ibn Jubayr commented in the record of ʿAbdur-Razzāq. Their own lives and property had been protected simply upon professing the faith, feeling safe with the believers because of the attestation that there is no god but Allah and that Muḥammad is the Messenger of Allah, before the Emigration. The Qur'ān had already reminded them: "And remember when you were few and were reckoned weak in the land" (8:26).
