They were never asked to prove their Islam, never asked to let their hearts be examined, never ordered to produce evidence before being counted Muslims. The simple recital of the kalimah was enough. The duty that follows from memory is plain: take anyone who recites the kalimah as a Muslim.

**"So be sure!"** returns the command with weight: discriminate, lest a believer be killed, and treat those entering the religion as they were once treated. The word also carries a hint, for the Jews and the Christians all claimed to be believers, so some investigation is meant, not none.

**"Indeed, Allah is All-Aware of what you do"** ends with the threat and the warning, as Saʿīd ibn Jubayr stated, for nothing done is hidden from Him and He requites.

### When a Muslim may not be called a kāfir

The ruling that comes from this verse concerns the one who professes Islam, whether by reciting the kalimah or by joining himself to some marked feature of Islam, the adhan and the ṣalāh among them. Such a person is to be treated as a Muslim. Muslims deal with him as with any other Muslim, and they do not wait and worry over whether the embrace was wholehearted or done out of expediency. Even his doings are not a criterion of expulsion. Someone may skip the ṣalāh, not fast, and be involved in all sorts of sins, and still no one has the right to say he has left the pale of Islam or to treat him as a disbeliever. The great Imām Abū Ḥanīfah said that no sin makes the people of the Qiblah kāfirs by our tongue. A similar statement runs in the narrations: never call the people of the Qiblah kāfirs, however sinful and given to evil they may be.

The boundary nonetheless stands. A person may profess Islam and attest to faith, then disgrace himself by uttering words of disbelief, prostrating before an idol, denying an injunction of Islam that is absolute and obvious, or taking up a religious way or mark of the disbelievers. Such a person is declared a kāfir on the proof of his deeds, and this is the hint carried by the word of caution in the verse. Musaylimah the Liar is the standing case. He professed the creed and practised the adhan and the ṣalāh, and in his adhan his muezzin said the testimony that there is no god but Allah, followed by the testimony that Muḥammad is the Messenger of Allah. Yet he also claimed to be a prophet and a messenger receiving revelations, an open denial of the binding injunctions of the Qur'ān and the Sunnah. On that basis the Companions declared him an apostate by consensus, and a jihād force was sent against him.

The correct course therefore runs: take everyone who recites the kalimah and adheres to Islam, one of the people of the Qiblah who turn to the direction of the Holy Kaʿbah in prayer, as a Muslim. His heart is not ours to inspect. Let Allah be the judge. When you see one professing faith yet doing what contradicts it, take him to have apostatised only on the condition that the deed be absolutely and certainly contrary to the dictates of faith, admitting no other probability or interpretation. The terms Kalimah-reciter and people of the Qiblah are technical terms applied solely to one who, after professing Islam, does nothing by word or deed that can be classed as infidelity.

The passage also casts its law wider over crime. It lays down the premeditated and unpremeditted modes, but it suggests ways of dealing with other serious crimes of the public realm. As it is a duty not to deprive others of life, so it is commanded not to disgrace people, rob them, deprive them of livelihood, or victimise them in any way that seriously disturbs their peace of mind. Harm done by mistake calls for accepting the blame quickly, with repentance before Allah and compensation for the loss of the one affected. Harm intended deliberately ranks as the equivalent of deliberate homicide, differing only in its degree of gravity.

### The inner reading

When you strike forth on the path of Allah, look clearly. Read by allusion, the journey of the wayfarer is a journey toward one of the friends of Allah, that he may be the intimate of his days and the witness of his heart and spirit. However far a traveller goes, he is never at ease from seeking, and never holds back the foot of effort. The friends are the favourites of the Exalted Threshold, accepted in the Presence of Divinity, and not everyone sees them, nor does every eyesight perceive them. When found, give ear, and when seen, hold fast, for hearts grow bright by witnessing them and felicity without end sits in their company. The pīr of the ṭarīqah, Junayd, was once asked to weigh two cycles of voluntary prayer against an hour in the presence of the poor. He took the hour with the poor, for that witnessing is the love of Allah, who has made it incumbent on Himself to love those who love each other in Him and visit each other in Him. Bringing that love to hand is an obligatory act, and leaving an obligatory act aside for a supererogatory one is not the work of the clever, nor the conduct of the chevaliers.

### In short

- The verse answered real killings: the shepherd of Banū Sulaym, the camel rider at Idam, the wealthy man of the Miqdād expedition, and Mirdās ibn Nuhayk al-Farārī killed by Usāmah ibn Zayd.
- No action on guess, in travel or at home, for haste belongs to Shayṭān and discernment to Allah.
- The salām, or the profession of faith, establishes Islam on its face, and no one may dig for hypocrisy without proof.
- With Allah are plenteous spoils, and the memory of one's own hidden faith should close the hand.
- The people of the Qiblah are never called kāfir for sin, apostasy comes only on certainty, and Musaylimah, who prayed and yet claimed revelation, marks the boundary.
- The traveller of the path looks clearly for the friends of Allah, whose witnessing outranks voluntary prayer.

95.text:
The rank of the striver: "are not equal to those who strive in the cause of Allah with their wealth and their lives. Allah has elevated in rank those who strive with their wealth and their lives above those who stay behind" (4:95). The verse sets the mujāhid above the sitter, then guards the sitter who has a reason, and the balance of both duties runs through the whole discussion.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Those who stay at home"** are the believers who sit away from the struggle while suffering no disabling hurt, and the verse says plainly that they are not the equals of those who strive in the way of Allah with their possessions and their lives. The exception came down by revelation itself. Al-Barāʾ said that on the coming down of the verse, a summons went to Zayd from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ with the command to write it. Then Ibn Umm Maktūm arrived and spoke of his blindness, and the exception came down by revelation. Sahl ibn Saʿd as-Saʿʿadī told the fuller form, from Marwān ibn al-Ḥakam, from Zayd ibn Thābit, who dictated the verse for the Prophet ﷺ and was leaning his thigh on his when Ibn Umm Maktūm came, saying that if he had power he would surely take part in jihād, for he was blind. Revelation descended on the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and the weight on Zayd's thigh grew so heavy that he feared it would be crushed, until the exception came down and the weight lifted. Al-Bukhārī recorded both forms, and Muslim carries the second from Bundār and Ghundar, both relating it from Shuʿbah, with az-Zuhrī in the chain of the fuller version. At-Tirmidhī recorded from Ibn ʿAbbās the identification of the two parties as those kept from the battle of Badr and those who went to it. As Badr drew near, the question had come from Abū Aḥmad ibn Jahsh and Ibn Umm Maktūm: blind men both, they asked what excuse could cover them. The school gloss names them ʿAbd Allāh ibn Umm Maktūm and ʿAbdullāh ibn Jahsh al-Asdī, and the answer was the exception. Whoever has a disability, blindness, a limp or an illness preventing him from joining, is not compared with the mujāhidīn as the able sitter is.

**"Allah has elevated in rank those who strive with their wealth and their lives above those who stay behind"** gives the preference its measure: a degree, since both may hold the same intention, and the extra degree goes to the one who carried the struggle through. Allah made those who fight stand above those who sit at home, not hindered by any disability.

**"Allah has promised each a fine reward"** keeps the sitter from despair. Unto each, the fighters and the sitters alike, Allah has promised good, meaning Paradise and tremendous rewards. In his Ṣaḥīḥ, al-Bukhārī records from Anas the word of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ:

> There are people who remained in al-Madinah who were with you in every march you marched and every valley you crossed.

Asked how that could be while they stayed in al-Madinah, he said that only their disability had hindered them. The verse thus indicates that jihād is not a duty on each and every individual, but a duty of sufficiency.

**"those who strive will receive a far better reward"** states the difference in kind: a huge reward above the common promise.

### The duty of sufficiency

According to the leading exegetes, this verse teaches that jihād is fard ʿalā al-kifāyah under normal conditions. As opposed to fard ʿalā al-ʿayn, the obligation of every individual, the duty of sufficiency works this way: should some people fulfil it, the rest of the Muslims stand relieved, subject to the condition that those engaged are sufficient for that jihād. If the situation is otherwise, jihād becomes an absolute obligation on all Muslims living in the neighbouring areas, who must come forward to help.

In the terminology of Islamic law, the duty of sufficiency covers obligations the fulfilment of which is not mandatory on every individual. Most activities of a collective nature fall under the category. The teaching of the religious sciences and their wider dissemination is one such obligation: if enough people devote themselves to it, the rest are absolved, but if nobody discharges it where the need stands, everyone becomes a sinner. The ṣalāh for the deceased, with the washing and the shroud, is likewise a collective obligation and a requirement of Islamic law, the right of a Muslim brother that a brother discharges. The building of mosques and religious schools and the running of public welfare come under the same rule. Injunctions of collective need are classed this way of necessity, so that all duties are discharged under the principle of distribution of work: some engaged in jihād, others in education and daʿwah, and others attending to the remaining Islamic and human needs. The escalation returns when defence is short: if the fighters need support, jihād becomes an absolute obligation first on the neighbouring Muslims, then on those nearby, and in the last resort on every Muslim of the East and the West.

The wider teaching reads the same scale. Muslims fall broadly into two categories by their actions. One adopts the Islamic way of life within the confines of the obligatory injunctions, worshipping Allah and living discreetly, heeding the lawful and the unlawful. The other lives at the level of sacrifice, exerting itself to carry the message to people, willingly enduring the difficulties, placing life and possessions in jeopardy for the cause. Both are sincere, and both receive their shares of grace, but the status of the second differs. Their offerings in the path of Allah were not measurable, so neither will the requital of their efforts be. They joined the mission without consideration of expediency, and accordingly the grace and mercy returned to them will be beyond measure. In the inward reading, the favours of the Real gather all His friends together, yet the degrees keep their distinctions. Rich or servant, anyone finds someone richer. Greatness always meets a greater. The stars glisten, and the moon stands above them, but the sun, once risen, dims every light with its own.

### In short

- The sitter without excuse is not the equal of the striver, and the exception for disability was revealed while Zayd ibn Thābit's thigh bore the weight of it.
- Both parties are promised good, the sitters of al-Madinah counted present at every march through their hindrance alone.
- Jihād is a duty of sufficiency in normal conditions, relieving the community when enough respond, and pressing outward neighbour by neighbour when they do not.
- The two levels of religion, obligation and sacrifice, both receive grace, and the sacrifice that cannot be measured is requited beyond measure.

96.text:
The reward itemised: "far superior ranks, forgiveness, and mercy from Him. And Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful" (4:96). The great reward of the previous verse opens into its parts.

### Phrase by phrase

**"far superior ranks"** are degrees, stations one higher than the other in honour, rooms in Paradise that Allah gives the strivers along with His forgiveness and the descent of mercy and blessing, as a favour and honour from Him. In the Two Ṣaḥīḥs, Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī narrates that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that there are a hundred grades in Paradise prepared for the mujāhidīn in His cause, the distance between each two grades being as the distance between heaven and Earth. Forgiveness covers the sins, and mercy is what saves from torment. One reading of the grammar folds the parts together, the forgiveness and the mercy standing as the object of the preferring, so that the degrees and the pardon come in one gift. **"forgiveness, and mercy from Him"** divide the gift further, forgiveness covering the sins and mercy saving from torment, and the grammar of the passage folds them into one act of preferring.

**"And Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful"** names the Giver: Forgiving toward those who repent of staying back and go out, Merciful toward him who dies in a state of repentance. The ruling stands alongside: no obligation of jihād falls on the lame, the crippled, the blind or the sick, nor on others the Islamic law holds excusable.

### In short

- The huge reward divides into degrees, one station above another, and the highest reach a hundred grades for the mujāhidīn.
- Forgiveness and mercy ride with the ranks, as one gift of the preferring.
- The disabled and the sick stand excused from the obligation entirely.

97.text:
The death of the wronged soul: "When the angels seize the souls of those who have wronged themselves" (4:97). The verse turns from the one who stayed behind with excuse to the one who stayed where staying was sin.

### The occasion of the warning

Al-Bukhārī recorded from Muḥammad ibn ʿAbdur-Raḥmān, Abū al-Aswad, that the people of al-Madinah were forced to prepare an army against the people of ash-Shām during the khilāfah of ʿAbdullāh ibn az-Zubayr at Makkah, and he was enlisted. Meeting ʿIkrimah, the freed slave of Ibn ʿAbbās, he told him of it, and ʿIkrimah forbade him strongly, then related that Ibn ʿAbbās had told him that some Muslims used to go out with the idolaters, increasing the size of their army against the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. An arrow would hit one of them and kill him, or a sword would strike his neck, and Allah sent down this verse. Aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk stated that it came down about the hypocrites who stayed behind from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, kept to Makkah, marched out with the idolaters to Badr, and fell among the fallen there. One report counts them among fifty who had left Islam and were all killed at Badr, and another describes them as people who professed Islam outwardly but were hypocrites inwardly, joined the idolaters against the Muslims, and had their faces and backs struck by the angels as they were taken. The verse thus concerns residence among the idolaters while able to emigrate and unable to practise the faith, an injustice against the self and a prohibition by consensus.

### Phrase by phrase

**"scolding them, 'What do you think you were doing?'"** is the angels' question at the taking. It asks after their condition, why they stayed and never made the hijrah, what their religion stood in at the end.

**"they will reply, 'We were oppressed in the land.'"** is the excuse offered: we were weak and oppressed, unable to leave the land or move about in the earth, unable to establish religion in the land of Makkah.

**"The angels will respond, 'Was Allah's earth not spacious enough for you to emigrate?'"** rejects the excuse, for emigration from the land of unbelief to another land stood open, as others had done. The rule behind the rebuke was stated by the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, in the record of Abū Dāwūd from Samurah ibn Jundub:

> Whoever mingles with the idolater and resides with him, he is just like him.

**"It is they who will have Hell as their home"** gives the end of the matter, an evil destination and an evil journey's end.

The Prophet ﷺ knew the trap and prayed against it. Al-Bukhārī records from Abū Hurayrah that while he was leading the ʿIshāʾ prayer, he said before prostrating:

> O Allah! Save ʿAyyāsh ibn Abī Rabīʿah. O Allah! Save Salamah ibn Hishām. O Allah! Save al-Walīd ibn al-Walīd. O Allah! Save the weak Muslims. O Allah! Be very hard on the Mudar tribe. O Allah! Afflict them with years of famine similar to the famine years of the time of the Prophet Yūsuf.

The lesson beneath the law reaches every soul. A believer naturally wants a free environment where his believing personality finds room to express itself, and if the environment turns unfavourable, he had better change his surroundings, which is the reality of hijrah. Take a person attached to an organisation dominated by certain personalities, where his room shrinks to glorifying the personalities, with no room left for glorifying Allah. If he compromises with that atmosphere for the sake of self-interest, fails to proclaim the truth as he sees it, and breathes his last in that state, then he has perpetrated an injustice against his own soul.

The inward reading sharpens it further. The verse alludes to the person whose hour arrives with him still penned in the lower self and enslaved to its desires, and he has no excuse, for he never sought the shelter of his Lord's nearness, the shelter that would have delivered him from the self's contemptible nature. There is no veil between a person and this talk except his own whims.

### In short

- Muslims who marched with the idolaters against the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and died at Badr are the occasion, and residence among idolaters while able to leave stands prohibited by consensus.
- The angels' question dismantles the excuse of oppression, for Allah's earth was spacious.
- Whoever settles with the idolater becomes as he is, and the Prophet ﷺ prayed by name for those trapped, weak Muslims.
- The trap is inward as much as outward, for the soul that never left its whims died wronged.

98.text:
The exception: "Except helpless men, women, and children who cannot afford a way out" (4:98). After the warning comes the mercy.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Except helpless men, women, and children"** names the weak ones, the elderly and the infirm among men, and the women and the children, in Makkah unable to plan a way out and not shown one.

**"who cannot afford a way out"** explains the inability: they have no strength to emigrate and no substance, and they do not find the way to it, as Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah and as-Suddī stated. Allah gives this excuse because such people are unable to free themselves from the idolaters, and even if they managed it, they would not know which way to go.

Ibn ʿAbbās put himself inside the verse, in the report that came through Ayyūb and Ibn Abī Mulaykah, saying that he and his mother were among those weak ones whom Allah excused.

### In short

- The helpless of men, women and children stand outside the warning.
- Their excuse is real inability, no plan, no way, no strength, no substance.
- Even Ibn ʿAbbās and his mother counted themselves among those Allah excused.

99.text:
The hope: "it is right to hope that Allah will pardon them. For Allah is Ever-Pardoning, All-Forgiving" (4:99). The exception ends not in bare acquittal but in expectation.

The word of likelihood here means certainty: Allah shall pardon them for not migrating, for He is Ever-Pardoning, Oft-Forgiving, clement toward the likes of these and forgiving of those among them who repent.

### Phrase by phrase

**"it is right to hope that Allah will pardon them"** rests the hope on the exemption. Those truly helpless and incapable of support are spared the condition laid on the able. When a call of truth is raised and others refuse to leave their cocoons of self-interest, failing to join and support the caller, dying in that state is the injustice to their own lives, and it is from this that the helpless are exempted.

**"For Allah is Ever-Pardoning, All-Forgiving"** seals the hope with two names of pardon.

The wider lesson of the set runs on. The inward reading of the exception reaches the life of the spirit.

It alludes to those overwhelmed and annihilated by meanings, who then continue on as those who act on His behalf. Of themselves they own neither force nor strength, and what reaches them is only what He lets flow over them of the decrees. Once the self has returned through the reality of the Real, the ḥaqq of the ḥaqq, they are effaced from themselves. No way guides them to anything but Him, and no breath of theirs goes to anything but Him. On the outward aspect of the verse, the reading of the scholars is that the Real's pardon shall surely reach those whose excuses held them back from choosing to emigrate.

### In short

- The likelihood of pardon is a promise in the language of hope.
- The truly helpless receive the exemption, while the able who merely chose comfort stand under the warning.
- In the life of the spirit, the overwhelmed and effaced have their own portion of the exception.

100.text:
The promise to the emigrant: "Whoever emigrates in the cause of Allah will find many safe havens and bountiful resources throughout the earth" (4:100). The verse closes the set with the widest promise of all, held out to whoever leaves home for Allah.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Whoever emigrates in the cause of Allah"** names the act first, and the act has a definition. In the lexicon, hijrah with its sisters ḥijrān and hajr names displeasure with a thing and the leaving of it. Common speech applies it to leaving one's home country. The Sharīʿah gives it the technical sense of quitting Dār al-Kufr, the homeland of disbelief, for Dār al-Islam, in the definition of Rūḥ al-Maʿānī. Mullā ʿAlī al-Qārī notes in Sharḥ al-Mishkah that leaving a home country for religious reasons also comes under it. The verse "Those who have been driven away from their homes" (59:8), revealed about the emigrating Companions, adds a further case: the expulsion of Muslims from a country of disbelievers, on account of their faith, counts as hijrah with them. The Muslims who left the subcontinent for Pakistan out of disgust with the abode of disbelief, or were driven out for their faith, were muhājirs in the legal sense, while those who moved for business or employment are not entitled to the name in that sense. Then there is the hadith of al-Bukhārī and Muslim in which the Prophet ﷺ says that the true muhājir abandons all that Allah and His Messenger have prohibited. Its first sentence sets the frame: a Muslim is the one from whom all Muslims remain safe, from his tongue and from his hands, as at-Tirmidhī records in the Book of Īmān. A true and successful emigrant does not treat migration from his homeland as the ultimate obligation. He leaves everything else the Sharīʿah has declared unlawful, for, as the poets of the path put it, when you change into the iḥrām garment, change your heart too.

### The merits of hijrah

The merits fill the Qur'ān. Sūrat al-Baqarah says: "As for those who believed and those who migrated and carried out jihād in the way of Allah, they do hope for Allah's mercy" (2:218). Sūrat at-Taubah says: "And those who believed and emigrated and took up jihād in the way of Allah with their wealth and lives are greater in rank in the sight of Allah" (9:20). And this very verse promises the many places of refuge and the wide resources. Some narrations tie the verse to Khālid ibn Hizām, who set out from Makkah with the hijrah to Ethiopia in view. A snake bit him on the road and brought on his death. In a hadith, the Prophet ﷺ says that hijrah undoes all the sins committed before it.

### The blessings of hijrah

The blessings have their verse in sūrat an-Naḥl: "And those who migrated for the sake of Allah after they were subjected to injustice, to them We shall give a good place to be in the world" (16:41). The word muragham in the promise is a verbal noun meaning the moving from one land to another, and it also names the place to which one moves and settles. The good place has been read variously, Mujāhid explaining it as lawful sustenance, Ḥasan al-Baṣrī as a good home, and others as superiority in excellence, honour and power over antagonists. The truth is that all these elements are included in the sense of the verse. History bears witness. Ibrāhīm migrated to Syria from his homeland in Iraq, and Allah gave him all those things. Mūsā (Moses) and Banū Isrāʾīl migrated from Egypt for the sake of Allah, and He gave them the land of Syria, a better homeland, and then Egypt too. When the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions left Makkah for Allah and His Messenger, Madinah received the blessed emigrants with the best of shelter, better far than what Makkah had held, and honour and power and peace and prosperity followed, apart from the transitory hardship of the early period.

The events related to the poverty and hunger of the noble Companions belong to that early period, or to a volitional acceptance of poverty, a dignified readiness to live with less. They did not care for worldly wealth, spending what they received in the way of Allah without delay, and the Prophet ﷺ lived in that state, his lack of means and his patience in hunger voluntary, for he simply did not choose to be rich. In the sixth year after Khayber, sufficient means were available to him and his family, and the same held for the righteous caliphs. When Islam needed support, Abū Bakr came forward and donated everything in his house. Zaynab, the Mother of the Faithful, gave her whole stipend to the poor and lived contentedly in want, earning the name Mother of the Needy. On the other side, many rich ones among the Companions left wealth and property behind, and many poor ones, like Abū Hurairah, were made rich after the hijrah. When he was appointed governor of a province, he would address his own past with relish:

> O Abū Hurairah, you are the same man, the servant of a tribe. Your salary was what you could eat, your duty was to walk with those who rode, and to collect their firewood when they broke journey. Today, because of Islam, you are here, so high from so low, and they call you the Commander of the Faithful.

The promise nonetheless carries a condition, that they be true emigrants for the sake of Allah, not migrating for worldly wealth, office, power, recognition, honour or influence. In a hadith of al-Bukhārī, the Prophet ﷺ said that the migration of those who migrate for Allah and His Messenger is precisely for Allah and His Messenger, while those who migrate to make money or to marry a woman receive exactly what they migrated for. The Two Ṣaḥīḥs, with the Musnad and the compilers of the Sunan, record from ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb the foundation of it all, that actions go by intentions, so that each emigrant receives according to what he set out for. Groups of emigrants in distress today are either passing through the transitory hardship that marks early hijrah, or they are not muhājirs in the real sense. Their course is to correct the intention and take charge of their circumstances, and the truth of Allah's promise will then show itself to their own eyes.

### The dying emigrant

The closing words secure the reward even at the roadside: whoever leaves his home as an emigrant to Allah and His Messenger, and death overtakes him, his reward is incumbent upon Allah. The case stands in the records. Jundaʿ, or Jundab, ibn Damura al-Laythī, an old man of Makkah, set out for Madinah and died on the road at aṭ-Ṭanʿīm. His reward matched the reward of those who completed the journey, and he died with his endeavour highly praised. Another report ties the verse to Aktham ibn Sayfī likewise. Whoever starts emigrating and dies on the way acquires the reward of those who emigrate for Allah.

### The three sorts of emigrants

In this verse the Lord of the Worlds sets a mark of His mercy before the servants, the knowing and lovingly kind inviting the faithful to emigrate. Three sorts set out. The first goes for the sake of this world, taking up trade or the hunt for livelihood. The Sharīʿah allows it, yet no one can say where such a journey will finally lay its head. Muṣṭafā said that love for this world is the beginning of every offense, and he also said not to take a landed estate, lest eagerness for this world grow. Such an emigrant stays in suffering and hardship, caught by thieves and on the verge of destruction, hoping to gain something allowed while leaving aside something obligatory, and in the end he loses the basis of both, as the word says: "You desire the chance goods of this world" (8:67).

The second sort are the renunciants, whose emigration serves the afterworld, their travelling a journey through meanings. On the feet of aspiration they cross the way stations of obedient acts and the stages of worship, making the hajj, going out to battle, striving, performing the prayers, remembering the name, meditating on the blessings. Of them the hadith says:

> Concerning them God's Messenger said: Travel! The solitary will be the preceders. They said: O Messenger of God, who are the solitary? He said: The engrossed, those engrossed by the remembrance of God. Remembrance has lifted away their loads, and they come forth unburdened on the Day of Resurrection.

Of them the Exalted Lord says: "Whosoever desires the afterworld and strives after it with due striving" (17:19).

The third sort are the recognizers, and the Patron himself is the object of their emigration. Their journey runs within their own makeup. Curtain by curtain they pass through the soul until the heart, through the heart until the spirit, and through the spirit until union with the Beloved.

### In short

- Hijrah means leaving what displeases, the homeland of disbelief, or every prohibited thing, and the forced expulsion for faith counts within it.
- The verses of merit run from al-Baqarah through at-Taubah to this very passage, and hijrah undoes what came before it.
- The good place of the world and the great reward of the Hereafter are proved by Ibrāhīm, by Mūsā and Banū Isrāʾīl, and by the emigrants of Madinah, with intention the one condition.
- The emigrant who dies on the road, like Jundaʿ ibn Damra al-Laythī at aṭ-Ṭanʿīm, arrives all the same.
- Of the three sorts of emigrants, the worldly traveller risks losing both worlds, the renunciant travels by meanings, and the recognizer emigrates through the soul to union with the Beloved.

101.text:
The concession of the road: "When you travel through the land, it is permissible for you to shorten the prayer" (4:101). Jihād and hijrah both run through travel, and travel in that age ran through danger, so the verse opens the concessions of the ṣalāh.

### Phrase by phrase

**"When you travel through the land"** uses the word for striking through the land, which means to travel in it. The Qur'ān says elsewhere: "He knows that there will be some among you sick, others travelling through the land, seeking of Allah's bounty" (73:20). The Sunna fixes the sense of travel as the long-distance journey, put at roughly 50 miles.

**"it is permissible for you to shorten the prayer"** means reducing the units from four to two. The wording of no sin marks a dispensation and not a requirement, which is the opinion of al-Shāfī.

**"if you fear an attack by the disbelievers"** names the fear that prevailed when the verse came down. In the beginning of Islam and after the hijrah, fear attended most Muslim travel. Their movements ran mostly to large or short military expeditions, for most areas were the ground of combatant enemies of Islam and its people. When the prevalent circumstances cease, a decree of this nature may no longer apply. The word about slave girls and chastity (24:33) answers a condition of its time in the same way. The fear condition itself has passed into leniency. Yaʿlā ibn Umayyah asked ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb about the verse, since Allah had granted the Muslims safety. ʿUmar answered that the same thing had puzzled him, until he asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who said:

> A gift that Allah has bestowed on you, so accept His gift.

Muslim and the collectors of the Sunan recorded this hadith, and at-Tirmidhī called it ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ. ʿAlī ibn al-Madīnī vouched for it: preserved by no route besides this one, every narrator known. From the record of Abū Bakr Ibn Abī Shaybah comes the question of Abū Ḥanzalah al-Ḥaḏāʿ to Ibn ʿUmar about the qaṣr prayer. Two rakʿahs, came the answer. Asked then about the fear mentioned in the verse, with safety now prevailing, he said that this is the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Al-Bukhārī recorded from Anas the journey from al-Madinah to Makkah with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. He prayed two rakʿahs until they returned, ten days spent in Makkah, and the Group recorded it. Imām Aḥmad recorded from Ḥārithah ibn Wahb al-Khuzāʿī the memory of the Ẓuhr and ʿAṣr at Minā behind the Prophet ﷺ. The crowd was huge and the safety complete, and the prayer was two rakʿahs. The Group recorded it with the exception of Ibn Mājah, and al-Bukhārī's narration reads that he led two rakʿahs at Minā during the peace period.

### The remembrance beneath the rules

No sin therefore attaches to the shortening, and no apprehension of sin is warranted, for the qaṣr is itself a rule of the Sharīʿah, following which brings reward. The purpose beneath the rules is the remembrance itself. All acts of religion have the ultimate purpose of remembering Allah, the prayer and the zakāh, the propagation of the word and the struggle for the cause alike. Their aim is a person who lives with the thought of Allah at every moment. He fears Allah in apprehension and longs for Him in hope. His attention turns to Him in gain and loss alike, until the whole inner existence is lost in His majesty and grace. So important is the matter that even in war the prayer is said in some form. Face to face with death, a person is reminded of what is of real value, to be carried along to the Hereafter.

The inward teaching reads the concession as pure kindness. The shortening of prayers is the recommended practice in travel. Though first legislated in a time of fear, it remained in force without the fear, as a kindness to the servants. Travel licensed the shortening of the obligatory prayers, and a further leave covered the supererogatory devotion of the camel mounts. No search for the qibla was required, the mount turning as it pleased, and the same held for one on foot. Thus it became known that permission to engage in talk with Allah is ongoing at any time, to be taken up at will or set aside at will. This is the most extraordinary kindness. It protects the practice of fulfilment and consummates the true meaning of friendship. Even the sujūd, the prostration appointed by the Sharīʿah of Islam as a part of the ṣalāh, stands within this open door.

### In short

- Travel shortens the four-unit prayers to two, with the distance and the fifteen-day stay setting the boundaries of the concession.
- The fear condition described the early era, and the Prophet ﷺ called the continuing concession a gift to be accepted.
- The ʿUmar, Ibn ʿUmar, Anas and Ḥārithah reports all show two rakʿahs prayed in safety.
- The shortening is no sin but reward, an open door of talk with Allah that travel merely widened.

102.text:
The prayer under threat: "When you ˹O Prophet˺ are ˹campaigning˺ with them and you lead them in prayer, let one group of them pray with you" (4:102). The verse teaches the fear prayer, the ṣalāt al-khawf, in which worship and war stand in one line.

### The occasion

Imām Aḥmad recorded from Abū ʿAyyāsh az-Zurraqī the day in the area of ʿUsfān, near Makkah. The idolaters met them under the command of Khālid ibn al-Walīd, positioned between them and the qiblah, with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ among the company. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ led them in the Ẓuhr prayer. The idolaters said among themselves that the Muslims had been busy with something during which a chance to attack had passed. They added that a prayer would come next, dearer to the Muslims than their children and themselves. Then Jibrīl came down with these verses between the Ẓuhr and the ʿAṣr. When the time for prayer came, the command went out to hold the weapons, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ made them stand in two lines behind him. At his bow they all bowed, and at the raising of his head they all raised theirs. Then came the prostration with the first line, while the rest stood on guard. Those finished and rose, the lines exchanged positions, and the others sat and made their prostration under the guard of the first. The second rakʿah ran the same course, and then the Prophet ﷺ performed the taslīm and ended the prayer. He performed this prayer twice, at ʿUsfān and in the land of Banū Sulaym. The two shaykhs, Bukhārī and Muslim, report the like of it from Baṭn Nakhlah. Abu Dāwūd and an-Nasāʾī recorded this narration, which has an authentic chain and many supporting texts. The other records add their colours. In one the coming prayer is more beloved to the Muslims than their own fathers, in another than their wives and wealth, and the plot never changes: raid them while they are performing it. Allah then revealed to His Prophet the verses to their end, informing him of the plot and teaching the prayer of fear within them.

### Phrase by phrase

**"When you ˹O Prophet˺ are ˹campaigning˺ with them and you lead them in prayer"** addresses the Prophet ﷺ in person, and the restriction belongs to the situation of the time. In his presence no uncommanded imam of prayer can stand. After him, whoever is the imam stands deemed in his place and he leads the fear prayer, and all the leading religious authorities agree that the injunction remains operative and was never abrogated. The same permission extends to being gripped with fear of hurt from a beast, a lion or a python, when little time remains for the ṣalāh.

**"let one group of them pray with you"** divides the company, and the verse continues with the rotation. Before the detail stand the boundaries of the shortening shared with all travel prayer. A journey shorter than 48 miles keeps the full prayer. A stay intended for less than fifteen days keeps the journey rules, while fifteen days or more makes the place a residence where the full prayer returns. The shortening applies to the fard of Ẓuhr, ʿAṣr and ʿIshāʾ only, never to Maghrib or Fajr, nor to the sunnah and witr prayers, all as the Sharīʿah fixes it. One party stands with the imam, taking their arms. When they finish their prostrations they take their positions in the rear, and the other party, which has not yet prayed, comes up and prays with him under full precaution, bearing arms. The records differ in the completion. Al-Bukhārī has Ibn ʿAbbās describing the Prophet ﷺ leading the fear prayer, the people bowing in part and prostrating in part. Standing for the second rakʿah, he was joined by the second party, while those who had prayed the first left and guarded their brothers. All the people were in prayer, and all were guarding one another. Imām Aḥmad recorded from Jābir ibn ʿAbdullāh the version in which the Prophet ﷺ led those behind him with one rakʿah and two prostrations. They moved to the position of those who had not prayed, and he performed one rakʿah and two prostrations with the others and said the salām. He had prayed two rakʿahs while they prayed one. An-Nasāʾī recorded the hadith, Muslim has other wordings, and the collectors of the Ṣaḥīḥ, Sunan and Musnad collections carry it. Ibn Abī Ḥātim recorded from Sālim, from his father, the form in which each group received one rakʿah from the Prophet ﷺ, then completed one more on its own while the other stood guard. The Group collected it with Maʿmar in the chain, and it has many other chains from several Companions, gathered by al-Ḥāfiẓ Abū Bakr Ibn Marduwyah, as did Ibn Jarīr. After the salām, the hadith says, the two groups completed their one rakʿah each on their own. The detail is found in the books of Islamic fiqh.

The fear prayer takes more forms than one. The enemy may stand toward the qiblah or away from it. The prayer itself may run to four rakʿahs, to three as with Maghrib, or to two as with Fajr and the travel prayer. It is prayed in congregation when that is possible, but when the battle is raging and congregation fails, each person prays by himself, facing the qiblah or otherwise, riding or on foot, walking and fighting while performing the acts of the prayer. Some scholars held that in that last case only one rakʿah is prayed. Ibn ʿAbbās narrated that by the words of the Prophet ﷺ, Allah ordained the prayer of four rakʿahs while residing, two during travel, and one during fear, recorded by Muslim, Abu Dāwūd, an-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah, and this is the view of Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal. Al-Mundhīrī counted ʿAṭāʾ, Jābir, al-Ḥasan, Mujāhid, al-Ḥakam, Qatādah and Ḥammād of the same view, with Ṭāwūs and aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk preferring it. Muḥammad ibn Naṣr al-Marwazī added that the Fajr prayer also becomes one rakʿah during fear, the opinion also of Ibn Ḥazm, and Isḥāq ibn Rāhawayh said that amid raging battle a single rakʿah with a nod of the head suffices, and failing that, one prostration, the prostration being itself remembrance of Allah.

**"The disbelievers would wish to see you neglect your weapons and belongings, so they could launch a sweeping assault on you"** states the reason for the arms. The enemy longs for the moment of heedlessness, the forgotten weapons and baggage, to descend upon the praying company all at once, and herein lies the reasoning behind keeping weapons on oneself. A group of scholars therefore said that holding the weapons during the fear prayer is obligatory according to the verse, and one of two opinions held by al-Shāfī makes it compulsory whenever no excuse exists, the other counting the precaution a sunna, and this is the more preferable opinion.

**"But there is no blame if you lay aside your weapons when overcome by heavy rain or illness"** gives the dispensation: intense rain impeding, or sickness and wounds, lift the carrying, which implies that without such excuse the carrying stands.

**"but take precaution"** keeps the guard in every case, as best as the company can.

**"Indeed, Allah has prepared a humiliating punishment for the disbelievers"** closes the passage on the enemy whose plot it answered.

The inward reading carries the law to its root: no servant, while a breath of choosing remains in him, is ever released from the obligation of prayer. Not in fear and not in security, not in the state of separation where the precepts of the law predominate, nor when overwhelmed by the authority of reality, at the wellspring of gathering.

### In short

- The fear prayer was taught at ʿUsfān through Jibrīl when Khālid ibn al-Walīd stood between the Muslims and the qibbah of their prayer.
- One group prays behind the imam while the other guards, then they exchange, and the records vary on whether the completion comes before or after the salām.
- The forms multiply with the battle: four, three, two or one rakʿah, each alone when the fighting presses, down to a single prostration, which is remembrance.
- The weapons are the point of the verse, obligatory in one reading, sunna in the more preferable one, laid aside only for rain or sickness.
- Prayer is never lifted from the servant while a breath of choice remains.

103.text:
The remembrance after: "When the prayers are over, remember Allah" (4:103). The verse moves from the form of the prayer under fear to the spirit that outlasts every form.

### Phrase by phrase

**"When the prayers are over, remember Allah"** commands the dhikr after the fear prayer in particular, though such remembrance is encouraged after every prayer in general. In the fear prayer it is urged even more, because the pillars of the prayer are diminished, the praying company moving about within it, unlike other prayers. The Sacred Months run the same logic: "so wrong not yourselves therein" (9:36), though injustice is prohibited all year long, it is particularly outlawed in those months for their sanctity and honour.

**"whether you are standing, sitting, or lying down"** means in all conditions, standing for the healthy, sitting for the sick, reclining for the wounded. The remembrance itself is spelled out: the tahlīl, declaring His Oneness with the words lā ilāha illallāh, the tasbīh, saying subḥān Allāh, and the praise, saying alḥamdulillāh, in whatever posture is possible.

**"But when you are secure, establish regular prayers"** restores the full form. In safety, tranquillity returning and fear subsiding, the prayer is performed as commanded, fulfilling its obligations with humbleness, completing the bowing and the prostration, four units for the resident, who may not postpone the prayer from its appointed time without valid reason, while the traveller joins and shortens.

**"Indeed, performing prayers is a duty on the believers at the appointed times"** fixes the law. The word of the verse means enjoined, as Ibn ʿAbbās stated, and he said that the prayer has a fixed time, just as the ḥajj does. The same report runs from Mujāhid, from Sālim ibn ʿAbdullāh, from ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn and Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī, from al-Ḥasan and Muqātil, and from as-Suddī with ʿAṭiyyah al-ʿAwfī.

### The eminence of the prayer

The prayer is the secret whispering between Allah and the servant, and in the whispering there is both need and joy. Today the need, tomorrow the joy. Today suffering, tomorrow the treasure. Today a heavy burden, tomorrow "repose and ease" (56:89). Today the bowing and the prostration, tomorrow the finding and the seeing. The Exalted Lord mentioned the prayer 102 times in the Qur'ān, and that eminence carries into its names, thirteen in all: prayer and devotion, Qur'ān and glorification, book and remembrance, bowing, prostration and praise, the asking of forgiveness, the declaring of greatness, beautiful deeds, and subsistent things. Muṣṭafā said:

> The prayer is the miʿrāj of the person of faith.

He said also that the prayer is the banquet of Allah in the earth. The ʿulamāʾ of the past called the prayer the throne of the desirers, the delight of the recognizers, the sinners' means of approach, and the scented garden of the renunciants. Seven generous bestowals, they said, come to its performer, running from guidance and sufficiency, through expiation and mercy, on to proximity, degree and lastly forgiveness. The first step in associationism is to leave the prayers, for the Exalted Lord will ask, "What brought you into Saqar?" (74:42-43), and the answer of the guilty runs: we did not pray. He placed the very name of faith on the prayer, where He says, "But Allah would never leave your faith to waste" (2:143), that is, your prayer. He promises daily provision with prayer, where He says, "And command your folk to the prayer" (20:132). Five is the number of the obligatory prayers, in conformity with the roots of the rules, for Muṣṭafā said that the submission is built on five. The servant who performs the five prayers with their stipulations and at their times receives the reward of all the roots. Four are the guises of the prayer: standing, bowing, prostrating and sitting.

The wider teaching of the passage keeps the balance of reliance and means. Though Muslims rely entirely on Allah, they are instructed to be ready with the means of defence against their enemies, for help from Allah reaches the recipient through tangible means, and to refuse preparation is to refuse the receptacle through which the help could arrive. The difficulties faced in this world are part of the scheme of trial, by which it is judged who remains steadfast and who turns reckless, and when defeat and harm come in the struggle of truth and untruth, the pessimism they breed misses the providence hidden in adversity, which comes so that repentance may grow and the turning to Allah may make a person more deserving of His benevolence.

### In short

- The dhikr after the fear prayer repairs the diminished form, as the sacred months concentrate the year-round ban on injustice.
- Tahlīl, tasbīh and praise fill every posture, standing, sitting or lying.
- Security restores the full prayer at its fixed times, a duty as fixed as the ḥajj.
- The prayer is the whispering with Allah, His banquet, the miʿrāj of the believer, and the bearer of the name of faith itself.

104.text:
The pursuit: "Do not falter in pursuit of the enemy" (4:104). The verse was revealed after Uḥud, when the Prophet ﷺ dispatched a group to seek out Abū Sufyān and his companions, and they complained of their wounds.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Do not falter in pursuit of the enemy"** means do not weaken the resolve in the chase. Rather, pursue vigorously, fight and be wary.

**"if you are suffering, they too are suffering"** sets the ledger straight. Just as you suffer injuries and death, the same happens to the enemy, who shrinks from nothing and yet bleeds alike: "If you suffer a harm, be sure a similar harm has struck the others" (3:140).

**"But you can hope to receive from Allah what they can never hope for"** gives the asymmetry. You and they are equal in the injuries and the pain, but you hope for Allah's reward, victory and aid, as He promised in His Book and by the words of His Messenger ﷺ, and His promise is true. Your enemies hope for none of this. It is you, not they, who should be eager to fight, to establish the Word of Allah and raise it high.

**"And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise"** seals it. He is most knowledgeable and wise in all He decides, decrees, wills and acts upon, in the worldly and the religious ordainments alike, and He is worthy of praise in all conditions.

### The lesson of the pursuit

The pursuit itself belongs to a pattern of trial. The difficulties faced by the Muslims in this world are part of the plan by which conditions of trial are created, so that it may be seen who remains steadfast and who turns into a reckless victimiser of his fellow men. In the struggle between truth and untruth the believers are sometimes defeated and harmed, and pessimism spreads among some of them, yet in such adversities the providence of Allah lies hidden. They come so that repentance may be the greater, and so that the turning to Allah in them makes a person more deserving of His benevolence. The wounded of Uḥud, sent out again with this verse ringing in their ears, are the proof that the plan never abandons the believers to their pain.

The inward reading sets the same charge at a steeper angle. Stand up for Allah and let the trust be in Allah in the struggle of jihād. The enemy shares the experience of suffering, but stands apart from you in what the heart witnesses. Yours is the seeing they cannot reach, and yours the inward finding that never enters their hearts. To trail behind such opponents in effort and struggle would be unseemly.

### In short

- The verse answered the wounded after Uḥud who hesitated to pursue Abū Sufyān.
- Pain is common to both sides, but reward, victory and aid are hoped for by one.
- The believer's eager fight establishes the Word of Allah, and the wisdom of the All-Knowing covers both armies.
- What the heart witnesses is the difference no wound can measure, and lagging behind the enemy in effort is unseemly.

105.text:
The judge and the Book: "Indeed, We have sent down the Book to you ˹O Prophet˺ in truth to judge between people by means of what Allah has shown you. So do not be an advocate for the deceitful" (4:105). The verse sets the standard of judgement and then guards the judge against the pull of loyalty. Behind it stands a case of theft that nearly went the wrong way.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Indeed, We have sent down the Book to you ˹O Prophet˺ in truth"** means that the Book truly came from Allah, every narration and every commandment of it. Gabriel, in the idiom of one rendering, brought it down to show the true from the false. The passage revealed over this incident runs all the way to the word "Whoso ascribeth partners unto Allah hath wandered far astray" (4:116).

**"to judge between people by means of what Allah has shown you"** means judging by what Allah taught and showed in the Qur'ān, not according to whims and fancy. The inward reading hears the precision. The command is not to judge between them blindly, but by what He unveiled from the lights of insight, until the matter is understood by His teaching and His directing. The same holds for those of the community who judge with truth.

The office is human, and the Prophet ﷺ said so himself. In the Two Ṣaḥīḥs, Zaynab bint Umm Salamah relates from Umm Salamah the day the noise of disputing people rose close to the door of his room. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ went out to them saying:

> Verily, I am only human and I judge based on what I hear. Some of you might be more eloquent in presenting his case than others, so that I judge in his favour. If I judge in one's favour concerning the right of another Muslim, then it is a piece of the Fire. So let one take it or leave it.

Imām Aḥmad recorded from Umm Salamah the case of two men of the Anṣār who came with a dispute regarding some old inheritance, without evidence. He told them that they brought their disputes to a man who was only human. Some are more persuasive than others, and he judges only by what he hears:

> Whomever I judge in his favour and give him a part of his brother's right, let him not take it, for it is a part of the Fire that I am giving him, and it will be tied around his neck on the Day of Resurrection.

The two men wept, and each forfeited his right to his brother. He then told them to go, divide the inheritance, try to be just in the division, draw lots, and each forgive his brother thereafter.

**"So do not be an advocate for the deceitful"** names the case. Tuʿmah ibn ʿUbayriq, of Banū Ẓafar ibn al-Ḥārith, one of the Helpers, stole a coat of mail from his neighbour Qatādah ibn an-Nuʿmān. The mail lay in a sack of ground wheat, and as he took it, wheat spilled from a hole and left traces in his house. He hid the mail with a Jew named Zayd ibn al-Samin. Searched, his house yielded nothing, and he swore by Allah that he had not taken it and knew nothing of it. The owners followed the trail of ground wheat to the Jew's house. The Jew said that it was Tuʿmah who had left the armour with him, and Jewish witnesses testified to it. The clan then came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and asked him to argue for their man. Otherwise, they said, their man was doomed and exposed, and the Jew would come out innocent. He was on the verge of doing as requested, for his heart was with them, and of punishing the Jew, when Allah revealed the verse.

### The pull of the clan

The warning reaches everyone who judges. The context here is the hypocrites. While the passage dealt with the open disbelievers, the Qur'ān turned to the hypocrites, whose kufr was the common denominator with them, and a particular episode of theirs now begins. Behind the episode lies the standing temptation of communal bias, the mentality that says my community right or wrong. A man of one's own circle is supported even in error, while the outsider receives nothing though right. The command of Allah is the standard instead, and whoever errs is checked without prejudice, and whoever stands for truth is supported whatever his group.

The inward reading turns the warning inward. Do not defend the masters of worldly concerns, but be with the children of Allah's rights. The worshipper of whim betrays the taqwā his soul was given in trust. The one who banks on the pull of the lower desires betrays the shame owed before the eyes of the Protector.

### In short

- The Book came in truth, and judgement runs by what Allah shows, never by eloquence or partiality.
- The Prophet ﷺ judged by what he heard, and a wrongly awarded right is a piece of Fire hung around the neck.
- Tuʿmah ibn ʿUbayriq's theft of the mail, hidden with Zayd ibn al-Samin, nearly took the Jew's hand, until revelation set the case upright.
- Community loyalty is no standard of right, and the master of worldly concerns has no defence.

106.text:
The word to the judge: "And seek Allah's forgiveness" (4:106), "indeed, Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful". The verse stands between the standard and the prohibition, and it holds the story that gives all five verses their setting.

### The episode of Banū ʿUbayriq

The nine verses from 105 to 113 belong to one episode, and in the characteristic style of the Qur'ān the instructions are not peculiar to it. They form a set of basic principles beneficial to Muslims of every time. The episode centres on the clan of Banū ʿUbayriq in Madinah. A man of the clan broke into the house of Rifāʿah, the uncle of Qatādah ibn an-Nuʿmān, and committed a theft. His name prints as Bashīr in the narration of Tirmidhī and Ḥākim, and as Tuʿmah in that of al-Bāghawī and Ibn Jarīr. The Tirmidhī narration adds that the man was in reality a hypocrite. Living in Madinah, he was yet audacious enough to compose poetic satires insulting the noble Companions, publicising them in the names of others with his own identity concealed.

The theft belonged to the early period of the hijrah, when the Muslims lived straitened, facing need, hunger and deprivation. Their common food was barley bread or dates. Wheat flour was scarce, hardly available in Madinah, coming only occasionally from Syria, whereupon some would buy it for guests or a special need. Rifāʿah bought some wheat flour, put it in a bag, laid arms on top and stashed it in a small room of the house. Ibn ʿUbayriq came to know, broke in and made off with the bag. Morning brought the discovery, and Rifāʿah went with his nephew Qatādah to investigate in the locality. The light of a fire had been seen at the Banū ʿUbayriq house in the night, people said, probably for cooking the stolen goods. When Banū ʿUbayriq learned their secret was out, they came charging that the thief was Labīd ibn Sahl, a man well known as a sincere and pious Muslim. Labīd came out of his house with his sword in hand. The blade, he declared, would not return to its sheath until the truth of the theft became clear. The clan quietly assured him that nobody was blaming him and that this was not the sort of thing he would do. The narration of al-Bāghawī and Ibn Jarīr then has the clan charging a Jew with the theft. Their clever work was a trail of seemingly falling flour, trickling from a slit in the bag, from Rifāʿah's house all the way to the Jew's, and the stolen arms and armours were carried to the same man for safe keeping. The goods were recovered from his house in the investigation, and the Jew declared on oath that they had been given to him by Ibn ʿUbayriq. To harmonise the two narrations, the clan likely charged Labīd first, and when the ruse failed, targeted the Jew.

The circumstantial evidence convinced Qatādah and Rifāʿah overwhelmingly that this was the work of Banū ʿUbayriq, and Qatādah carried the theft and his strong suspicion to the Prophet ﷺ. Banū ʿUbayriq came too, complaining that Qatādah and Rifāʿah blamed them without valid legal proof, despite the property found in the Jew's house. Their appeal to the Prophet ﷺ was to restrain the two, failing which the suit should go to the Jew. The outside appearance inclined even the Prophet ﷺ toward the probability that the theft was the Jew's work. So far, according to al-Bāghawī, that he intended to inflict on the Jew the punishment of theft and sever his hand. Matters worsened when Qatādah appeared before him and was admonished for accusing a Muslim family without proof. Qatādah was grieved, wishing he had never spoken even at the loss of his property. Rifāʿah, hearing what had been said, exercised patience with the words that from Allah alone is all help sought.

Not much time passed before a whole section of the Qur'ān came down about the episode. The reality was shown to the Prophet ﷺ, general instructions were given for such cases, the theft of Banū ʿUbayriq stood exposed and the Jew acquitted. They had no choice but to return the stolen property, which the Prophet ﷺ had restored to Rifāʿah, and Rifāʿah finally endowed all those arms for use in jihād. When the exposure came, Bashīr the son of ʿUbayriq ran from Madinah and landed in Makkah among the disbelievers. A hypocrite before, he became an acknowledged disbeliever, and if he had been a Muslim, an apostate now. The curse of his antagonism to Allah and His Messenger gave him no peace even there. The woman at whose house he had taken residence, learning of the episode, threw him out. He came to loitering in the streets until the day he broke into yet another house, where the wall he went in by collapsed and killed him, as al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ records.

### Phrase by phrase

**"And seek Allah's forgiveness"** asks the Prophet ﷺ to seek forgiveness, and the reason lies in the station. The obvious circumstances and evidence were such that a tilt toward the Jew's probable guilt was no sin, yet it stood contrary to the actual fact. The station of prophets is very high, and from them Allah does not favour the issuance of even something so insignificant. One rendering reads it as repentance for being on the verge of striking the Jew, Zayd ibn al-Samin. The gloss adds that Allah is Forgiving of the transgression about to be committed, Merciful toward him.

**"indeed, Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful"** keeps the door open behind the correction. The inward reading widens it: pray for forgiveness for your community, for the word already suffices about the forgiveness of what is past, "that Allah may forgive you what is past of your sin" (48:2).

### In short

- One theft, a bag of Syrian wheat, arms and a forged trail of flour, ran through nine verses of the Book.
- Labīd ibn Sahl was the first false target, then the Jew, and the Prophet ﷺ nearly ruled by appearances before revelation corrected the case.
- The clan's own exposure cost them the property, and Bashīr died under a collapsing wall in Makkah, an apostate among disbelievers.
- Even an inclination short of sin, in a prophet's station, calls for seeking forgiveness, for Allah does not favour the least departure from truth in them.

107.text:
The prohibition repeated: "Do not advocate for those who wrong themselves. Surely Allah does not like those who are deceitful, sinful" (4:107). The emphatic assertion returns so that the lesson of the episode becomes a standing law.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Do not advocate for those who wrong themselves"** forbids pleading for people who have betrayed themselves by disobedience, whose betrayal falls back on their own heads. The rule for every judge follows: do not argue for a person who commits a sin and denies it, until more is known of the matter.

**"Surely Allah does not like those who are deceitful, sinful"** defines the pair. Treacherous through the stealing itself, sinful through the lying oath and the false accusation of an innocent, and the one Allah does not love is the one He will punish.

The teaching beneath runs to the conscience. Abandoning the truth is like abandoning oneself, for a man is dishonest to himself before he is dishonest to anyone else. In every heart Allah has implanted a conscience as His representative, and whoever intends to go against the truth is stopped by this invisible representative, so that the inner voice must first be suppressed before justice is traded for injustice. All too often he supports some erring person because of the importance attached to him, and social relations and expediencies lead him to turn a blind eye. Refusing to keep apart from a follower of the path of untruth costs a person his nearness to Allah, and whoever supports untruth for the esteem of men in this world loses Allah's company in the Hereafter.

The inward reading gives the same verdict in its own terms. Those who prefer their worldly concerns over His rights, and are content in the familiar territories of whim without moving to the waystations of contentment, are not loved by Allah. He will humble them and most assuredly will not honour them.

### In short

- The prohibition stands: no defence for those who wrong themselves, and no argument for a sinner who denies.
- Deceit and sin pair as the theft and the lying oath paired.
- The conscience must first be silenced before injustice is done, and that first silencing is the real betrayal.
- Worldly concerns preferred over rights end in humiliation, not honour.

108.text:
The strange shyness: "They try to hide ˹their deception˺ from people, but they can never hide it from Allah" (4:108). The verse studies the psychology of the deceitful and finds it upside down.

### Phrase by phrase

**"They try to hide ˹their deception˺ from people"** chastises the hypocrites for hiding their evil works from the people so as not to be criticised. They feel shy before other people like themselves and conceal the theft from them.

**"but they can never hide it from Allah"** exposes the inversion. Before Allah the evil lies disclosed, under His perfect watch over their secrets and His knowledge of their hearts, yet before Him they feel no shame at all.

**"in Whose presence they plot by night what is displeasing to Him"** means that His knowledge attends their night plotting and its words, which He does not approve, their resolve being to swear by Allah, deny the theft and accuse the Jew. The shyness is strange: shy before men, and never before Allah, who is with them always and watches everything they do, above all when they conspired together to fix the blame on the Jew, then came to the Prophet ﷺ complaining against Rifāʿah and Qatādah, charging false accusation, and appealing for support against the Jew.

**"And Allah is Fully Aware of what they do"** closes the file. He encompasses what they do, secretly and openly, nothing hidden from Him, and He will repay them for their actions.

The inward reading marks the divide. What created beings can see or not see dominates such hearts, and the ones branded with separation have no awareness that the Real looks down upon their hearts.

### In short

- Shyness before people and none before Allah is the deceitful heart turned inside out.
- The night plotting, the oath, and the framing of the Jew all stood in Allah's presence.
- He is Fully Aware and encompassing, and the repayment is certain.

109.text:
The advocate out of office: "Here you are! You ˹believers˺ are advocating for them in this life, but who will ˹dare to˺ advocate for them before Allah on the Day of Judgment? Or who will come to their defence" (4:109). The verse moves the courtroom to the Hereafter.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Here you are! You ˹believers˺ are advocating for them in this life"** addresses the clan of Tuʿmah, the Banū Ẓufr in one gloss, who contested on behalf of their man in the life of this world. Suppose such people gain the verdict from the rulers in their favour, since rulers judge according to what is apparent to them.

**"but who will ˹dare to˺ advocate for them before Allah on the Day of Judgment?"** asks the question no one can answer. Before Allah, who knows the secret and what is yet more hidden, what will their condition be? Who will stand as their advocate on that Day? None will support them then.

**"Or who will come to their defence"** asks for a guardian to take charge of their affair, and the silence answers: no one.

The verse works twice over, admonishing them and holding the hazards of the Hereafter before their eyes, so as to persuade them to repent and turn to Allah. The inward reading hears the address to the Prophet ﷺ in it: out of respect for you, Muḥammad, they are defended, since you are among them. But how will they stand on the Day of Resurrection, once your blessing, O believers, has been taken from them?

The wider frame is the trial of this world. Everyone may commit mistakes here, toward Allah and toward His servants, and when someone errs, the right course is sincere repentance, seeking Allah's guidance, begging forgiveness, and praying for assistance to do only virtuous deeds. One who seeks Allah's shelter so sincerely will certainly receive it. But the one who does wrong and will not admit it, justifying himself, gathering supporters and fighting those who merely informed him of the mistake, stands with his supporters among the worst criminals in the eyes of Allah, whose eloquence will become meaningless and whose host of supporters will be of no avail in the Hereafter.

### In short

- Verdicts won in this world rest on appearances, and the Day of Judgement rests on the secret and what is more hidden.
- No advocate, no guardian, no defender stands for the deceitful before Allah.
- The verse admonishes and invites repentance, for the advocate of this life is withdrawn in the next.

110.text:
The open door: "Whoever commits evil or wrongs themselves then seeks Allah's forgiveness will certainly find Allah All-Forgiving, Most Merciful" (4:110). The verse keeps the sinner from despair after the passage has finished with the deceitful.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Whoever commits evil or wrongs themselves"** covers both kinds, the sin by which another is harmed, as when Tuʿmah falsely accused the Jew, and the sin whose consequences stay with the doer alone. The wise way of the Qur'ān is at work here, saving sinners from total disappointment by saying that a sin is a sin, big or small, and that both stand at the same open door.

**"then seeks Allah's forgiveness"** means repenting, with regret admitted and the sin left. The persuasion is deliberate: those who have committed sin still have the time and the hope to desist and turn back sincerely, and nothing is lost.

**"will certainly find Allah All-Forgiving, Most Merciful"** is the promise. ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that Allah informs His servants of His forgiveness, His forbearing generosity and His expansive mercy. Whoever commits a sin, minor or major, and then seeks His forgiveness, finds Him ready to pardon, whatever the pile of it, even a heap greater than the heavens, the earth and the mountains.

### The practice of the door

Imām Aḥmad recorded from ʿAlī the practice of that door:

> Abu Bakr told me, and Abu Bakr has said the truth, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: No Muslim commits a sin and then performs ablution, prays two rakʿahs and begs Allah for forgiveness for that sin, but He forgives him.

He then recited this verse together with the word "And those who, when they have committed Fahishah or wronged themselves with evil" (3:135).

The inward reading finds a generosity past all deserving. The word then indicates extended time: lives pass in useless activities and opposition, and at the end comes the prayer for forgiveness. Finding is the ultimate event. The disobedient seek only forgiveness, but Allah brings a person to the utmost by His grace if He wills, for His way is to bring about more than what one hopes for.

### In short

- Evil done to others and wrong done to oneself meet at one door, and repentance opens it.
- The forgiveness outlasts any measure, even sins greater than the heavens, the earth and the mountains.
- Ablution, two rakʿahs and the begging of forgiveness seal the promise, as ʿAlī learned from Abū Bakr.
- The way of Allah is to give beyond what is hoped for.

111.text:
The private ledger: "And whoever commits a sin" (4:111), "it is only to their own loss. Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise". The verse closes the account for those who refuse the open door.

### Phrase by phrase

**"it is only to their own loss"** means the sin is earned against the self alone, like the word of the Book that no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another. No one avails anyone else, and every soul, and none besides it, carries its own burden. The choice not to repent brings no harm to Allah, or to His Messenger, or to the Muslims, for the sad nemesis of a person's evil deed is faced by the person himself. The gloss keeps the case in view: the one who steals and falsely swears by Allah earns only the punishment of that sin, and Allah is Knower of the one who stole the armour, Wise in commanding that his hand be cut.

**"Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise"** adds the governance: this occurs by His knowledge, wisdom, fairness and mercy.

The inward reading frees the whole affair of any need on Allah's side. The Real has no need for the obedience of the obedient or for the avoidance of error by the disobedient. The one who obeys acquires his good fortune, fa-ḥaẓẓuhu, and the one who disobeys has abandoned his own.

### In short

- A sin unrepented harms only the sinner, for no soul carries another's burden.
- The theft and the false oath of the episode stand in the ledger under one name only.
- Allah needs neither obedience nor its absence, and the fortune lost by sin was the sinner's own.

112.text:
The double sin: "And whoever commits an evil or sinful deed then blames it on an innocent person, they will definitely bear the guilt of slander and blatant sin" (4:112). The verse takes the trick of the episode and makes it a standing rule of conduct.

### Phrase by phrase

**"And whoever commits an evil or sinful deed"** covers the mistake and the minor sin, the grave sin, the theft and the false oath sworn afterwards.

**"then blames it on an innocent person"** names the second crime, the casting of the deed upon one innocent of it, as the theft was thrown upon Zayd ibn al-Samin. The pattern repeats wherever people deliberate: a man steals something and, facing discovery, hides it in someone else's house, then raises the cry that another man is the thief. A man intends to outrage the modesty of a woman, and when the pious woman does not relent, defames her with fabricated stories. Two partners run a business, and one, feeling his interests harmed, manages its closure while putting the blame on the other. All such activities are deliberate efforts to implicate others and lay the blame at their door.

**"they will definitely bear the guilt of slander and blatant sin"** totals the account: calumny by the false accusation, and a manifest sin evident on account of what was committed. Whoever commits a sin and then ascribes it to an innocent man has doubled and hardened it. He earns the punishment of his own sin, then adds the punishment of the lie and the false accusation. The misdemeanours only increase the guilt and never absolve the doer, and the wrongdoers are advised, through the immense bounty of Allah, to accept their faults without argument, to shun arrogance built on the strength of supporters, to remain humble out of fear of Allah, and to pray, if retaliation ever comes their way, for deliverance from becoming tyrants.

The inward reading watches the tables turn. Whoever attributes his own disgraceful acts to an innocent person finds that Allah clothes the innocent one with the robe of the accuser's good deeds and pulls the garment of pardon over the innocent one's bad deeds, while the situation of the aggressor is reversed by the exposure of his behaviours to his own peers.

### In short

- Blaming the innocent doubles the sin: the deed plus the calumny.
- The thief, the defamer and the cheating partner all follow the pattern of Banū ʿUbayriq.
- The guilt only grows, never transfers, and the supporters' strength buys nothing.
- The innocent comes out robed in the accuser's good deeds, and the accuser stands exposed before his own.

113.text:
The rescue of the judge: "Had it not been for Allah's grace and mercy, a group of them would have sought to deceive you ˹O Prophet˺" (4:113). The verse closes the episode by telling the Prophet ﷺ what saved him, and then opens outward into the widest statement of what he was given.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Had it not been for Allah's grace and mercy"** reads the rescue. The bounty is the bestowing of prophethood, and the mercy the sending of Gabriel with the Qur'ān. The party concerned is the clan of Tuʿmah, resolved and planning to mislead him in the issuing of the right judgement. It was Allah's grace and mercy that revealed to him the reality behind the event of the theft, otherwise these people would have misled him into error. Since he is not alone, and the grace and mercy are with him, they can never do so.

**"Yet they would deceive none but themselves, nor can they harm you in the least"** turns the plot on its plotters. They themselves fall into the error they dug, and the hurt befalls those who committed the perjury.

**"Allah has revealed to you the Book and wisdom and taught you what you never knew"** moves from the rescue to the endowment. Before this revelation came down, he knew not, as the Book itself says: "And thus We have sent to you a Ruh, a revelation and a mercy, of Our command. You knew not what is the Book" (42:52). And again: "And you were not expecting that the Book would be sent down to you, but it is a mercy from your Lord" (28:86). What he was taught runs from the lawful and the unlawful through judicial decision to the legal rulings and punishments, and matters of the Unseen with them.

**"Great ˹indeed˺ is Allah's favour upon you"** sums the ledger of the gifts, infinite in the receiving.

### The Prophet ﷺ and ijtihād

From verse 105, which opens this passage, five rulings are established. First, situations not covered by any explicit authority of the Qur'ān lay open to his judgement. Many a decision of major importance he took by his own ijtihād. Second, an ijtihād counts as trustworthy in the sight of Allah only when based on and deduced from Qur'ānic principles and the clear authority of the text. Simple opinions and views are not trustworthy, nor can they be termed ijtihād in the sense recognised in the Sharīʿah. Third, his ijtihād was not like that of the mujtahid imams, in whom the probability of error always remains. Any possible error in his judgement stood corrected by Allah Almighty. When he decided by ijtihād and nothing against it came from Allah, the decision was thereby indicated as finding favour and being correct in His sight. Fourth, what he understood from the Qur'ān was nothing but what Allah Himself made him understand, and the possibility of misunderstanding simply did not exist. Other scholars and mujtahids are unlike him here, for their understanding cannot be attributed to Allah in that sense. This is the force of the words about judging by what Allah has shown you. When someone said to ʿUmar, decide as Allah shows you to, he scolded him, saying that this is special to the Prophet of Allah ﷺ. Fifth, pursuing or advocating a false case or a false claim, or seconding and supporting one, is totally ḥarām.

### The reality of repentance

From verse 112 the passage had already shown that a sin ascribed to an innocent man doubles and hardens itself. What remains is the teaching on the way back.
