All sins, whether they violate the rights of human beings or the rights of Allah, can be forgiven by repenting and praying for forgiveness, but the reality of the act must be known. All sins, whether they violate the rights of human beings or the rights of Allah, can be forgiven by repenting and praying for forgiveness, but the reality of the act must be known. Mere verbal declarations of seeking forgiveness and turning back are not repentance as such. The scholars by consensus hold that the person involved in a sin, unashamed of it, not leaving it and not resolving to leave, makes of his declaration an open mockery of the act. For repentance to be genuine, three things are necessary. One is being ashamed of past sins. The second is immediately leaving the sin one is in. The third is resolving to stay away from sin in the future. Forgiveness for sins touching the rights of Allah's servants has, in addition, to be sought from the wronged party. What was due must first be paid, and what was denied fulfilled. These are binding conditions.

### The Book and the Wisdom

By pairing al-Kitāb, the Book, with al-Ḥikmah, the Wisdom, the verse points out that the wisdom, which is the name of the Sunnah and the teachings of the Prophet ﷺ, was also sent down by none but Allah. The difference is that its words are not from Allah, which is why they are not part of the Qur'ān, while its meanings, like the meanings of the Qur'ān, are certainly from Allah, and it is therefore obligatory to act in accordance with both. This is what some jurists mean by revelation being of two kinds. The revelation which is recited, matlūw, is the Qur'ān, its words and meanings both from Allah. The revelation which is not recited, ghayr-matlūw, is the hadith of the Messenger, its words from the Prophet ﷺ and its meanings from Allah. The words that He taught him what he did not know also settle a dispute about his knowledge. His knowledge of the entire universe was never the all-comprehending knowledge equal to Almighty Allah that some ignorant people insist upon. What is true is that his knowledge ran to the measure of what Allah bestowed, and the knowledge bestowed upon him is beyond doubt greater than all the knowledge of created beings combined.

### The inward reading

Bounty is beneficence, iḥsān, beyond what is due, and it alludes to the protection, ʿiṣma, of Muḥammad, singled out for him alone. The Real shielded him from abandoning His right, and shielded him likewise from the deception of His creatures. No one has any way of leading him astray, for the grip of the divine power holds him fast. What is guarded is secure from everything else. Allah conferred distinction upon him with the revelation of the Book and made him a special intimate in the ways He preferred and approved, and there is nothing like the knowledge granted to him alone. It may be the knowledge of Allah and His majesty, or the knowledge of his own servanthood, and of what his state is worth in strength and in beauty. It is said that He taught him the proprieties of service, with a deep knowledge of reality unambiguous to him. It is said that He left him in no need of instruction from any others, so that no one would hold a light except what is borrowed from his. Those who do not walk under his banner will not reach the entirety of the beneficence, nor receive the good fortune of nearness and communion. The bounty is ever great in all eternity without end, and he was recognised in the most exalted degree and honourable rank in all eternity without beginning. It is said that he was taught the sublimity of his rank over all others, and it is said, finally, that one can only value the measure of Allah to the degree one conforms to His command.

### In short

- The grace and mercy revealed the truth of the theft and turned the clan's plot back on their own heads.
- The Book, the wisdom and the unknown knowledge together outweigh every deception.
- Ijtihād belonged to the Prophet ﷺ in a corrected and protected form, false advocacy is ḥarām, and repentance means shame, departure from the sin, and resolve.
- The Sunnah is revelation unrecited, words his and meanings Allah's, and his knowledge, given by measure, exceeds all creation's combined.
- The bounty toward him runs from eternity without beginning to eternity without end.

114.text:
The good whisper: "There is no good in most of their secret talks" (4:114), "except those encouraging charity, kindness, or reconciliation between people". The passage turns from the theft and the conspiracies of cover-up to the uses counsel can be put to.

### Phrase by phrase

**"There is no good in most of their secret talks"** means the talks people hold with each other and the plans they make for transitory worldly gain, unmindful of the concerns of the life-to-come, are devoid of good. One gloss reads the secret conferences as those of the clan of Tuʿmah. A hadith sets the measure: speech harms its speaker somehow, whatever it is, save the remembrance of Allah, the bidding of the Fair and the forbidding of the Unfair. The bidding of the Fair, the command of what is good, covers every action the Sharīʿah counts good and those who know it patently recognize. The forbidding of the Unfair, Nahy ʿan al-Munkar, covers every action the Sharīʿah counts undesirable, squarely unrecognized by those who know. The bidding includes all imperatives and motivations through which people are led to what is good and right, and helping the oppressed, assisting the needy with loans and guiding the lost all fall under the broad category.

**"except those encouraging charity, kindness, or reconciliation between people"** names the talk that carries real good. Charity and reconciliation belong to that wider category, yet receive their own mention, for their benefit travels from person to person and lifts the collective life of the community. These two fields cover what is most essential about public service, bringing benefit to Allah's creation and protecting people against pain and loss, for charity spreads benefits among people and reconciliation stops mutual pain and loss. The scholars of tafsīr agree that sadaqah, charity, carries a general sense here, running from the obligatory zakāh through voluntary giving to anything that brings a person benefit. The glosses keep the case in view: the encouragement of alms to the poor, the kindness that gives a loan, and the reconciliation between Tuʿmah and Zayd ibn al-Samin, the Jew.

The merit of peacemaking stands in the records. Imām Aḥmad recorded that Umm Kulthūm bint ʿUqbah, one of the immigrant women who pledged allegiance to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, heard him say:

> He who brings about reconciliation between people by embellishing good or saying good things, is not a liar.

She said she never heard him allow what people say of lies except in three cases: in war, in bringing peace between people, and in the man's invented compliments to his wife and her speech to her husband. The Group recorded this hadith, with the exception of Ibn Mājah. Imām Aḥmad also recorded from Abū ad-Dardāʾ that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> Should I tell you what is better than the grade of fasting, praying and sadaqah? Bringing reconciliation between people. Spoiling the relationship between people is the destroyer.

Abū Dāwūd and at-Tirmidhī recorded it also, at-Tirmidhī calling it ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ. The parallel reports run the same way: an act far superior in rank to fasting, prayers and charity, namely the removal of discord, the making of peace between two persons and the elimination of bickering, and the warning that mutual discord among people is what really shaves, for it does not shave the head but shaves off the faith.

**"seeking Allah's pleasure"** sets the condition. The deeds of bidding charity and fair action and reconciliation are worthwhile and acceptable only when undertaken sincerely and exclusively for the pleasure of Allah, awaiting the reward with Him, the Exalted and Most Honored, without any trace of personal or material interest.

**"We will grant them a great reward"** answers the sincerity with an immense, enormous and tremendous reward, a vast wage in Paradise.

### The call and its answer

The verse has its setting in the fate of every genuine call to truth. Such a call amounts to the establishment of Allah's balance of justice on the earth, and everyone feels himself being weighed in its scale, which removes the veneer from a person and leaves him as he actually is. Those exposed this way are infuriated to an extreme, and the preacher of Allah's word bears the brunt. Finding themselves valueless in the scales of truth, such people are overcome with haughtiness and pride, and they oppose and obstruct whatever casts doubt on their reputation as lovers of truth. Rumours fly against the call and the caller. Others are dissuaded from extending financial help. Every effort is made to keep Allah's servants from rallying around the bearer of the divine message, by planting doubts about what he carries. To those who have kept their consciences alive, Allah gives the ability to surrender before the preacher of His word, to extend full support and mould their lives by his guidance. Speech, their God-given faculty, goes to the open acknowledgement of truth. They urge the spending of time and wealth on the mission, encourage charity and welfare works, and labour to persuade people to quench old enmities and settle grievances. Truth acknowledged, a positive psychology wakes as a natural result, and its disposition runs to positive deeds.

### The inward reading

Three things in this verse hold the best of the servants' deeds: charity, the honourable, and the making-wholesome of the people. The good of them is not specified for one individual, for its profit reaches others. The wonder is not that a person should open a door for himself. The wonder and the chivalry are that he should open a door to himself for another. Pīr Bū ʿAlī Siyāh put it plainly: to please yourself is a small thing, for the real work lies in pleasing another. Muṣṭafā alluded to it in the word that the worst of men is he who eats alone. Charity itself runs to three sorts. With the possessions, it gives comfort to the poor by spending blessings on them. With the body, it takes up for them the duty of service. With the heart, it stays loyal to the beauty of intention and the consolidation of aspiration. There is also charity toward the rich: acting with munificence toward them, not exposing one's need to them, taking back one's hope from their charitable gifts, and coveting nothing from them. Where charity, the honourable and the making-wholesome gather in one person, veneration itself stands from head to foot, the oyster shell of the mysteries of lordhood, welcomed by the witnesses to the divinity. Men will speak of him as the sincerely truthful, and on the morrow his gathering will be with the sincerely truthful. This is the tremendous wage the Exalted Lord has promised.

### In short

- Most secret talk serves the transitory gain and holds no good, save the word of remembrance and the bidding of the Fair.
- Charity, kindness and reconciliation stand out for reaching beyond the speaker, and charity here includes the zakāh and every benefit given.
- Reconciliation outranks fasting, prayer and charity, embellished words in its service are no lie, and discord shaves off faith.
- Sincerity for Allah's pleasure alone makes the deed acceptable, and its wage is tremendous.
- The best deeds open a door for another, and their doer is gathered with the sincerely truthful.

115.text:
The breach: "And whoever defies the Messenger after guidance has become clear to them and follows a path other than that of the believers" (4:115). The verse names the crime that closes every door of return, and it rests on the authority of the whole community.

### Phrase by phrase

**"And whoever defies the Messenger after guidance has become clear to them"** speaks of the deliberate turn, the choosing of a way other than the Law revealed to the Messenger once the truth stands clear, apparent and plain. The defiance is a breach, and one gloss keeps the episode in view: Tuʿmah opposing regarding Allah's divine Oneness and His judgement, preferring idolatry, the religion of the people of Makkah, to the religion of the believers.

**"and follows a path other than that of the believers"** names a conduct closely related to the contradiction of the Messenger ﷺ. The contradiction could take the form of opposing a text of the Qur'ān or the Sunnah, or of opposing what the Ummah of Muḥammad ﷺ has agreed on. When they all agree on something, that Ummah stands immune from error, a miracle that increases their honour on account of the greatness of their Prophet.

### The authority of consensus

Two crimes are identified in the verse as great and as causes of consignment to Hell. The first is opposing the Messenger of Allah, which is obviously kufr and a terrible curse. The second is the violation of the universal Muslim consensus, the abandoning of something carrying the agreement of all Muslims and the opting for another way against them. This shows that the consensus of the Muslim community is a valid religious authority. Following the injunctions of the Qur'ān and the Sunnah is obligatory, and by the same token, a universal agreement of the Muslim Ummah carries an equally obligatory following, opposition to it being a grave sin. The hadith of the Prophet ﷺ runs that the hand of Allah is on the Muslim community, and the one who splits off from it is himself split off for Hell. Imām al-Shāfī was once asked whether the validity of the authority of the consensus of the Muslim Ummah could be proved from the Holy Qur'ān. He devoted three full days to the recitation of the Qur'ān, completing three recitals during each day and night, and the proof he finally came up with was this verse. When he cited it before the scholars, they all agreed that the proof was sufficient to confirm the authority of ijmāʿ, the consensus of the Muslim community.

**"We will let them pursue what they have chosen, then burn them in Hell"** describes the punishment as a handing over. Going down the wicked path draws its own punishment: the evil way is made to look good in the heart, beautified, so that the temptation deepens. He is turned over to what he turned to, made a leader of the misguidance he followed, left in this world to what he chose and admitted in the Hereafter into the Fire where he burns. The parallels of the Qur'ān run the same course: "Then leave Me Alone with such as belie this Qur'ān. We shall punish them gradually from directions they perceive not" (68:44). "So when they turned away, Allah turned their hearts away" (61:5). "And We shall leave them in their trespass to wander blindly" (6:110). The destination is assembled: "Assemble those who did wrong, together with their companions" (37:22). And the criminals "shall see the Fire and apprehend that they have to fall therein, and they will find no way of escape" (18:53).

**"what an evil end"** seals it: an evil destination, an evil journey's end, an evil return.

The inward reading carries the same law into the life of the heart. Thoughts that come from the Real are His emissaries to the servant, and whoever opposes the subtle directives the inner path demands draws down the punishments of hearts, blinded eyes among them, shut to the perception of what is right. Resisting consensus in the outward religion casts a person out of the fold, and resisting recognized truth, once the path has become clear, works the same falling away.

### In short

- Defying the Messenger after clear guidance, or following a path other than the believers', is the breach that seals the Fire.
- The Ummah's agreement is a miracle and an authority, and al-Shāfī found its proof in this very verse after three days of recitation.
- The punishment is a handing over: the evil path made beautiful in the heart, then the Fire.
- The parallels run from gradual punishment to the assembly of the wrongdoers with their companions.
- In the inward life, resisted directives blind the eyes to the right, as resisted consensus leaves the fold.

116.text:
The unforgiven and the forgiven: "Surely Allah does not forgive associating ˹others˺ with Him ˹in worship˺, but forgives anything else of whoever He wills. Indeed, whoever associates ˹others˺ with Allah has clearly gone far astray" (4:116). The mention of jihād in the preceding verses reached every force hostile to Islam, yet the verses described only the Jews and the hypocrites, leaving the pagans, far greater in number, outside the description. The passage now turns to their beliefs and the punishment they will face, a coherence of its own in this place, for the thief of the earlier episode became an apostate, and the lasting punishment he earned now becomes evident.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Surely Allah does not forgive associating ˹others˺ with Him ˹in worship˺"** states the one sin that stands outside pardon. The verse has appeared before in this sūrah, at verse 48, in the same words save for the ending. There the ending read that whoever ascribes a partner to Allah has designed a great sin, and here it reads that he has gone far astray. The reason for the difference lies in the addressees. The earlier verse spoke to the Jewish people of the Book. Through the Torah they knew the truth of Allah's Oneness, the falsity of shirk and the veracity of the Prophet's ﷺ mission, and yet they entered shirk regardless, acting as though this were the Torah's own teaching, a total forgery and a false accusation. That earned the word of the great sin. The present verse speaks to the pagans of Makkah, who had no background of Book or Prophet, though the rational arguments for the Oneness of Allah were all too clear, and taking stones crafted by their own hands as objects of worship was ineffectual and false even to ordinary common sense. That earned the word of going far astray.

**"but forgives anything else of whoever He wills"** keeps every other sin at the door of His mercy, forgiven to whoever is fit for it, out of His mercy and grace, even where the sinner dies without repentance.

**"Indeed, whoever associates ˹others˺ with Allah has clearly gone far astray"** totals the loss: other than the true path, away from guidance and righteousness, the self destroyed in this life and the Hereafter, and contentment lost in both.

### The permanence of the punishment

Some people doubt the proportion here. The crime of kufr and shirk is committed within the limited time of one life, so why should its punishment be limitless and permanent? The answer lies in the doer's stance. The kāfir and the mushrik simply does not regard what he does as a crime. He takes it as good and proper, worth his while, accompanied by the firm intention to remain so always. Holding that position to the last breath, he has committed a permanent crime to the full extent of his choice and volition, and the punishment for it must be permanent. The scholars count three kinds of injustice. The first Allah will never forgive, and it is shirk. The second could be forgiven, and it is falling short in the rights of Allah. The third meets retribution, and it is the violation of the rights that Allah's creatures hold over one another.

The reality of shirk is equality. Shirk in its reality is the placing of any created being beside Allah in worship, or in love, or in reverence. The words of the disbelievers on arrival into Jahannam are recorded in the Book: "By Allah, we were in obvious error when we had equated you with Allah, the Lord of all the worlds" (26:97). Even the polytheists did not believe their idols were the Creator and Master of the universe. It was under other erroneous assumptions that they regarded them as equal in worship, love and reverence, and this was the shirk that caused their entry into the Fire, as Fatḥ al-Mulhim notes. In short, whoever sets any created being level with Allah in His particular attributes, Creator, Provider, Absolute Master, Knower of the Seen and the Unseen, has committed shirk.

The wider teaching sharpens the edge. Opposition to the call of truth and victimisation of its followers are unforgivable, for while other sins flow from human weakness, opposing the call flows from insolence and haughtiness, and such rebellion is not forgiven unless a person confesses his mistakes and abandons the stance. The call brought in its pure and original form is a divine mission under the special succour of Allah, and to oppose it is to stand against Allah Himself. The believer has his roots in Allah and rejoins them whenever he turns back, while whoever attaches himself to anyone besides Allah is deprived of the true base in the universe. Good actions rooted in polytheism have only surface value, nullified by the slightest jolt and swept away in this world, whereas the good action based in monotheism unfolds its results in the Hereafter.

The inward reading strips the matter to the atom. To acknowledge anything other than Him, imagining even an atom as a cause of origination, is the very essence of shirk. No pardon is possible for it, while pardon remains possible for other things. Whoever seeks access to Allah through what he imagines is joining partners to Him without realizing it. No, He is Allah, the One.

### In short

- Shirk alone lies outside forgiveness, and the earlier verse 48 named it the great sin for the People of the Book who knew better, while this verse names straying for the pagans who crafted their own gods.
- The punishment is permanent because the crime is permanent, held by firm intention to the last breath.
- Three kinds of injustice divide all sin, never forgiven, forgivable, and retributed.
- Shirk is equality given to a created being, in worship, in love, in reverence, or in the attributes of Lordship.
- Even an atom imagined as a cause beside Him is the essence of the unforgiven.

117.text:
The idols and their instructor: "Instead of Allah, they only invoke female gods and they ˹actually˺ invoke none but a rebellious Satan" (4:117). The verse looks at what the pagans worship and finds the worshipper of stones to be, in reality, the worshipper of the devil.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Instead of Allah, they only invoke female gods"** describes the idols with feminine names, al-Lāt and al-ʿUzzā, and Manāt with them, which can neither benefit nor harm anyone. Juwaybir reported from aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk the claim behind them: the idolators said that the angels are Allah's daughters and that they worshipped them only so that they would bring them closer to Allah. Thus the angels became gods to them, the shapes were carved as girls, and the verdict followed that these idols resembled the daughters of Allah being worshipped. The Qur'ān answers them: "Have you then considered al-Lāt and al-ʿUzzā" (53:19), The angels are called females in their reckoning, though angels are but servants of the Most Gracious, and a kinship has been invented between Him and the Jinn (37:158). The gloss names the worshippers as the people of Makkah, who took lifeless idols in place of Allah.

**"and they ˹actually˺ invoke none but a rebellious Satan"** names the true object of the worship. This worship was Shayṭān's command to them, made to look fair and beautiful in their eyes, so that the worship paid him in reality. Allah said: "Did I not command you, O Children of Adam, that you should not worship Shaytan" (36:60), and the angels shall proclaim on the Day of Resurrection about the idolators who worshipped them: "Nay, but they used to worship the Jinn, most of them were believers in them" (34:41). By obeying him in this worship of female idols, they pray to a rebel intense in his rebellion.

### The enemy of every soul

The teaching beneath names that enemy. Man's real challenge in this world is from Satan, who has no real power, yet lures human beings with fanciful promises to fulfil wishful, imaginary desires, making them deviate from the straight path. His way of misguiding runs by two main types, superstition and interference in creation. Faith in superstition means expecting from something results that have no relation to it, as when a person believes, on self-styled suppositions, that someone other than Allah controls the affairs of the world, or immerses himself in worldly pursuits and hopes by wishful thinking to achieve the Hereafter without having worked for it.

The inward reading sees the mechanism. Lifeless things were set up and given names, and the delusion plunged ahead. The errors of conjecture were made the support, and so the truth was left far behind.

### In short

- The female idols, al-Lāt, al-ʿUzzā and Manāt, were daughters pretended for Allah, and the angels made into girls of stone.
- Behind the stones stands the rebel who made the worship seem fair, so the worshipper of idols is the worshipper of Shayṭān.
- Satan's lure runs by superstition and interference, promise without power, hope without work.

118.text:
The claim of the cursed one: "I will surely take hold of a certain number of Your servants" (4:118). The verse lets the outcast speak, and his boast sets the proportions of the peril.

### Phrase by phrase

**"cursed by Allah"** means expelled and banished from His mercy and His grace, removed from all good, distanced by the Real and sent away by His distancing.

**"I will surely take hold of a certain number of Your servants"** is his oath before his Lord, the taking of an appointed portion, a fixed and known share. Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān counted the share: of every one thousand, a single one for Paradise, the remaining nine hundred and ninety-nine for the Fire. One rendering prints it in figures, 999 of every thousand destined for the Fire, and adds that what Iblīs imprints in a person becomes that person's obligation and command.

The inward reading keeps the boast in proportion. None other than Iblīs is what they pray to, Iblīs whom the Real has distanced from His mercy. Yet the grip of God turns even Iblīs about, according to what the Creator desires. Did even an atom of self-sufficiency in him admit affirming, divinity would have an associate in him. It does not. Only the Real brings about in created beings their states and circumstances, and only He creates what follows the whisperings in the being led astray, the Ḍalālan. He is the Guide and the One who leads astray, the One of free disposal over all. He creates the power of expectations, the āmālan, in human hearts after the whisperings, and He makes their ugly actions, the aʿmālan, seem beautiful in their eyes.

### In short

- The curse is banishment from mercy, and the boast is a fixed share of servants.
- The share is fearsome in the arithmetic given, one of a thousand escaping.
- Even the outcast is turned in the grip of God, for guidance, misguidance and the heart's expectations are created by the Real alone.

119.text:
The programme of corruption: "I will certainly mislead them and delude them with empty hopes. Also, I will order them and they will slit the ears of cattle and alter Allah's creation" (4:119). The verse lists the rebel's four projects, and each one found takers.

### Phrase by phrase

**"I will certainly mislead them and delude them with empty hopes"** covers the inner work: leading them from the true path, tempting them to feign repentance, arousing false hopes, encouraging delay and procrastination with righteous deeds, and casting into hearts the thought of life enduring, of no rising and no reckoning to come, so that the misguidance itself turns attractive.

**"I will order them and they will slit the ears of cattle"** names the first outward corruption, the slitting that designated the animals as Bahīrah, Sāʾibah and Waṣīlah, as Qatādah and as-Suddī stated, the she-camels called bahāʾir among them.

**"and alter Allah's creation"** names the second. Al-Ḥasan ibn Abī al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī read it as tattooing. In his Ṣaḥīḥ, Muslim recorded the prohibition of tattooing the face, one wording of which runs the curse of Allah on whoever does it. The Ṣaḥīḥ also records from Ibn Masʿūd the word:

> May Allah curse those who have tattoos and those who do it, who pluck their facial hairs and the one who does it for them, and those who make spaces between their teeth for the purpose of beauty, changing what Allah has created.

And why, he asked, should he withhold his curse from those the Prophet ﷺ had already cursed, the Book of Allah itself commanding it, citing the word "And whatsoever the Messenger gives you, take it, and whatsoever he forbids you, abstain from it" (59:7). Another reading takes the alteration further still, the changing of Allah's religion, the substituting of His religion with unbelief, making lawful what Allah has made unlawful and unlawful what He has made lawful.

**"And whoever takes Satan as a guardian instead of Allah, has certainly suffered a tremendous loss"** totals the account. The word walī, guardian, marks the following and the obeying, and the loss is manifest: this life and the Hereafter both gone, a loss that cannot be compensated or restored, ending in the Fire made perpetual.

### The division of the work

The inward reading assigns the work exactly. Misguidance is consigned to Iblīs only as a secondary cause. Otherwise, who is Iblīs? His job is the instilling of disquiet, no more. In the tracks of that disquieting, the Exalted Lord creates the misguidance, for guidance and misguidance, felicity and wretchedness, come from God: "Whomsoever God guides, he is guided, and whomsoever He misguides, you will not find for him a guiding friend" (18:17).

### In short

- The empty hope, the deferred repentance, the slit ears and the altered creation are his four projects, and all found takers.
- Tattooing, plucking and teeth-spacing drew the curse of Ibn Masʿūd, on the authority of the Messenger ﷺ and the command of the Book.
- Reading the alteration as the corruption of religion extends it to every lawful turned unlawful.
- The guardian taken instead of Allah costs both worlds, a loss nothing restores.
- Even here the disquiet is his, but the misguidance created after it belongs to the Real.

120.text:
The promiser unmasked: "Satan only makes them ˹false˺ promises and deludes them with ˹empty˺ hopes. Truly Satan promises them nothing but delusion" (4:120). The verse reads the fine print of every promise the rebel ever made.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Satan only makes them ˹false˺ promises"** lists the goods promised: long life, the attainment of worldly hopes, the assurance that there is no resurrection and no reckoning, even the whisper that there is no Paradise and no Hell. Deceit is the manner of his promising, and his supporters are tempted into believing themselves winners in this life and the Hereafter.

**"and deludes them with ˹empty˺ hopes"** exposes the goods as hopes with no reality, mere wishes inspired and held.

**"Truly Satan promises them nothing but delusion"** is the verdict: falsehood and lies, nothing else in the package. The end of the transaction is written in the Book: "And Shaytan will say when the matter has been decided: Verily, Allah promised you a promise of truth. And I too promised you, but I betrayed you. I had no authority over you" (14:22), and the passage runs on to the painful torment of the wrongdoers.

The inward reading sees the decree beneath. For those whose allotment is being led astray in the present state, punishment has been decreed in the end. What appears, appears by His deliberative power, and no sliver of being astray or being guided belongs to any other. To fully grasp the truth of Allah's Oneness is a rare and precious thing, and those who have mastered it are few.

### In short

- The promises run from long life to the denial of the Rising, and the deliverer of them owns nothing he promises.
- On the decided Day he confesses the betrayal and admits he had no authority.
- Delusion is the whole of the package, and the mastery of Oneness remains the rare escape from it.

121.text:
The address at the end of the road: "It is they who will have Hell as their home, and they will find no escape from it" (4:121). The verse hands the story to its setting.

### Phrase by phrase

**"It is they who will have Hell as their home"** names the people, those who liked and preferred what Shayṭān was promising and assuring them of, and names the home, the destination and abode on the Day of Resurrection.

**"and they will find no escape from it"** closes every exit: not able to avoid, avert, evade or elude the Fire, no escape and no sanctuary, no alternative to it.

### In short

- Hell is home to those who preferred the promises of the deluder.
- No exit, no refuge and no alternative awaits them there.

122.text:
The other address: "And those who believe and do good, We will soon admit them into Gardens under which rivers flow, to stay there for ever and ever. Allah's promise is ˹always˺ true. And whose word is more truthful than Allah's" (4:122). After the home of the misled, the verse opens the home of the guided.

### Phrase by phrase

**"And those who believe and do good"** describes the people. Truthful in heart and obedient in limb, they performed the righteous acts commanded and left off the evil they were prohibited from doing.

**"We will soon admit them into Gardens under which rivers flow"** describes the welcome. The rivers of Paradise, of wine, water, milk and honey, flow beneath its rooms and habitations, and its palaces overlook the streams. The plenty obeys its people, for the rivers are made to flow wherever their people think of them flowing.

**"to stay there for ever and ever"** fixes the term: without end or removal, never to die, never to be moved out.

**"Allah's promise is ˹always˺ true"** vouches for the whole: a true promise from Allah, which shall come to pass, promised and fulfilled in truth.

**"And whose word is more truthful than Allah's"** asks the closing question, and the answer is none, for no one is more truthful in statement and narration than Allah, and there is no deity worthy of worship nor Lord except Him. The proclamation of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ ran in his speech:

> The most truthful speech is Allah's Speech, and the best guidance is the guidance of Muhammad. The worst matters are the newly invented in religion, every newly invented matter is an innovation, and every innovation is a heresy, and every heresy is in the Fire.

### The second way of Satan

The teaching of the passage names that second way, the interference in the divine scheme. Allah has created man with an innate desire to turn all his attention to Him. To interfere is to divert the attention toward things other than Allah, or to push acquisition through self-devised ways instead of the natural course He set. In this manner Satan interferes with man's observance of Allah's divine plan for the entire universe.

The inward reading reads the promise from the divine side. Those made fortunate by decree and speech were helped at the time they were brought into existence by generosity and power, and then surely what had been promised in reward was brought about through what they were given in a place of good return.

### In short

- Truthful hearts and obedient limbs receive the Gardens, where the rivers run wherever their people think.
- The stay is for ever and ever, and the promise binding it is true and fulfilled.
- No word is more truthful than Allah's, and the Prophet's ﷺ proclamation stands on that word.
- The second way of Satan is interference with the innate attention to Allah, and the fortunate were helped from their coming into existence.

123.text:
The end of boasting: "˹Divine grace is˺ neither by your wishes nor those of the People of the Book! Whoever commits evil will be rewarded accordingly, and they will find no protector or helper besides Allah" (4:123). The verse arose from a contest of boasting and cut it short with a scale.

### The dispute of the communities

Qatādah said the Muslims and the People of the Scriptures once traded virtues. The People of the Scriptures claimed the earlier Prophet and the earlier Book, and with them the greater right to Allah. The Muslims answered that the greater right was theirs, their Prophet being the Final Prophet and their Book superseding all before it. Then Allah sent down the verse, and His later words backed the Muslims' side of the argument against the opponents of other religions. Similar statements are attributed to as-Suddī, Masrūq, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk and Abū Ṣāliḥ. Al-ʿAwfī reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that the followers of the various religions disputed, each naming its best, the Christians their man, the Jews Mūsā, the Muslims the Last of them. One report has the adherents of the Tawrah, the Torah, and of the Injīl, together with the adherents of other religions, sitting in one place, each claiming to be better than the rest, when the verse came down. The ruling inside it is general: no religion is accepted on the strength of wishful thinking or mere hopes. The accepted religion relies on what resides in the heart and is made truthful through actions. A claim does not attain its object merely by being uttered. Nor is every claimant to the truth counted such, until the claim gains merit with proof from Allah. Safety is not acquired by wishing, for either side. The key is obeying Allah and following what He legislated through the words of His honourable Messengers.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Whoever commits evil will be rewarded accordingly"** sets the scale, and the Qur'ān repeats it: "So whosoever does good equal to the weight of an atom, shall see it. And whosoever does evil equal to the weight of an atom, shall see it" (99:7-8). When these verses were revealed they became hard on many of the Companions. Ibn Abī Ḥātim recorded that ʿĀʾishah said she told the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that she knew the hardest āyah in the Qur'ān, and when he asked which, she named this one, and he answered:

> That is what strikes the believing servant, even the problems that bother him.

This hadith stands recorded also with Ibn Jarīr and with Abū Dāwūd. Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr recorded from Abū Hurayrah that the verse was hard on the Muslims, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ told them:

> Be steadfast and seek closeness. Everything that afflicts the Muslim, even the thorn that pierces his skin and the hardship he suffers, will be an expiation for him.

Imām Aḥmad collected this wording through Sufyān ibn ʿUyaynah, and Muslim, an-Nasāʾī and at-Tirmidhī also recorded it. The reports multiply the comfort. Abū Hurairah's version has the Companions grieved that the minutest evil in their deeds would be requited. The answer came back: do not worry, keep doing what you can, for whatever hardship or pain afflicts you makes amends, down to the thorn that pinches a foot. Another narration says that any sorrow, pain, sickness or anxiety afflicting a Muslim becomes an expiation of sins. Abū Bakr's case stands in the Jāmiʿ of at-Tirmidhī and in the record of Ibn Jarīr. When the Prophet ﷺ recited the verse to him, he felt as if his back was broken. Asked what was the matter, he submitted that hardly anyone among them could claim to have done nothing bad, so who could hope to go unscathed if every evil deed was to be requited. He was told that he and his believing brothers need not worry, for the worldly hardships they face make amends for their sins. Another narration puts it as a question about sickness, about the tests of distress and sorrow. All this does happen, came his answer. That, he was told, is the requital of whatever evil may have been done. In a hadith of Abū Dāwūd, ʿĀʾishah reports that a discomfort faced in fever, a pain however it comes, even the pinch of a thorn, all become expiation, down to the small effort of someone looking for a thing in one pocket and finding it in another. The division of the requital runs between the two abodes. Believers are recompensed in this world or after death, before entering Paradise, and unbelievers in the Hereafter, before entering the Fire. The People of the Scripture, for their part, wished their day's sins forgiven by night and their night's sins by day.

**"and they will find no protector or helper besides Allah"** closes the escape, for no relative will benefit and no defender save from the torment. ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah reported from Ibn ʿAbbās the one exception: unless he repents and Allah forgives him.

The wider teaching reads the verse against the hopes of every community. When the People of the Book become engrossed in the world, they do not deny Allah or the Hereafter outright. They believe in these realities formally, while devoting all effort to worldly acquisition, very serious about honour and glory here. For Paradise, wishful thinking alone is believed to suffice, whether the blessing of some saint, the membership of a certain group, or the reciting of words and phrases, cheap formulae and superficial acts hoped to save from the Fire and usher into Heaven. Such wishful thinking, in whatever beautiful words couched, will not come to the rescue. The system of Allah is established on realities, not wishes, and in His court everyone will be judged exactly in accordance with his actions, with nothing but the law of justice He Himself promulgated to influence His decisions.

The inward reading gives the same law in images. Whoever plants colocynth will not harvest roses and jasmine, and whoever drinks deadly poison will not find the taste of honey. The duty of service, once squandered, leaves no firm standing on the carpet of nearness. Whoever is branded with misfortune will not be provided with the best of the best, and whomever the divine decree rejects has no helper in creation. Yet whoever labours in Allah's service will not be kept from attaining His blessing. Whomever He has made rich in seeking Him, He honours in finding Him, and whomever He has made to drink from the cup of longing for Him, He brings to the intimacy of meeting Him.

### In short

- The boasting of Muslims and People of the Book over Prophets and Books was answered with one scale, the deed.
- The āyah weighed heavy on the Companions until the Prophet ﷺ taught that every affliction, down to a thorn, is an expiation.
- Abū Bakr's breaking back was steadied by sickness and sorrow as requital, and ʿĀʾishah counted even the search through pockets.
- Repentance remains the one exception to the friendless requital.
- Neither saint nor formula purchases Paradise, and the colocynth yields no roses.

124.text:
The other scale-pan: "and have faith will enter Paradise and will never be wronged ˹even as much as˺ the speck on a date stone" (4:124). The verse answers the previous severity with a mercy as exact.

### Phrase by phrase

**"But those who do good—whether male or female—and have faith"** sets the one condition under all the good: deeds that issue forth from true faith. The doing is of acts of obedience, that which lies between the servant and his Lord, and the faith is genuine in the one who holds it, male or female alike. Allah mentions His kindness, generosity and mercy in accepting the good deeds of His servants on condition that they embrace the faith, and the reading of the verb runs both ways, they shall be admitted and they shall enter, the receiving and the coming meeting in one word.

**"will enter Paradise and will never be wronged ˹even as much as˺ the speck on a date stone"** measures the justice. Nothing of their righteous deeds will be withheld, not the weight of a naqīr, the speck on the back of a date-stone, and the rewards will not be diminished even by the size of the dint in a date-stone.

### The measures of smallness

The Qur'ān keeps a set of weights for the minute. The naqīr is the speck on the back of a date-stone. The Fatīl is a scalish thread in the long slit of the stone, and the Qiṭmīr the thin membrane stretched over it, and all three measures have their places in the Book. The point of the weighing is comfort. The justice that requites an atom's evil also guards an atom's good, and the believer's account is kept to a measure finer than anything a hand can hold. He who combines faith with practice enters Paradise fully rewarded. The entry is not a bare admittance but a payment in full, every deed counted, nothing docked, nothing shorted, down to the thread in the slit.

The hint inside the verse divides the communities. Good deeds may exist among the People of the Book and other non-Muslims, yet with an unsound faith those deeds find no acceptance. The Muslims, with sound faith and good deeds, are the successful ones, standing above the rest.

### In short

- Faith is the condition under every good deed, and Paradise receives both the man and the woman who meet it.
- The speck on the date stone is the outer limit of the wronging, and no reward is cut even by the thread in the slit.
- Good deeds without sound faith find no acceptance, while sound faith with good deeds stands above every community.

125.text:
The best religion: "And who is better in faith than those who ˺fully˺ submit themselves to Allah, do good, and follow the Way of Abraham, the upright? Allah chose Abraham as a close friend" (4:125). The verse names the criterion and then its living proof.

### Phrase by phrase

**"who ˺fully˺ submit themselves to Allah"** means the surrender of the face, and the face is the whole personality. The verse calls the same person a muḥsin, a beautiful-doer, for the surrender and the beauty of the deed are one station. Turning the face toward Allah is turning with the whole existence. It is to act for His good pleasure with all the sincerity at one's command, never staining the deed with hypocritical or materialistic motives.

**"do good"** names the second half of the criterion: the way of acting must itself be correct. The correct way is no invention of the self. It is the way of Islam pure and unalloyed, founded on the injunctions Allah Almighty sent down and on the teachings of His noble Messenger ﷺ. Two conditions therefore govern the acceptance of any deed, sincerity of intention and soundness of action, accordance with the Sharīʿah and the Sunnah. Sincerity belongs to the heart, the innermost human dimension, and conformity to the Sharīʿah to the exterior. The deed becomes outwardly correct by following the Sunnah and inwardly correct by sincerity, and whoever fulfils both finds exterior and interior perfectly synchronized. When sincerity is lost, the doer becomes a hypocrite showing off for people, and when the Sharīʿah is not followed, he becomes an ignorant, wicked person. Lacking either pillar, the deed becomes null and void, and whoever combines both performs the deeds of the faithful believers, whose best deeds are accepted and whose errors are erased.

### The two downfalls

The history of nations and faiths shows that all deviant groups have either lacked sincerity or not acted right. These are the two groups identified in sūrat al-Fātiḥah as those who left the straight path. Those referred to as incurring wrath are the people who lack sincerity, victims of desires, and those called astray are the people who have not acted right, victims of doubts. Everyone understands the first condition, the need for sincerity. The second, good conduct as the following of the Sharīʿah, is the condition many Muslims ignore, thinking a good deed a good deed wherever done. The Qur'ān and the Sunnah say otherwise, that good conduct rests exclusively on the teachings of the Prophet ﷺ and the following of his example. Doing less and doing more are both crimes. Three rakʿahs of Ẓuhr in place of the prescribed four is a crime, and so is the offering of five, a sin of the same nature. The condition set by Allah and His Messenger ﷺ for any act of worship is final. Additions or restrictions of one's own, or forms other than the one laid out, are impermissible, however attractive the surface. All new alterations in the established religion, the innovations the Prophet ﷺ declared straying into error, are of this nature. The ignorant perform them with sincerity, as worship worthy of reward, while the deed goes waste or turns sinful in the light of the Sharīʿah. Hence the stress on good conduct in the Book: "So that He tests you as to who among you is good in deed" (67:2), said in sūrat al-Mulk, where the words are good in deed, not outnumbering in deeds, for the good deed is precisely the deed done by the Sunnah's measure. The proper effort, spoken of in the verse that says whoever desires the Hereafter and strives for it with due striving (17:19), is the same: intended purely for the Hereafter and carried out as the Prophet ﷺ explained by word and deed, with any shift, increased or decreased, outside acceptance. In all the deeds of ṣalāh, sawm, ḥajj, zakāh and charity, in the dhikr of Allah, the blessings on the Prophet and the salām, the way is to find how the Messenger of Allah did them and what instructions he left.

**"and follow the Way of Abraham, the upright"** names the pattern. The hanīf is the one who avoids shirk intentionally and with knowledge, goes attentively to the truth, and lets no one hinder him or stop him from it. He inclines away from every religion to the upright religion, the creed that accords with the creed of Islam and its Oneness. The command was given: "Follow the religion of Ibrahim the Hanif, and he was not of the Mushrikin" (16:123), and the claim is defined: "Verily, among mankind who have the best claim to Ibrahim are those who followed him, and this Prophet" (3:68), for "Ibrahim was an Ummah, obedient to Allah, a Hanif, and he was not one of the Mushrikin" (16:120).

**"Allah chose Abraham as a close friend"** crowns the pattern. The grade of Khalīl is the highest grade of love, the ultimate closeness to Allah that the servants seek. Ibrāhīm attained it through obedience to his Lord, who tried him with certain commands and he fulfilled them (2:124). Al-Bukhārī recorded from ʿAmr ibn Maymūn that when Muʿādh came back from Yemen he led the people in the Fajr prayer and recited this verse, and one of the men present commented that surely the eye of Ibrāhīm's mother had been comforted. Ibrāhīm bears the name Khalīl for the great love his Lord bore him, love earned through the acts of obedience that Allah loves and prefers. In the Two Ṣaḥīḥs, Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī said that in his last speech the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> O people! If I were to take a Khalīl from the people of the earth, I would have taken Abū Bakr ibn Abī Quḥāfah as my Khalīl. However, your companion is the Khalīl of Allah.

From Jundub, from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr and from ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd comes the same word: Allah chose His Prophet as His Khalīl, even as He chose Ibrāhīm as His Khalīl.

### The inward reading

In this verse the Lord of the Worlds praises the self-purifiers, showing His pleasure with self-purification in deeds. Muṣṭafā was the first to dress the Kaʿbah of deeds in that cloak, and his word was that deeds are only through intentions. Self-purification does the work of colour in jewels. A jewel without the cape of colour is a worthless stone, and the deed without self-purification is spent effort that never strikes the mark. Maʿrūf Karkhī used to beat himself with a whip, saying: O soul, purify thyself and be delivered. It has been said that knowledge is the seed and deeds the planting, with self-purification the water. By self-purification the work is done, in it lies salvation, and in it endless felicity, yet it is exalted, coming down just anywhere to no one and showing its face to just no one, for the Exalted Lord said that it is one of His secrets, deposited in the hearts of those whom He loves among His servants. Of its hiddenness there is a story. A worshipper among the Children of Israel was told of a tree in a certain place that people worshipped. For the sake of Allah and the zeal of the religion he grew angry, took a mattock on his shoulder and set out to dig the tree up by its roots. Iblīs met him on the road in the attributes of an old man, asked where he was going, and heard the errand. He told the worshipper to go back and busy himself with his worship, for this would not be done by his hand, then struggled with him and fell, and the worshipper sat on his chest. Iblīs begged to be let go, promising beautiful words, and once released, said: O worshipper, Allah has prophets. If this tree needed to be dug up, He would command a prophet to dig it up.

### In short

- The best religion is the full surrender of the self, the good deed and the way of Ibrāhīm the upright.
- Sincerity and correctness are the two pillars, and either loss names its people, the hypocrites of showing off and the astray of self-invented ways.
- Good conduct means the Sunnah, no less and no more, for three rakʿahs and five rakʿahs of Ẓuhr offend alike.
- Ibrāhīm, who fulfilled the commands, holds the highest grade of love, and the Prophet ﷺ would have taken no earthly friend but Abū Bakr.
- Self-purification is the colour of the jewel, a secret deposited in the hearts of the beloved, as the worshipper with the mattock learned.

126.text:
The possession of everything: "To Allah ˹alone˺ belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. And Allah is Fully Aware of everything" (4:126). The verse closes the passage with the ground the whole scale stands on.

### Phrase by phrase

**"To Allah ˹alone˺ belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth"** means that everything and everyone are His property, His creatures and His servants, with the dominion of all of it in His hand alone. No one exists who could avert His decision or question His judgment, and what He does, He is never asked about, for His might, ability, fairness, wisdom, compassion and mercy place Him beyond accounting. His is the kingdom in the heavens and the earth, and His planning runs over everything He created.

**"And Allah is Fully Aware of everything"** means that His knowledge holds all things, and nothing concerning His servants is hidden from Him. Not even the weight of an atom escapes His observation in the heavens and the earth, nor anything smaller or bigger than that, and His power and His planning surround His creation as His knowledge does.

### The three admonishments

The inward reading counts the refrain. Three times in these verses it is said that to Allah belongs everything in the heavens and the earth, and each is an admonishment for a different group, specific to a designated meaning. Each of the three sayings carries its own meaning for its own hearers. The first admonishes the common Muslims, the second the worshipful servants and the godwary, the third the sincerely truthful and the elect. First, He says for the common Muslims that everything in heaven and earth is His possession and kingdom, all His creation and artisanry, His knowledge reaching all. He has made certain rightful dues incumbent among them and set apart obligatory acts, so they are to comply with the rightful due of women, orphans and the weak. The commands are to be put into action, and comfort and peace are to be sought. In good and in bad, in peace and in war, the reality stands that He knows and He sees, for all is His creation and His artisanry, and no maker is blind to the work of his own hands. "Does He who created not know, while He is the Gentle, the Aware?" (67:14).

The teaching that hangs on the verse reaches every soul in its hiding place. Allah is the Lord of the universe, the possessor of all kinds of power, yet He has chosen to remain invisible in this world, and man commits all kinds of evil because he does not see Him, assuming freedom to do as he pleases. The believer of the better faith is the one like Ibrāhīm, whose loyalty belongs to his Lord alone, whose dealings in the world run by justice and modesty, and who keeps scrupulously clear of injustice and arrogance. And were a person to realise how utterly powerless human beings are, he would know the helplessness that awaits on the Day of Judgement, when all realities are laid bare.

### In short

- Everything in the heavens and the earth is His property and creation, and no one averts His decision or questions His judgment.
- Not an atom, nor smaller nor bigger, escapes His observation.
- The refrain speaks three times, to the common Muslims, the worshipful, and the elect, and the first hearing is a charge to the rights of women, orphans and the weak.

127.text:
The question about women: "They ask you ˹O Prophet˺ regarding women. Say, “It is Allah Who instructs you regarding them. Instruction has ˹already˺ been revealed in the Book concerning the orphan women you deprive of their due rights but still wish to marry, also helpless children, as well as standing up for orphans’ rights”" (4:127). The verse answers a question the people put to the Prophet ﷺ directly, and behind the question stood the practices of the age of ignorance.

### The question and its occasion

At the beginning of this sūrah, injunctions relating to orphans and women were given, with stress on fulfilling their rights. In the days of jāhiliyyah some people refused women and children any part of the inheritance, others unlawfully ate up what they received, and still others married the women while withholding the full dower. When no abrogation came of the new rules, some who had waited for one decided to go to the Prophet ﷺ and ask him outright. This question, in the reports of Ibn Jarīr and Ibn al-Mundhir, was the very reason for the revelation of the verse, and the verses that followed carried additional rulings about women. One record names the questioner ʿUyaynah, and the report reaches ʿĀʾishah through Ibn Wahb, from Yūnus, from Ibn Shihāb, from ʿUrwah, with Muslim carrying it from Ḥarmalah from Ibn Wahb.

### Phrase by phrase

**"concerning the orphan women you deprive of their due rights but still wish to marry"** opens the answer, and ʿĀʾishah explained the case. The verse concerns the man taking care of a female orphan, her caretaker and inheritor, whose money is joined with his to the point that she shares with him even the branch of a date he owns. For the material gain he would rather marry her himself, and he cannot bear that another man should marry her and share in the money through her. So he refuses to let her marry anyone, and the verse came down. Al-Bukhārī recorded this, and Muslim also. She added that the words also cover the opposite desire of the guardian, who avoids marrying the orphan under his supervision when she lacks property or beauty. What was forbidden to the guardians was marrying the orphan girls of property and beauty without being just to them, as they generally refrained from marrying the plain and the poor. The recited instruction of the Book is the earlier word of this sūrah: "If you fear that you shall not be able to deal justly with the orphan girls, then marry other women of your choice" (4:3). The basis stands in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs. ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah reported from Ibn ʿAbbās the old custom. The guardian of a fatherless girl would throw his rope over her as a mark of possession, and once marked, she was unmarriageable. A beautiful one he married and took control of her wealth. A plain one he held back from every suitor until she died, and then he inherited her money. Allah prohibited and outlawed the practice. The reading of the phrase runs two ways, and both expose a wrong. Read as and they tend to marry them, it names those who, attracted by the beauty of the orphan girls, married them without giving them the due rights of a wife. Read as and you avoid marrying them, it names those who would not marry them for their unattractive features yet let them marry no one else, wanting the wealth to stay in their hands. One gloss names the wronged ones as the daughters of Umm Kuhhah. The command that follows covers both: when a caretaker wishes to marry the orphan in his care, he must give her the suitable dowry that other women of her status receive, and if he will not, let him marry other women, for Allah has made the matter easy. And when he does not desire her, he is forbidden to prevent her from marrying another man out of fear that the husband would share in the money.

**"also helpless children"** recalls the second practice of jāhiliyyah. Young children and females were denied a share of inheritance. The verse prohibits the practice and fixes the share of each, "To the male, a portion equal to that of two females" (4:11), with no regard to youth or age, as Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and others stated.

**"as well as standing up for orphans' rights"** closes the charge with the golden rule, in the words of Saʿīd ibn Jubayr: just as you would want to marry her and have her for yourself when she is beautiful and wealthy, so marry her and have her for yourself when she is neither wealthy nor beautiful.

**"And whatever good you do is certainly well known to Allah"** encourages the good deeds and the fulfilment of the commandments. Allah is knowledgeable of all of it, and He rewards it in the best and most perfect manner.

The occasion teaches the condition of all law. The questions people brought to the Prophet ﷺ about the sharīʿah's social rules always drew answers weighted toward goodness, justice, fraternity and piety. A law serves its purpose only when the one who must enforce it is God-fearing and truly desirous of justice. Social reform takes hold only when the evil-doer realises he is ultimately accountable to Allah, who cannot be fooled even if people are. The doer of good carries on whether appreciated or not, in the belief that Allah is watching and will reward, deterred from injustice by the dread of the Fire, and given courage by the hope of Paradise to endure the losses of a truthful life.

The inward reading hears the threat inside the mercy. Allah prohibited coveting what leads to harm or wrong against oppressed women and orphans, explained that Allah is their avenger, and showed that whoever is heedful of Allah regarding them loses nothing on His account but finds a beautiful recompense, while whoever abuses them suffers a painful tribulation.

### In short

- The question about women's rights followed the waiting of those who expected the inheritance rules to be abrogated.
- The guardian who trapped the orphan's wealth, by marrying her or by preventing every other marriage, is the target of the instruction, and the rope of jāhiliyyah is cut.
- Children and females receive the fixed shares, and the standing rule is to want for the plain orphan what one would want for the beautiful one.
- Allah knows the good done to the weak, repays it perfectly, and avenges their abuse.

128.text:
The strained marriage: "If a woman fears indifference or neglect from her husband, there is no blame on either of them if they seek ˹fair˺ settlement, which is best" (4:128). The verse opens the Qur'ān's instruction for the hard part of married life, the part every couple meets at one stage or another.

### The situation and the occasions

Mutual displeasure and tension, left unchecked, bring the couple severe problems. At times the evil travels outward to families and tribes, into confrontation and even killing. The Qur'ān introduces a system of family life that keeps the whole range of feelings in view. Followed, it makes a home a paradise, love replacing whatever bitterness there was. Should separation become inevitable, the parting is smooth and painless, leaving no fallout of enmity or hurt. Verse 128 concerns the strain that comes for reasons beyond the couple's control. The husband lacks amorous feeling for the wife, and she has no control over the means that would change his heart. She may be plain or aged while he is handsome, and neither can be blamed for what each is.

The occasions show the verse at work. Abū Dāwūd aṭ-Ṭayālisī recorded from Ibn ʿAbbās that Ṣawdah feared the Messenger of Allah ﷺ might divorce her, and said: do not divorce me, give my day to ʿĀʾishah. He did, and Allah sent down the verse. Ibn ʿAbbās added that whatever legal agreement the spouses mutually agree to is allowed, and at-Tirmidhī recorded it, calling it ḥasan gharīb. In the Two Ṣaḥīḥs, ʿĀʾishah tells of Ṣawdah bint Zamʿah growing old, forfeiting her day to ʿĀʾishah, while the Prophet ﷺ spent Ṣawdah's night with ʿĀʾishah. By keeping her among his wives, his ummah received the pattern of this kind of settlement, for what he kept, others may keep. Al-Bukhārī also recorded from ʿĀʾishah her reading of the verse over the case of a man married to an old woman he no longer desires and seeks to divorce. Her answer is to say that she forfeits her right on him, and the verse was revealed. The records add more cases, one through ʿAbd ar-Raḥīm ibn Sulaymān, from Hishām, from ʿUrwah, from ʿĀʾishah. One is the woman who bears no children while the husband seeks divorce. Another is the woman with friends and children she cannot leave, who offers her husband the exchange of keeping her while she forgoes every right due to her. Muslim carries the report from Abū Kurayb from Abū Usāmah. And Ibn al-Musayyab related the case of the daughter of Muḥammad ibn Maslamah, married to Rāfiʿ ibn Khadīj, who wanted to divorce her over something he disliked in her, arrogance or the like. The report came through Ibn al-Rabīʿ, from al-Shāfiʿī, from Ibn ʿUyaynah, from az-Zuhrī. Her answer was to tell him not to divorce her, leaving him free to apportion whatever he liked for her, and Allah revealed the verse. One school gloss even names the pair, ʿUmayrah the wife and Asʿad ibn ar-Rabīʿ the husband, with his young favourite beside the old wife.

### Phrase by phrase

**"If a woman fears indifference or neglect from her husband"** describes the state precisely. Indifference means his looking down on her, his refraining from intimacy, his keeping the maintenance short. The cause is his aversion and his eye set on someone more beautiful. Neglect means his turning from her altogether, no word to her, no sitting with her.

**"there is no blame on either of them if they seek ˺fair˺ settlement"** allows the concession. The wife may forfeit all or part of her rights, provisions, clothing, dwelling and so forth, and the husband may accept. The wording of no sin covers a deal that on the surface looks like a bribe, with the husband tempted by forgiven dower and claims while the bond stays intact. The statement of the Qur'ān makes clear that this is not bribery. It is expediency, wise consideration under complex circumstances, the parties surrendering initial claims and agreeing to a moderated mean, and it is permissible. The words between them carry their own hint, as al-Mazharī notes. The compromise is best made by the two alone. A third person may make the very compromise impossible, and even where it is reached, the weaknesses of the couple stand exposed before an outsider without need. Staying safe from that is expedient for both.

**"which is best"** ranks the settlement above divorce, and the wording is general. It certainly covers the husband-wife dispute of the context. It covers as well every kind of family difference and every mutual dispute, altercation and litigation of worldly life, for the words of the Qur'ān are general: the compromise is better. The parties fare better when they avoid stubbornness over the fulfilment of demands in full, forgo something from each side, and meet on middle ground. The Prophet ﷺ said:

> Every compromise is permissible between Muslims, except a compromise in which something unlawful has been made lawful or something lawful has been made unlawful. And Muslims must abide by accepted conditions, except a condition in which something lawful has been made unlawful.

It is not permissible, for example, to compromise with one's wife on the condition that he also marry her sister, since Islamic law prohibits combining two sisters in marriage. Nor may the condition be that he stop fulfilling the rights of the other wife, which turns a lawful thing unlawful. From the generality of the hadith, Imām Abū Ḥanīfah deduced that all kinds of compromise are permissible. One kind is made with an avowal, as when the defendant confesses a debt and the plaintiff surrenders part or takes something in lieu. Another comes through the defendant's silence, a wish to settle whatever the truth of the claim. A third comes despite a disclaimer, part being paid to end the dispute. On the last two kinds some jurists differ. One boundary matters in the marriage settlement itself. If the woman surrenders rights whose fulfilment was already incumbent, such as a dower due before the compromise, the right lapses wholly or partly and her claim is gone. But rights whose fulfilment falls due only in the future, such as future expenses or the right to privacy, do not lapse forever. She may declare at any time that she no longer forgoes them, and the husband then has the choice of releasing her, as al-Mazharī and others rule.

**"Humans are ever inclined to selfishness"** explains why the concession works. The word names extreme niggardliness, and souls are ever in its presence. The woman's greed lies in her desire to protect the future of her children, fearing that release would ruin it or that life elsewhere would prove more bitter. The husband is tempted by what she does, the dower forgiven in whole or part, the other claims stopped, and a wife kept in the bargain, so that getting along comes to seem easy. A woman would scarcely allow another to share her husband. A man would scarcely let her enjoy him if he fell in love with another. Between these two selfishnesses the compromise finds its room.

**"But if you are gracious and mindful of Allah"** opens the third way. The husband had the legal choice of release on grounds of incompatibility, and the licence of compromise where she offers to surrender claims. Beyond both stands the conduct of grace: keeping the fear of Allah in the heart, being benign and accommodating despite the incompatibility, and fulfilling her rights as due. The text stops at the words that Allah is All-Aware of what you do, without spelling out the return. The hint is that the reward is far more than one can ever imagine.

### The summary of the law

The whole map runs as follows. When the husband feels estranged and his rights unfulfilled, he should first correct what lies within the wife's range, by coldness, hard advice, or in the last resort soft disciplining, as the early verses of this sūrah have set out. If correction fails, or the fault is not in her control at all, the law gives him divorce, a release conducted decently and without altercation. But if he chooses to carry on under the same conditions, ignoring his own rights and fulfilling hers in full, that conduct is highly meritorious and deserving of a great reward. The reverse case mirrors it. Where the husband fails the wife's rights and she wishes release, the course is open if he is willing, and if he is not, she may reclaim her freedom through the Islamic court, or she may brave his cold and crooked ways with patience, surrendering her claims while fulfilling his rights, which is as highly meritorious in her as in him. The guideline in essence: the Qur'ān gives both parties the legal right to remove difficulty and receive their due, while prompting both toward high morals and patience with the loss of rights, so that the relationship is severed only at the farthest limit of possibility, the general command standing as it was revealed: "retain in an honourable manner or part amicably" (2:229).

### The inward reading

When the companionship of created beings disconnects from the discourse of the Real, alienation and blame threaten, and aversion and disgust mix into it. Whoever rejects, ʿaraḍa, Allah in his heart finds created beings rejecting consideration for his right. They come out against him together, finding his affair pathetic and holding his worth cheap. But whoever returns to Allah in his heart finds the affair brought back into balance, whole and in its parts. The chest expands until it can bear the bad traits found in others, the cloak of pardon is drawn over the defects of all, and reconciliation is preferred to his own portion, given up in favour of theirs. To ignore one's aversion to those who quarrel is more appropriate and more advantageous than arrogance with the foe, the wanting of revenge and the claim of privileges, and most people sit in the fetters of this tribulation. The greed of the lower self is the servant's concern for his worldly portion. Veiled from witnessing the Real, a person is inevitably returned to witnessing the lower self. Being gracious, iḥsān, is to worship Allah as if you see Him. The fear commanded is to stop looking at your own status and worth, and to look rather to your Lord, so that in seeing Him you are annihilated from every vision of your own worth. And once you have been annihilated from yourselves and your acts, Allah suffices as Knower (4:70), and He suffices as the Giver of existence following your effacement.

### In short

- Strain beyond control is the setting, and the verse answers it with three doors: settlement, grace, or release.
- Ṣawdah's forfeited day, the childless wife's offer, and Rāfiʿ ibn Khadīj's wife's apportionment are the standing occasions.
- The settlement is no bribe but expediency, best made between the two alone, better than divorce, and lawful in every form that does not trade lawful for unlawful.
- Rights already due lapse when surrendered, future rights do not, and the reward of gracious forbearance is left unspoken because it exceeds imagination.
- The heart that rejects Allah is rejected by all, and the heart that returns finds the cloak of pardon and the expansion of the chest.

129.text:
The limit of the heart: "You will never be able to maintain ˺emotional˺ justice between your wives" (4:129), "no matter how keen you are". The verse sets the boundary of obligation exactly where human power ends.

### Phrase by phrase

**"You will never be able to maintain ˹emotional˺ justice between your wives"** states the impossibility: perfect justice between wives in every respect is beyond anyone. Even with the nights divided justly, degrees remain in love, desire and intimacy, so stated Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿUbaydah as-Salmānī, Mujāhid, al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk ibn Muzāḥim, for love lies outside a person's control. The verse is a clarification of the earlier ruling of this sūrah. The words of verse 3, that a man holding more than one wife is duty-bound to maintain justice and equality, and that whoever fears failure should keep to one woman (4:3), could give the impression that the obligation covers even the heart's inclination. This verse clarifies the matter: in things outside one's control, equality is not obligatory. Equality is obligatory in what lies within one's power, the nights spent with them, the living standards and the cost of maintenance. ʿĀʾishah said that the Prophet ﷺ took the greatest care to treat his wives equally, and while doing so he prayed:

> O Allah, this is my division in what I own, so do not blame me for what You own and I do not own,

meaning his heart. Imām Aḥmad and the collectors of the Sunan recorded it, and this is the wording Abū Dāwūd collected, with a sound chain. Who could be more in control of his self than the Prophet ﷺ? Yet even he ruled the matter of emotional inclination to be outside his control and prayed to be excused on that count.

**"So do not totally incline towards one"** draws the practical line. Liking one wife more is given, but the liking must not be exaggerated into treatment, and though equality of inclination is not in one's power, one must not lean so far toward the favourite as to prefer her even in the matters that do lie within one's power and control.

**"leaving the other in suspense"** names the crime of the muʿallaqah, the suspended wife, and the glossers of the word run from Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr through al-Ḥasan, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk and ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas to as-Suddī and Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān, all with one meaning: neither divorced nor married. She is like a prisoner, without a husband to fulfil her right and without the freedom to seek another. Abū Dāwūd aṭ-Ṭayālisī recorded from Abū Hurayrah the warning of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ:

> Whoever has two wives and inclines to one of them too much, will come on the Day of Resurrection with one of his sides dragging.

**"And if you do what is right and are mindful of Allah"** gives the promise: justice and equal division in what one has power over, with the fear of Allah in all conditions, and Allah forgives the favouritism of the heart that could not be helped.

### The verse cannot be used against polygamy

Some juxtapose this verse with verse 3 to argue that since equality between wives is impossible, keeping more than one wife must be impermissible. Allah has Himself phrased the two verses with the material that removes the misunderstanding. The present verse says only do not incline totally, and the earlier verse said: "But, if you fear that you will not maintain equity, then, keep to one woman" (4:3). The condition if you fear openly indicates that justice between wives is not beyond possibility or ability, else the extended wording would serve no purpose. Consider the comparison with the forbidden degrees. The verse of prohibitions lists the women forbidden for marriage (4:23) and then declares the combining of two sisters in marriage unlawful (4:23). Had the absolute prohibition of more than one wife been intended, one sentence would have sufficed, and the restriction of the sisters would have been redundant. Instead the Qur'ān avoids the lexical brevity and spends two full verses on the detail, which indicates that the restriction of the two sisters itself suggests the justification of combining more than one woman in marriage, permissible on the condition that they not be sisters.

### The wider teaching and the inward reading

The differences between husband and wife, and between any two persons, largely result from greed, one party wanting demands met without consideration for the other, which breeds distrust. The proper course is for each to weigh the other's problems and, with due allowances, reach a consensus. As Allah desires consideration between people, so He shows the maximum consideration to His servants. He does not seize a person for natural weaknesses, but takes to task the deliberate excesses, the acts of injustice out of haughtiness and insolence. Whoever fears Allah and carries the urge of reform in his heart finds his rightly intended acts pardonable in the Hereafter. Nor should anyone nurse the thought that he is behind the success of another, for Allah alone is the provider, and His help may come under diverse sets of circumstances.

The inward reading turns the same light on the heart. When the concern is for oneself, the state of the union together is overturned and what was sound becomes ruined. When the concern is Allah, the balance of the life together is restored and cleared of turmoil. If Allah has decreed some deficiency as a person's state, no competence of yours will set it right. The command do not turn altogether away is a command not to stray from the clear path. Stop where the stopping was ordered, and do what there is to do. The suspended one is harmed in two ways, nothing to be had from the husband and no way to be with another, and this harm is very grave.
