The allusion within it is that when the path to your share in worldly things closes, Allah opens to you the witness of His reality toward you and the finding of His kindness. Whoever's annihilation is in Allah, the Real is his substitute. And when what is between you and created beings is set right, with trust placed in what lies between you and the Real, then Allah is forgiving of your failings and merciful in pardoning your sins.

### In short

- Perfect equality of the heart is impossible and not owed, and the Prophet's ﷺ prayer divided what he owned from what Allah owns.
- The owed equality is the nights, the maintenance and the living standard, and the forbidden thing is the suspended wife.
- The one who inclines too far comes on the Day of Resurrection with his side dragging.
- The verse clarifies verse 3 rather than repealing it, and the two-sisters restriction shows the way the rule runs.
- Greed divides people, consideration mends them, and the heart concerned with Allah keeps its balance.

130.text:
The open door of parting: "But if they choose to separate, Allah will enrich both of them from His bounties" (4:130). The verse closes the passage by answering the fear that separation means ruin.

### The case behind the passage

One record names the couple of the occasion, Asʿad ibn al-Rabīʿ, who had beside his old wife another young wife whom he favoured. Allah forbade him the favouring and commanded that the young and the old be treated equally. The passage that closes here thus grew out of a real household, and the closing verse answers the fear of ruin that hangs over every parted couple.

### Phrase by phrase

**"But if they choose to separate"** names the third case between husband and wife, reached when every effort at setting things right has failed. The separation may come by divorce issued by the man or by khulʿ initiated by the woman.

**"Allah will enrich both of them from His bounties"** is the comfort. Allah will suffice them, giving him a better wife and her a better husband. Another home and a source of support await the woman, and another woman the man, each compensated out of His plenty. There is no cause for concern and no reason to lose hope. Let each think of the life before the marriage, two strangers with no bond between them, whom Almighty Allah then joined as husband and wife. The same can happen again, for the power of Allah is extensive.

**"And Allah is Ever-Bountiful, All-Wise"** seals it. His favour is tremendous and His bounty enormous, and He is Wise in all His actions, decisions and commandments. The dimensions of His capacity are the most extensive, and everything issuing from Him rests on wisdom. In the separation itself may lie the readiest solution of the problem, and the time after it may bless each with a mate by whom life grows good to live.

The inward reading carries the comfort to its root. The essential companionship is the companionship of the heart in perpetual need of Allah, since nothing separates a person from the Real. Everything other than the Real leaves human beings needing one another in the external sense alone, and that is the thinking of the people of separation. The people of realisation hold no doubt that the need of created beings runs entirely to Allah.

### In short

- When all mending fails, separation by divorce or khulʿ opens, and poverty is not among its results.
- Allah enriches both from His plenty, as He united them when they had been strangers.
- The separation itself may be the wisdom, and the real companionship, which is of the heart, never parts from the Real.

131.text:
The standing counsel: "To Allah ˹alone˺ belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. Indeed, We have commanded those given the Scripture before you, as well as you, to be mindful of Allah" (4:131). After the rules of behaviour toward women and orphans, the passage returns to the promise for those who abide and the warning for those who contravene, the usual style of the Qur'ān.

### Phrase by phrase

**"To Allah ˹alone˺ belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth"** states the ownership and the supreme authority over both. The refrain repeats through this passage with three shades in it, the first being the boundless reach of the power of creation, which lacks nothing.

**"We have commanded those given the Scripture before you, as well as you, to be mindful of Allah"** means that what was recommended to the People of the Scripture is recommended to you: taqwā of Allah, the worship of Him alone without partners. The people of the Torah were charged in the Torah, the people of the Gospel in the Gospel, and every Scripture people in its Scripture, and the community of Muḥammad ﷺ in its Book.

**"But if you disobey"** carries no threat to Allah, only to the disobedient. As Allah said in the word of Mūsā to his people: "If you disbelieve, you and all on the earth together, then verily, Allah is Rich, Owner of all praise" (14:8). And as Allah said of those who disbelieved and turned away: "But Allah was not in need of them" (64:6). He is far too Rich to need His servants, and He deserves praise for every decision and commandment. The second shade of the refrain is this need-freedom: whoever denies the good counsel given takes nothing from Him, who stands ever-praised in His pristine glory. Over every soul He keeps perfect watch, knowing what it deserves, the Watcher and Witness of all things.

### The life the counsel builds

The point of the whole teaching is the life it builds. A believer's virtuous life is possible only as a God-worshipper at heart and soul. Discovering Allah as the Lord of the universe, fearing and trusting Him alone, and turning the full attention to the Hereafter, these enable the godly life in this world, and these were the focus of prophetic teaching.

The inward reading hears the direct address. Worshipper and abstainer alike are told to come fully into the street of godwariness, make godwariness their shelter, and leave the road of uncertainty and suspicion. So He commands, giving success to one group and placing another in the road of abandonment, and to all He gives the awareness:

> I am without needs. I have no benefit from the obedience of the one given success, nor any loss from the disobedience of the one abandoned. Everything in the heavens and the earth is My possession and kingdom. All are My predetermined things and artifacts. Had I wanted, I would have created all successful, or all abandoned. No one can protest against Me, and there is no turning away from My decree.

### In short

- The counsel of taqwā is one counsel, given to the Torah people, the Gospel people and the Qur'ān people alike.
- Disbelief harms none but the disbeliever, for the Owner of the heavens and earth needs nothing.
- The repetition teaches creation's limitless scope, Allah's need-freedom, and His perfect watch over every soul.
- The godly life is built on the God-worshipping heart, and godwariness is the shelter ordered for it.

132.text:
The Guardian: "To Allah ˹alone˺ belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. And Allah is sufficient as a Trustee of Affairs" (4:132). The refrain returns to ground the counsel a second time.

### Phrase by phrase

**"To Allah ˹alone˺ belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth"** is repeated, in the reading of one school, to reaffirm the reason why the fear of Allah is necessary. What is contained in the heavens and the earth belongs to Him, and He witnesses that belonging.

**"And Allah is sufficient as a Trustee of Affairs"** means He alone takes care of the affairs of His creation, the Guardian and Disposer of all, so that the trusting heart needs no other trustee.

### The world of trial

The wider teaching explains why the trustee must be feared as well as trusted. The present world is a world of trial, built to find out who is good and who is bad, and to serve that purpose it provides every kind of freedom. Here a person may even label his misdeeds good deeds. He may sin freely and pass himself off as pious, find beautiful words to justify himself, refute an open truth and dress the denial finely. He may build a life on honour-seeking, hoarding and self-glorification and still be hailed as a servant of truth, exploit Allah's religion for worldly purposes and flourish, or abandon the lawful for the unlawful and go scot free. Of all the aspects of a person's relationship with Allah, the most important is whether he fears Him, for the fear of Allah enables the responsible life. Without it nothing checks the path of evil, and evil here can be couched in beautiful words, injustice brings great advancement, and every tyrant finds fine words to hide his tyranny.

The inward reading addresses the sincerely truthful and the lovers. To them He says that the seven heavens, the seven earths and all within them are His. The face was not meant to turn toward them nor the heart to hang on them, held back from Him. Their purpose was to be shown and adorned for the soul, that once all is put aside and the face comes to Him, the whole of them enters service and lies in the hands. Of it the report says:

> O this world! Serve those who serve Me, and trouble those who serve you!

Sahl Tustarī's story has travelled far. The caliph of his day offered him great wealth, and he took nothing of it. Someone asked him why, and Sahl called upon Allah to lift the veil from the questioner's eyes, and the man looked and saw a whole realm of gems and pearls before him. Sahl said:

> O chevalier! I have no need for the wealth of the caliph. The whole world is at my command. The storehouses of the earth have been offered to me, but I do not want them.

And the word goes further:

> Why do you stay in this low place like crows looking for carrion? Break the cage and fly at once like peacocks to the heights. All on the face of gold and gems is unbelief. If you have the religion's fervour, step beyond the gold.

### In short

- The refrain grounds the fear, and the trusteeship of Allah covers every affair of creation.
- The world of trial permits evil to dress itself finely, and only the fear of Allah keeps the soul responsible.
- The heavens and the earth were made to be shown, not clung to, and whoever turns his face to Allah finds them all in his service.
- Sahl Tustarī refused the caliph's wealth with the storehouses of the earth already open to him.

133.text:
The replaceable: "If it is His Will, He can remove you altogether, O humanity, and replace you with others. And Allah is Most Capable to do so" (4:133). The refrain's third shade is the mercy behind the might.

### Phrase by phrase

**"If it is His Will, He can remove you altogether, O humanity"** means the power to take you away for disobedience, to destroy you and create in your stead beings better and more obedient.

**"and replace you with others"** is spelled out elsewhere in the Book, where the turning away of a people is answered by their exchange for another, unlike them in every good.

**"And Allah is Most Capable to do so"** closes the matter.

The inward reading weighs the might on eternity's scale. Whoever can do without others in all eternity without beginning, istaghnā ʿanhu fī āzālihi, needs nothing of them in all eternity without end. He, it is said, has no need for anyone, while the servant cannot do without Him for even a single breath. The things decreed know no limit: were it not this man, it would be that one, were it not one servant, it would be servants. The only one without substitute or replacement is the One, the Unique.

### In short

- Obedience is not a favour done to Allah, for humanity itself is replaceable at a word.
- The one needed from before beginning needs nothing after end, and every substitute but Him has a substitute.

134.text:
The two rewards: "Whoever desires the reward of this world, then ˹let them know that˺ with Allah are the rewards of this world and the Hereafter. And Allah is All-Hearing, All-Seeing" (4:134). The verse answers the one whose ultimate desire is this life.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Whoever desires the reward of this world"** addresses the one whose ultimate desire is this life, and the answer is the ownership: Allah holds the rewards of this life and the Hereafter, and whoever asks Him for both finds enrichment, award and sufficiency. The Qur'ān has drawn the two askers already. Some say only:

> Our Lord! Give us in this world!

and for such there is no portion in the Hereafter. Others say:

> Our Lord! Give us in this world that which is good and in the Hereafter that which is good, and save us from the torment of the Fire!

and for them there is a share for what they have earned. The scale is set in the Book: "Whosoever desires the reward of the Hereafter, We give him increase in his reward" (42:20), and on the other side, "Whoever desires the quick-passing, We readily grant him what We will for whom We like" (17:18), until the words "See how We prefer one above another in this world" (17:21). One school reads the verse as a rebuke. Why demand the lower reward? The higher is there for the sincere devotion, and whatever reward one seeks is found with Him alone. He is All-Hearing of what you say, All-Seeing of your works.

The inward reading sees the two corrections of the heart. To hearts attached to the transitory of this world He held out the hereafter, its blessing standing far above the aspirations of this paltry place. Then, when the search was raised to the hereafter, He cut the seekers off from every external and created thing, saying: "And Allah is better and more enduring" (20:73).

### In short

- Both rewards are with Allah, and the asker may ask for both, the good of this world and the good of the next.
- The one who asks for this world alone buys no portion in the Hereafter.
- The heart attached to the transitory is reminded of the Hereafter, and the heart fixed on the Hereafter is freed from everything created.

135.text:
The justice of the witness: "O believers! Stand firm for justice as witnesses for Allah even if it is against yourselves, your parents, or close relatives" (4:135). The verse instructs all Muslims in upholding justice and true witness, and removes, in a manner most eloquent, the things that stand in their way.

### The purpose of prophets and scriptures

The real purpose of sending prophets and scriptures stands here in the open. A verse of sūrat al-Māʾidah that follows this sūrah carries the same subject, nearly the same words, and sūrat al-Ḥadīd states the purpose outright. Sayyidna Ādam was sent as the vice-regent of Allah in this world, followed by the blessed prophets one after another with Scriptures and missions, so that justice would prevail in the world with peace coming in its wake, every human being, as a distinct individual, adopting justice as a hallmark within the circle of his or her influence. As for the chronically contumacious, whom good counsel, education and communication cannot bring to the path of justice, they are the ones to be compelled to observe it through legal process, due penalization and punishment. The words of sūrat al-Ḥadīd are these:

> We have sent Our messengers with clear signs, and We have sent with them the Book and the Balance, so that people stand firm with justice, and We have sent the iron, in which there is great awe and benefits for people. (57:25)

The sending down of iron, mentioned at the end of that verse, hints at the eventuality when counsel alone fails to make people abide by justice. Then the compulsive miscreant meets the deterrent of iron, the chain and the bar, in the best interest of establishing justice.

Establishing and maintaining justice is therefore not simply the duty of governments and courts. The instruction is given to every human being, obligating each to fulfil the demands of justice personally and to make efforts that others stay equally firm about seeing justice done. A certain level of justice does fall to government and its officials, when the wicked and the rebellious flout justice personally and stop others from carrying out its dictates, and on such occasions penalization and punishment become necessary, an enforcement only government can perform. In the world today, even fairly educated people think the dispensing of justice is the sole business of governments, and this attitude is a major reason why government and people stand as two confronting parties in every country, a gulf of conflict dividing the rulers and the ruled. Masses everywhere demand justice from their government yet are not themselves ready to uphold it, and the outcome is visible everywhere: law on hold, the crime wave riding high. Law-making bodies cost millions, elections shake the earth, the elected make laws with care, the machinery of government goes about enforcing them. Compare a hundred years of it, from 1857 to 1957, and the data will confirm that with every increase in law-making and every new kind of police, crimes escalated and people remained further deprived of justice, and more disorder showed up in the world.

The only guarantee of universal peace is the belief in the Hereafter and the fear of Allah. This twosome is the channel through which the obligations of the ruler and the ruled merge on a common platform, everyone pulsating with the sense of individual responsibility, and the masses can no longer say that respecting law was the job of the officials. The verses on justice end with exactly this article of faith. This sūrah ends with the reminder that Allah is all-aware of what you do. Sūrat al-Māʾidah first gives the instruction to observe taqwā and then the awareness. Sūrat al-Ḥadīd ends with the power and might. Seen together, the three verses do not rest at instructing officials and masses to uphold justice personally and see that others do. They go further, focusing all attention on the decisive reality able to generate a great revolution in human life: the power and domain of Almighty Allah, the thought of standing present before Him, of reckoning and retribution. That, in a nutshell, was the secret of the peace that prevailed in the less educated world of a hundred years ago, and its abandonment is what has deprived the modern, progress-claiming, satellite-borne world of genuine peace. Science can scale the skies, pitch camp on the stars and sound the depths of the seas, yet the end-product of all its equipment is found on none of them. It is in the message brought by the Prophet ﷺ who appeared in Arabia, within the belief in Allah and in the life-to-come and its reckoning: "Listen! Hearts rest at peace through the remembrance, the dhikr, of Allah" (13:28). Day by day, the discoveries of science do nothing but confirm the most perfect power of Almighty Allah and the mastery of His creation, before which every human claim to progress stands humbled. The Persian line asks it plainly: with no wisdom and no vision, what is the use of what you do?

To recapitulate, the Qur'ān has declared the establishment of justice the very purpose of a universal order, and proposed a system which, once adopted, would metamorphose this blood-thirsty and iniquitous world into a society of the virtuous. That is a Paradise now, present and immediate, well before the promised Paradise of the Hereafter. One explanation of the verse that promises two Paradises to the one who fears the high station of his Lord runs exactly so: the God-fearing have two Paradises, one in the Hereafter and one right here in this world. There is nothing utopian about it, for the feasibility was demonstrated by the harbinger of the message himself, who bequeathed it to posterity not as an unproven theory but as a practical and functioning system. After him came al-Khulafāʾ al-Rāshidūn, the rightly-guided caliphs, and many rulers who followed the Sunnah of the noble Prophet ﷺ strictly. Whenever they acted by the principles set for them, the lion and the lamb drank at the same water trough, the image of the ideal climate of justice for all, strong and weak, poor and rich, labourer and capitalist. Law was respected in bolted homes and in the darkness of nights. These are facts of authentic history, corroborated and confessed even by open-minded non-Muslims.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Stand firm for justice as witnesses for Allah"** opens with the word qisṭ, which, beginning with the vowel of i, means justice and fairness. The true sense of it is that every holder of a right be given the due in full, which includes the rights of Allah and all kinds of human rights. Upholding justice carries a wide thrust: nobody shall inflict injustice on anybody, the perpetrator of injustice shall be stopped, the victim shall be supported, appearing as witness shall not be avoided when it would restore a usurped right, the witness shall be true and factual as it really is, for or against anyone, and those who hold the reins of authority shall treat both parties equally and equitably, hearing the statements carefully, investigating every effort possible, and observing perfect justice in the verdict. Witnesses for Allah parallels the command to establish the testimony for Allah (65:2). The testimony is to be delivered precisely, for His sake, correct, truly just, and free of alteration, change or deletion.

**"even if it is against yourselves, your parents, or close relatives"** names the first impediment. Give correct testimony and say the truth when asked, even if harm follows, for with every matter of obedience Allah opens a way out and sends relief. Even against parents and kin, do not compromise, for the truth presides above everyone and is preferred to everyone. One record ties the verse to Miqyās ibn Ṣababah, who had something to testify against his own father. Another, reported through as-Suddi, tells of a poor man and a rich man who brought their dispute to the Prophet ﷺ. His inclination went toward the poor man, on the thought that a poor man cannot wrong a rich one, and Allah wished justice established over poor and rich alike, and the verse came down.

**"Be they rich or poor, Allah is best to ensure their interests"** removes the second pull. Do not favour the rich in testimony, nor pity the poor, for Allah is the caretaker of both, a better Protector than you, with better knowledge of their good, closer to the two than you are.

**"So do not let your desires cause you to deviate"** warns against the whole inner crowd, desire, lust and the hatred held against others. Stand for justice in all situations, as the command says: "And let not the enmity and hatred of others make you avoid justice. Be just: that is nearer to piety" (5:8). The hadith of Khaybar shows the command standing. ʿAbdullāh ibn Rawāḥah was sent by the Prophet ﷺ to assess the fruits and produce of the Jews of Khaybar for taxation, and a bribe was offered him, that he might go easy. His answer has stayed on record:

> By Allah! I have come to you from the dearest of the creation to me, and you are more hated by me than an equivalent number of apes and swine. However, my love for him and hatred for you shall not prevent me from being just with you.

On hearing it they said that this justice is the basis on which the heavens and the earth were created. The same removal of impediments appears in the other verse: malice against a people should not bid you to desert justice, for that too is nearer to taqwā (5:2).

**"If you distort the testimony or refuse to give it"** names the two corruptions of witness. The first word, Talwū, includes distortion and intentional lying, so read Mujāhid and several others among the Salaf. The Book says of a party that they distort the Scripture with their tongues (3:78). The second, Tuʿriḍū, includes hiding and withholding the testimony, as the word says: "Who hides it, surely, his heart is sinful" (2:283). And the Prophet ﷺ said that the best witness is the one who gives his testimony before anyone asks.

### The impediments and the address

Justice is normally impeded by two things. The first is love, kinship, friendship or linkage. It pushes the witness to testify in favour of someone, shielding him from loss or profiting by it, and moves the judge to decide for the party of his linkage. The second is hostility, which may take the witness to testify against someone and bend the judge to an unfavourable ruling. Love and hate are the two passions that carry a person off the path of justice into injustice and oppression. The verse of this sūrah removes the impediment of kinship, and the verse of sūrat al-Māʾidah removes the impediment of grudge and malice. A slight difference of address runs between them. Here it is: uphold justice, witnesses for Allah. There it is: be steadfast for Allah, witnesses for justice. Most readings take the change to show that both are interpretations of the same reality. Worth noticing too is the mode of expression. Both verses prefer multiple-worded sentences, though the command could have been given in the single word of the verse of sūrat al-Ḥujurāt, Aqsiṭu, do justice (49:9). The longer sentence indicates that accidental fairness in a single case does not settle the responsibility. Even the most evil and tyrannical ruler may find himself having done justice in some case. The word of the verse, upholders, qawwāmīn, makes justice a constant duty, at all times, in all conditions, for every friend and foe.

### The two principles of universal justice

The principles enunciated through these verses carry two major aspects. First, officials and masses alike are alerted to the supreme subduing power of Almighty Allah and the ultimate reckoning of the Day of Retribution. All are made to think, pause and hold back, or to face the consequences prepared. The masses themselves have to respect law, and the officials who enforce it have to keep the thought of Allah and the Hereafter before them, remaining servants rather than thoughtless masters of Allah's multitudes. Law is to be a source of service and betterment. It must never increase worry, never grind the victims of injustice in the mill of red tape, never multiply one injustice with others, never be sold for desires or paltry gains. By the words be steadfast for Allah, witnesses for Allah, both officials and masses are exhorted to act for Allah, with sincerity at its best. Second, the responsibility of establishing justice as a way of life rests on the shoulders of all human beings. The verses of this sūrah and of al-Māʾidah address the Muslim community by name, but the verse of al-Ḥadīd, saying that mankind should stand firm with justice, binds all human beings. And by saying even against yourselves, the instruction adds that justice is not something to be demanded from others only. It must be exacted from one's own self. Nothing is to be said against what is true and just, even where the declaration goes against oneself and brings loss. That loss is tiny and passing, while placating the self with flat lies buys the severe punishment of the Day of Retribution.

The divide runs through daily life. A person is often confronted with the path of desire and self-interest on one side and the path of justice on the other. Those unmindful of Allah, not convinced that He watches on all such occasions, follow the path of desire and count it an achievement to have ignored the call of truth. Those who fear Allah and regard Him as their guardian keep their eyes set on truth and justice, acting by their demands. Their sincere desire is to leave this world having done no injustice to anyone. Their desire for justice runs so high that behaviour short of its absolute standard becomes intolerable. Confronted with wrongdoing, they dare to proclaim the demands of truth, even against family interest or worldly considerations. From the standpoint of justice it is also very wrong to give the influential their due while denying the rights of the weak and without influence. A true believer deals justly with everyone, weak or powerful.

The inward reading defines the standing. Justice, qisṭ, is being fair and equitable. To be upright for Allah in fairness is to maintain His rights against your own self, and to seek them from everyone under your authority. The seeking goes by exhortation to kindness, by rebuke of the despicable, by direction to a legal issue, or by guidance to the right thing, the ḥaqq. The deepest realization never reaches the innermost self of whoever withholds from Allah what is rightly due. The foundation of religion is the preferring of the right of the Real over the right of created beings. Whoever prefers anyone, father, mother, child, kinsman or relation, to Allah, or withholds any portion owed to Him, stands not upright in justice.

### In short

- The purpose of prophets, scriptures and the Balance is universal justice, with iron held in reserve for the compulsive.
- The duty binds every individual, and the belief in the Hereafter with the fear of Allah is the only working guarantee of it.
- Testimony goes to Allah alone, over self, parents and kin, unbought by wealth and unsoftened by poverty, as Ibn Rawāḥah's answer at Khaybar shows.
- Distortion and withholding are the two corruptions, and the disclosed testimony stands highest.
- Love and hate are the two impediments, and the constant word qawwāmīn makes justice a standing duty. The heart that prefers any relation to Allah has left the ranks of the upright.

136.text:
The call upward: "O believers! Have faith in Allah, His Messenger, the Book He has revealed to His Messenger, and the Scriptures He revealed before" (4:136). After the subsidiary injunctions, with issues of faith, īmān, and of disbelief, kufr, appearing as a corollary to the dealings with antagonists, the sūrah now takes up these issues in detail, almost to its end. The first word commands faith to those who already have it.

### Phrase by phrase

**"O believers! Have faith"** is no redundancy. Allah commands His faithful servants to hold fast to every element of faith, branch, pillar and cornerstone alike. The command serves the completing of faith and its continual maintenance. The believer already proclaims in every prayer: "Guide us to the straight way" (1:6), which means make us aware of the straight path, increase us in guidance and strengthen us on it. The command to believe in Him and His Messenger stands likewise elsewhere: "O you who believe! Have Taqwa of Allah, and believe in His Messenger" (57:28). One school reads the address with perseverance built in: believe and keep believing. The teaching beneath runs the same: calling oneself a Muslim does not suffice to be held one in the eyes of Allah. A true Muslim is one who has made Allah the centre of his life, with his trust reposed in Him alone, whose belief in the Prophet ﷺ and his guidance excludes all else, whose hold on the revealed Scripture reaches the point that thought and feeling are subordinated to it, to whom belief in the angels means being surrounded by Allah's guardians constantly watching, and whose belief in the Hereafter is so profound that he examines all his words and deeds in its balance.

**"the Book He has revealed to His Messenger"** is the Qur'ān, and **"the Scriptures He revealed before"** are the previously revealed divine Books given to the messengers before him.

**"whoever denies Allah, His angels, His Books, His messengers, and the Last Day has clearly gone far astray"** gives the reverse: deviation from the correct guidance and distance from its path. Whoever falls short of that belief stands astray, whatever his own reckoning of himself as Muslim and believer, while whoever reaches it stands on the straight path to success in the Hereafter.

### The occasion of the call

One record reads the address over the people of an earlier covenant. The verse, it says, came down over a company of Torah believers: ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām, Asad and Usayd the two sons of Kaʿb, Thaʿlabah ibn Qays, Salam and Salāmah his nephews, and Yāmīn ibn Yāmīn. Their call ran: believers in Moses and the Torah, now believe in Allah and in His Messenger Muḥammad, in the Scripture revealed to him, and in every Scripture given to the prophets before. When the verse came down, all the people named embraced Islam.

### The two faiths

The inward reading hears two faiths inside the call, the one built on proof and the other on face-to-face vision. The road of inference and the employment of intellectual evidence make the first, while the second is the finding of the day of union and the arrival at its degrees. Read by allusion, the command runs: your faith by proof acquired, now strive for the faith of vision. And what is that? Gazing with the eye of response on the Responder, with the eye of solitariness on the Solitary, with the eye of presence on the Present, being near to Allah's nearness by being far from self, present with His generosity by being absent from self. He is not far from the strivers nor absent from the desirers, for He says: "We are nearer to him than the jugular vein" (50:16). The Pīr of the Ṭarīqah prayed it out:

> O Lord! You are found by the souls of the chevaliers, present to the hearts of the rememberers. They give marks of You up close, but You are far beyond that. They fancy You from afar, but You are closer than the spirit. Lovely idol! Are you then my beloved? Now that I look close, You are my spirit.

Another reading runs the verse as: the assent given, now give the realization. The Sharīʿah accepted, now accept the Ḥaqīqah, the reality. Then come the contrasts of the pair, in the record's own parallel:

> What is the Sharīʿah? What the Ḥaqīqah? The Sharīʿah is a lamp, the Ḥaqīqah a burn. The Sharīʿah is a bond, the Ḥaqīqah advice. The Sharīʿah is need, the Ḥaqīqah joy. The Sharīʿah is the outer pillars, the Ḥaqīqah the inner pillars. The Sharīʿah is not having evil, the Ḥaqīqah is not having self. The Sharīʿah is service based on conditions, the Ḥaqīqah exile based on witnessing. The Sharīʿah is by intermediaries, the Ḥaqīqah by unveiling.

Obedience kept and disobedience left aside is the way of the Sharīʿah's folk. The folk of the Ḥaqīqah flee themselves and take joy in oneness. Everlastingness and subsistent bliss are the hope of the former, while the latter boldly busy themselves with the Cupbearer.

### In short

- Faith is commanded to believers for its completion and maintenance, as guidance is sought in every prayer already received.
- The Qur'ān and the previous Scriptures stand together in the one assent, and denial of any pillar of faith is far straying whatever the self-naming.
- The Torah believers who answered the call, headed by ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām, are the occasion.
- Faith by proof is the road, faith by vision the arrival, and the Sharīʿah accepted must lead to the Ḥaqīqah realized, the lamp to the burn.

137.text:
The oscillating soul: "Indeed, those who believed then disbelieved, then believed and again disbelieved" (4:137), "Allah will neither forgive them nor guide them to the ˹Right˺ Way". The passage now details the censure of the hypocrites, and the first verse draws their curve.

### Phrase by phrase

**"believed then disbelieved, then believed and again disbelieved—˺only˺ increasing in disbelief"** describes whoever embraces the faith, reverts, embraces again, reverts again and remains on disbelief, increasing in it until death. Ibn ʿAbbās, in the report through ʿIkrimah, glossed the increase plainly: they remain on disbelief until they die, and Mujāhid said similarly. This is the characteristic of the hypocrites, believing and disbelieving by turns, and that is why their hearts become sealed.

**"Allah will neither forgive them nor guide them to the ˺Right˺ Way"** means no accepted repentance after death, and no deliverance from the plight to the path of correct guidance. Some read the verse over the Jews instead, as Rūḥ al-Maʿānī carries it. They believed, then took to the golden calf and disbelieved. They repented and believed, then rejected the prophethood of Sayyidna ʿĪsā (Jesus) and fell back into disbelief. Finally, refusing the prophethood of Sayyidna Muḥammad ﷺ, they increased the disbelief further. One school renders the curve in names: belief in Moses, disbelief after him, belief in ʿUzayr, disbelief in Christ after him, and then a firm stand of refusal toward Muḥammad ﷺ and the Qur'ān.

Read as a whole, the two halves teach that the repeated return to disbelief strips the very ability to receive true guidance. No door of repentance stays open, and none of believing remains. Otherwise, the definitive texts of the Qur'ān and the Sunnah lay down a general rule: the disbeliever, the kāfir, or the apostate, however hardened, has his past sins forgiven if the repentance he makes is sincere and true. Should such people change and repent, the law of amnesty and forgiveness stands open.

### The alternation as the ruin

The inward reading sees the wavering itself as the ruin. States that rise and fall, rise again and stumble, end sealed in their own unseemliness, struck by the arrows of the decree, the misery of fate their final state. The Real guides them to no purpose and leads them to no good sense.

> Give them tidings of separation without end, fa-bashshirhum bi-l-furqati al-abadiyya, and tell them of punishment uninterrupted, wa-akhbirhum bi-l-ʿuqūbati al-sarmadiyya.

The tussle runs through all of life. In every matter the mind tilts either to the demands of desires or to truth and justice. The tilt to desires denies the faith a person professes, and subservience to truth and justice makes the true Muslim. When truth comes before people, the modest acknowledge and the proud deny, the first response born of īmān, the second of faithlessness. The untrue believer loves worldly honour and prestige, and so gravitates to the like-minded who will add to his glory, even if they be deniers of the truth. He has no interest in those whose association adds nothing to his prestige, even if they be true God-worshippers.

### In short

- The alternating believer ends sealed on disbelief, and the increase is the dying state.
- Jews who cycled through calf, ʿĪsā and the refusal of Muḥammad ﷺ are one reading of the curve.
- Repetition can remove even the ability to repent, though the sincere repentance of any kāfir is otherwise always open.
- The proud tilt toward honour and the like-minded, and the modest tilt toward truth.

138.text:
The grim tidings: "Give good news of a painful punishment to hypocrites" (4:138). The verse names the addressees and the news in one breath.

The verse holds one word of irony and one list of names, and the two together are the whole of the warning.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Give good news"** is the word basharah, deliberately chosen, for everyone looks to some bright word about the future, and these people possess no other news than this.

**"of a painful punishment to hypocrites"** names the addressees, ʿAbdullāh ibn Ubayy and his followers, and every hypocrite after them until the Day of Judgement, with the command to announce it laid on the Prophet ﷺ himself, and the doom reaching into their hearts.

### In short

- The one announcement the hypocrites await is the painful punishment.
- Ibn Ubayy's company and every hypocrite after them are the addressees.

139.text:
The borrowed honour: "who choose disbelievers as allies instead of the believers. Do they seek honour and power through that company? Surely all honour and power belongs to Allah" (4:139). The verse exposes the motive and prices it.

### Phrase by phrase

**"who choose disbelievers as allies instead of the believers"** describes the hypocrites as the disbelievers' supporters in reality, giving them loyalty and friendship in secret. Alone with them, they say that they are with them and only mock the believers by pretending to follow their religion. One gloss names the allies as the Jews, sought for assistance and help.

**"Do they seek honour and power through that company?"** asks after the motive, and the answer dismantles it. The urge comes from the assumption that the outwardly visible influence, power and collective strength of the disbelievers may confer honour. Allah exposes the absurdity: honour is being sought from those who themselves have none. The ʿizzah, might and mastery, belongs to none but Allah, and whatever might anyone holds is given by Him. Gross is the failure of reason here: honour is courted by displeasing its owner and giver, and temporal honour is scrounged through His enemies. The Book says it twice over: "Whosoever desires honor, then to Allah belong all honor" (35:10), and "But honor belongs to Allah, and to His Messenger, and to the believers, but the hypocrites know not" (63:8). The addition of the Messenger and the believers in the verse of sūrat al-Munāfiqūn emphasizes that Allah alone owns real honour and bestows its portions on whom He wills, and since the Messenger and the believers are dear in His sight, honour and mastery are given to them, while the disbelievers and polytheists have none of it to give.

Sayyidna ʿUmar said that whoever seeks honour through human beings is disgraced by Allah, a word preserved by al-Jaṣṣāṣ. The same authority, Abū Bakr al-Jaṣṣāṣ, holds in the Aḥkām al-Qur'ān that the verse forbids seeking honour through friendship with disbelievers and sinners, while seeking honour and power through Muslims is not forbidden, for the verse of sūrat al-Munāfiqūn has made clear that Allah blessed His Messenger and the believers with honour. If the honour meant is the everlasting honour of the life-to-come, its applicability to the Messenger and the believers in the present world is obvious, for that honour never becomes the lot of a disbeliever. If it is honour in the present life, then, barring transitional periods and accidents, the honour and mastery are ultimately the right of Islam and the Muslims alone, as the whole world witnessed while Muslims remained Muslims in the true sense, and as will be seen again in the later period when Muslims reassemble around true Islam under the leadership of Sayyidna ʿĪsā. The weakness of the interim, born of weak faith and sins, does not go against the rule. In the Mustadrak of al-Ḥākim stands the address of Sayyidna ʿUmar to Sayyidna Abū ʿUbaydah, the governor of Syria:

> You were the lowest in numbers and the weakest in strength among the people of the world, then Allah made you exceed in numbers and strength with the grace of Islam. And you were the meanest in status among the people of the world, then Allah raised you in honour with the grace of Islam. So understand this very clearly: if you seek honour from any source other than Allah, Allah will disgrace you.

### The inward question

The inward reading asks the sharper question. To cling to a created being is to take refuge with other than the Protector, leaning on a shelter that never shelters, fallen into a bottomless abyss. Do they desire power from those who have themselves been humbled by the command to Be? How can those with no power extend power to anyone else? Shameless either way, seeking power while humbled by the divine subjugation, or imagining that power can come from anything other than Allah. Whoever seeks something from any direction other than Him finds failure the end of his effort. Power is of two kinds, the eternal power that is an attribute of Allah, and the contingent power He apportions to whom He wills.

### In short

- The secret alliance seeks borrowed honour from those who own none.
- Honour belongs to Allah, His Messenger and the believers, and seeking it from His enemies buys disgrace.
- ʿUmar's warning to Abū ʿUbaydah in Syria states the law for every age.
- The humbled cannot lend power, and the clinger to created beings shelters in a bottomless abyss.

140.text:
The company to leave: "He has already revealed to you in the Book that when you hear Allah's revelations being denied or ridiculed, then do not sit in that company unless they engage in a different topic, or else you will be like them" (4:140). The verse points back to an earlier command and then draws its line in the gathering.

### The earlier command

What was already revealed in the Book is the āyah of sūrat al-Anʿām, revealed in Makkah al-Mukarramah before the hijrah. It says: "And when you see those who engage in false conversation about Our verses by mocking at them, stay away from them" (6:68). Its addition runs: "And if Satan makes you forget, do not sit with the unjust people after the recollection" (6:68). The re-emphasis lands on people who have passed beyond mere sitting into friendship, taking the disbelievers for bearers of honour and wielders of power. The two verses carry the same sense. When a group is engaged in denying and deriding the verses of Allah, sitting with them to participate or observe is ḥarām for as long as the vain exercise lasts. The āyah of al-Anʿām generalizes a little more. Its reference to disputation in the divine verses includes disbelief and mockery, and the distorting of a verse's meaning as well, meanings deduced contrary to the explanation of the Prophet ﷺ and his blessed Companions, or against the consensus of the community. Ibn ʿAbbās, as reported by aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, included within the sense those who explain the Qur'ān erroneously, distort its meaning or invent what is not there. Hence the ruling. The teaching sessions of a person giving meanings contrary to the exegetical authenticity of the righteous early elders may not be attended. The authority is the Qur'ān itself, and attendance is a sin rather than a source of reward. In the Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ, Abū Ḥayyān drew the rule that the sin of saying extends to the hearing. What the tongue may not utter, the ear may not take in willingly. His poetic exhortation runs:

> Protect your ears from hearing the evil, as you protect your tongue from saying it.

### The questions of the gathering

For one who joined such company unknowingly, the rule is immediate departure once it is realised, for the point is not to sit with the unjust people when alerted. When they stop that strain of talk and digress to another topic, the scholars differ. Some hold that the prohibition was for the disparagement and distortion, and stops when they stop, so that sitting is no sin once the talk changes. Others hold the company of such disbelieving, sinning and unjust people incorrect even after the change, the position of Ḥasan al-Baṣrī. The verse of al-Anʿām says not to sit with the unjust people once you remember, and the unjust person remains unjust after the questionable conversation ends, as al-Jaṣṣāṣ argues. Qāḍī Thanāʾullāh Pānipatī found consistency in both views in his Tafsīr al-Mazharī. Once the comments of disbelief, mockery and distortion cease and another topic takes over, unnecessary sitting remains forbidden, while participation prompted by religious contingency or physical need is permissible.

Seclusion is better than bad company. Abū Bakr al-Jaṣṣāṣ said in the Aḥkām al-Qur'ān that a Muslim charged with forbidding evil, on witnessing sin in a gathering, should stop it by force if he has the strength. Lacking strength, he should at the least show displeasure, its lowest degree being to rise and leave. It is for this reason that ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz had some men arrested on the charge of drinking wine. Investigation found one of them fasting, a man who had drunk nothing but sat among the drunkards. He was punished too for the unexplained sitting, a case preserved in the Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ. And the hadith reported at this point in the record runs:

> One who believes in Allah and the Last Day should not sit to dine where liquor is being served.

The rule of leaving is hemmed by one condition: leaving must not entail a sin of one's own. Joining the congregation in the mosque is necessary. Should something contrary to the Sharīʿah start happening there, the congregational prayer is not abandoned over it, simple emotional displeasure being sufficient. The same holds for any gathering whose necessity stands proved. Abandoning duty because of others' sins paves the way for sinners to come and destroy the Sunnah and the Sharīʿah, as Ḥasan al-Baṣrī said. The forms of socialization with disbelieving or falsely-believing people sum up as five. Condescending to their infidelistic assaults is kufr. Showing repugnance when confronted with open disbelief is, without valid excuse, sinfulness. Socializing for some worldly need is allowed. Socializing to disseminate the injunctions of Islam is worship. And socializing under compulsion, exigency or helplessness is excusable.

### Phrase by phrase

**"or else you will be like them"** carries the warning inside the assembly. If, aware of the prohibition, one keeps sitting where the āyahs of Allah are rejected, mocked and denied, and sanctions the conduct, one has joined in the doing and shares the burden. The likeness can be read strictly, that satisfaction with disbelief is disbelief, for liking kufr is nothing but kufr, or more broadly, that by abetting the conspiracy against Islam and Muslims the sitter becomes an accomplice like them.

**"Surely Allah will gather the hypocrites and disbelievers all together in Hell"** closes the file. Just as the hypocrites participate in the kufr of the disbelievers, Allah joins them together in the Fire for eternity, dwelling in torment and punishment, enchained and restrained, drinking boiling water. The glosses name them: the hypocrites of Madinah under ʿAbdullāh ibn Ubayy, the disbelievers of Makkah under Abū Jahl, and the disbelievers of Madinah under Kaʿb. Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān held that this verse abrogated the part of the al-Anʿām verse leaving the exception, while the word of the exception itself stands: "Those who fear Allah, keep their duty to Him and avoid evil, are not responsible for them in any case, but (their duty) is to remind them, that they may have Taqwa" (6:69).

The teaching beneath explains why the command runs so hard. Whenever the call of Allah is addressed to any group, its basis is too strong to be refuted by arguments, so those who refuse it attempt to show its worthlessness by ridicule, heaping contempt to convey that the message is unworthy of acceptance. Such people demonstrate that they do not regard truth as a serious matter, and when people are not serious, arguing is of no use. Silence is better, waiting for the time the hearers are in a state of mind to give attention, and withdrawal from any company where the divine call is held low is itself the sign of seriousness about truth.

### The reason of the heart

The inward reading gives the reason of the heart:

> Do not make neighbours of those alienated in feeling and affection, for the darknesses of their souls extend to your hearts as you seek to inhale the fragrances they refuse.

Whoever sits with a people takes a share of their state. The companion of the intimate becomes intimate, and the companion of the darkened is estranged.

### In short

- The command predates this sūrah, given in Makkah in al-Anʿām, and this verse re-emphasizes it against those who went further into friendship.
- Sitting with mockery of the Book is ḥarām while it lasts, the corrupted tafsīr counts as mockery, and the ears share the tongue's sin.
- The unknowing joiner leaves on realisation, the changed topic divides the scholars, and need or duty may justify staying.
- The sitter becomes the accomplice, and liking kufr is kufr.
- The hypocrites and the disbelievers share one Fire, gathered as they were gathered in unbelief.

141.text:
The watchers: "˹The hypocrites are˺ those who wait to see what happens to you. So if Allah grants you victory, they say ˹to you˺, “Were we not on your side?”" (4:141). The verse draws the portrait of the double party to its finish.

### Phrase by phrase

**"those who wait to see what happens to you"** is the word alladhīna of the verse, substituted in the reading of one school for the same word of verse 139, and it means watching and awaiting the harm that befalls the believers, awaiting the time when the Muslim circumstances and religion dissolve and the state of kufr takes over. They lay in wait for hardship and the turn of events, hoping for misfortunes.

**"So if Allah grants you victory, they say, “Were we not on your side?”"** shows them at the moment of triumph, aid and booty, drawing close to the believers, claiming the same religion and asking a share of the gains.

**"But if the disbelievers have a share ˹of victory˺, they say, “Did we not have the advantage over you, yet we protected you from the believers?”"** shows the other face. The disbelievers gain victory over the believers sometimes, just as occurred during Uḥud, for the messengers are tested and the final victory is theirs. To them the hypocrites say that they helped in secret, divulging secrets, confusing the believers and weakening their resolve until the victory came. They claim the authority to capture and slay, exercised in sparing them, and the defence of them against the believers. The statement strengthens relations with the disbelievers, for the hypocrites pretend friendship with both parties to be safe from harm, out of weak faith and lack of certainty.

**"Allah will judge between ˹all of˺ you on the Day of Judgment"** answers the pretence. He judges by what He knows of them. The shade of Islamic law spread over them in this life, a protection existing only out of Allah's wisdom, deceives no one on that Day. The pretending brings no benefit there, the secrets of souls stand disclosed, the contents of hearts are gathered, the believers enter Paradise and the pretenders the Fire.

**"And Allah will never grant the disbelievers a way over the believers"** is the closing promise, and the reports gather around it. ʿAbdur-Razzāq recorded from Yāsiʿ al-Kindī that a man came to ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib and asked about the āyah, and he said:

> Come closer, come closer. Allah will judge between you on the Day of Resurrection, and He will not grant victory for the disbelievers over the believers.

Ibn Jurayj recorded from ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī that Ibn ʿAbbās dated it to the Day of Resurrection, and as-Suddī recorded the same from Abū Mālik al-Ashjaʿī, adding that the way means proof. It may also carry the meaning of this life, where the disbelievers are unable to exterminate the believers completely, though they sometimes gain victory over some Muslims. The final triumph belongs to the believers in this life and the Hereafter: "Verily, We will indeed make victorious Our Messengers and those who believe in the worldly life" (40:51). This rebuts the hopes of the hypocrites, who wish the believers destroyed and keep loyalty with the disbelievers, and the Book has drawn them already: "And you see those in whose hearts there is a disease of hypocrisy, they hurry to their friendship" (5:52), until the end where they stand regretful (5:52).

The portrait completes itself in the wider teaching. The hypocrite is outwardly religious and inwardly irreligious. Without principles, he watches for opportunities to turn events to his advantage, associating with any group that may help realise his worldly ambitions, believers or deniers alike. Into whichever gathering he goes, he speaks to please everybody. Worldly convenience associates him at times with the believers, yet he is no well-wisher of theirs. True believers, by their very existence, become a criterion of truth in a society, so those standing on false religiosity want such criteria demolished. Their mischief runs in this world alone, the believers being safe from it in the Hereafter. The hypocrite is bracketed with the deniers, for in Allah's judgement there is no difference between outward religiosity and blatant irreligiosity. Both states are identical in reality, and what matters to Allah is the inward state, not the outward appearance.

### The anatomy of the double

The inward reading adds the anatomy. Ikhlāṣ, sincerity in the truest sense, they lacked, and true conviction, ʿaqīda, they had never tasted, so their character differed from those who submitted within the decree, and the submitted and the disbelievers are not the same. The people of the Real must be wary of them and stay aloof. Then comes the beautiful expression of sufficiency, that Allah will never grant the disbelievers a way over the believers, an all-encompassing statement. Their deception, turned back on its authors, and their plotting, reserved for requital:

> The evil of their deception is diverted back to them, fa-inna wabāla kaydihim ilayhim maṣrūfun, and the requital for their plotting is reserved for them, wa-jazāʾa makrihim ʿalayhim mawqūfun.

And the two verdicts:

> The right and true reality, its people are aided from the power of the Real, wa-l-ḥaqqu min qibali al-ḥaqqi subḥānihi manṣūrun ahluhu, and the false, its foundation is uprooted through His help, mujtaththun aṣluhu.

### In short

- The watchers lay in wait for misfortune, claiming either side as fortune turns, safe in both camps and true to neither.
- The shade of Islamic law deceives them only in this life, for the Day of Judgement discloses the secrets of souls.
- ʿAlī, Ibn ʿAbbās and Abū Mālik al-Ashjaʿī carry the promise, and the way of the disbelievers over the believers never opens, in this life's final reckoning or the next.
- The believers are the criterion the false want demolished, and the deceived schemers find their own deceit returned upon them.

142.text:
The counterfeit worship: "Surely the hypocrites seek to deceive Allah, but He outwits them. When they stand up for prayer, they do it half-heartedly only to be seen by people" (4:142). The passage now draws the hypocrite's portrait from the inside, beginning with the deception that cannot work.

### Phrase by phrase

**"the hypocrites seek to deceive Allah"** cannot succeed, for there is no doubt that Allah is never deceived, having perfect knowledge of the secrets and what the hearts conceal. The attempt itself comes of their ignorance, scarce knowledge and weak minds. Once successful in deceiving people, with Islamic law as a cover of safety, they imagine a like standing with Allah on the Day of Resurrection. On that Day they will swear to Him they were on the path of righteousness, thinking the oath will benefit them. One gloss names them again, ʿAbdullāh ibn Ubayy and his followers, disbelieving in Him and opposing Him in secret while thinking they deceive Him. The beginning of sūrat al-Baqarah has said it: "They think to deceive Allah and those who believe" (2:9).

**"but He outwits them"** means the luring further into injustice and misguidance, and the prevention of the truth in this life and on the Day of Resurrection. The Book shows the scene: "On the Day when the hypocrites men and women will say to the believers: Wait for us! Let us get something from your light! It will be said: Go back to your rear! Then seek a light!" (57:13), until "And worst indeed is that destination" (57:15). A hadith states it briefly:

> Whoever wants to be heard of, Allah will make him heard of, and whoever wants to be seen, Allah will show him.

**"they do it half-heartedly only to be seen by people"** describes their conduct with the most honoured, best and righteous act of worship, the ṣalāh. They stand in laziness because they neither truly intend it nor believe in it, have no humility in it and do not understand it, and that is the outward attitude alone. The heart behind it has no sincerity, the showing off aimed at closeness to the watchers. From the prayers that can be hidden, the ʿIshāʾ and the Dawn, both prayed in darkness, they are often away. In the Two Ṣaḥīḥs, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said of them:

> The heaviest prayers on the hypocrites are the ʿIshāʾ and Dawn prayers. If they know their rewards, they will attend them even if they have to crawl. I was about to order someone to pronounce the adhan for the prayer, then order someone to lead the prayer for the people, then order some men to collect fire-wood, then I would burn the houses around men who did not attend the compulsory congregational prayer.

Another narration adds the pull of the table: a meat-covered bone, or a pair of rib-morsels, would have brought any of them in. It adds, too, that only the women and children in the houses kept the homes from being burned around their occupants.

**"hardly remembering Allah at all"** means that during the prayer they feel no humbleness and pay no attention to what they recite, inattentive and jesting, avoiding the good they were meant to receive. Imām Mālik reported, through al-ʿAlāʾ ibn ʿAbdur-Raḥmān, from Anas ibn Mālik, the word of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ:

> This is the prayer of the hypocrite, this is the prayer of the hypocrite, this is the prayer of the hypocrite. He sits watching the sun until when it goes down between the two horns of the devil, he stands up and pecks out four rakʿahs, without remembering Allah during them except little.

Muslim, at-Tirmidhī and an-Nasāʾī also recorded it, and at-Tirmidhī called it ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ. One note draws the line of the censure. The laziness rebuked here is doctrinal laziness, the sloth toward the articles of faith born of lacking true conviction. Laziness despite correct belief stands outside the censure, and if it comes of some excuse, sickness, fatigue or sleepiness, it is not even blameworthy. Without excuse, it is.

The inward reading sees the trick and its mirage. Hypocritical trickery displays conformity outwardly on the path, while the creed inwardly clings to association. The trickery of the Real toward them is the imagined salvation they count as entitlement. When the covering lifts, the certainty arrives: what they took for drink, sharāb, was a mirage, sarāb, for "there will appear to them from Allah that which they had never reckoned" (39:47). And the sign of hypocrisy stands exposed: energy when one can be seen by others, resolve lost when the opportunity to be seen passes.

### The religion beneath

The teaching beneath names the religion of such people. Those who have not surrendered themselves to Allah succumb to worldly interests, associating with anyone, religious or irreligious, by whom those interests are served. Their words and deeds, however religious in appearance, aim not at pleasing Allah but at showing others they too are believers, for opportunism is their real religion, though they are at pains to appear God-worshipping.

### In short

- The deception of Allah is attempted under the cover of the law and answered by the lifting of every cover on the Day.
- The heaviest prayers on the hypocrites are those prayed in darkness, and the burning of houses was only withheld for the women and children inside.
- The hypocrite's prayer is pecked out at the sun's setting, with no remembrance in it.
- The laziness rebuked is doctrinal, not the fatigue of the faithful, and the mirage awaits every entitlement imagined.

143.text:
The wavering: "belonging neither to these ˹believers˺ nor those ˹disbelievers˺" (4:143). The verse completes the portrait with the stance that belongs to neither camp.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Torn between belief and disbelief"** names the swaying. The hypocrites belong neither to the believers inwardly or outwardly, nor to the disbelievers inwardly or outwardly, keeping the believers outwardly and the disbelievers inwardly.

**"belonging neither to these ˹believers˺ nor those ˺disbelievers˺"** covers the fits of doubt, leaning toward these sometimes and toward those sometimes: "Whenever it flashes for them, they walk therein, and when darkness covers them, they stand still" (2:20). Mujāhid read the two parties as the Companions of Muḥammad ﷺ and the Jews. Ibn Jarīr recorded from Ibn ʿUmar that the Prophet ﷺ said:

> The example of the hypocrite is the example of the sheep wandering between two herds, sometimes she goes to one of them, and sometimes the other, confused over whom she should follow.

Muslim also recorded it. **"And whoever Allah leaves to stray, you will never find for them a way"** closes the verse. The word of the Book runs: for him you will find no walī, a guiding friend, to lead him to the right path (18:17), for whomsoever Allah sends astray, none can guide him. Those led astray from the paths of safety never find a guide to direct them or a saviour. There is none who can resist the decision of Allah. Of what He does He is never asked, while they all will be asked.

### The inward price

The inward reading adds the price of the wavering. The least worthy among created beings are those who remove the vest of servanthood and have not found the way to true freedom. They hold not even a sliver of precious nobility, nor an agreeable way of living, ʿīshatu ḥanīyya, in their heedlessness.

### In short

- The wavering heart keeps a foot in each camp and belongs to neither.
- The sheep between two herds is the standing image of it, and the light comes and goes for such people.
- Whom Allah sends astray has no guiding friend, and the vest of servanthood once removed leaves neither nobility nor ease.

144.text:
The proof offered: "O believers! Do not take disbelievers as allies instead of the believers. Would you like to give Allah solid proof against yourselves" (4:144). The command returns with the reason attached.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Do not take disbelievers as allies instead of the believers"** forbids the whole alliance, the friendship and association with the disbelievers, the advising of them, the intimacy with them, and the exposing of the believers' secrets to them. The Book has said it with the warning:

> Let not the believers take the disbelievers as friends instead of the believers.

No help from Allah comes to whoever does it, in any way, save under a feared danger, and Allah warns you against Himself, meaning His punishment.

**"Would you like to give Allah solid proof against yourselves"** asks the question that turns the choice sober. The manifest Sultan is the proof that warrants receiving the torment, as Ibn ʿAbbās said, for the word Sultan in the Qur'ān means proof, and his statement has an authentic chain. So also read ʿIkrimah with Mujāhid, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk with Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, as-Suddī, an-Naḍr ibn al-ʿArabī and Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Quraẓī. One gloss reads the address over the outward believers, ʿAbdullāh ibn Ubayy and his followers, seeking power from the Jews, the proof becoming a clear reason for action against them.

### The gravest of sins in the precepts of love

The inward reading weighs the friendship above the other sins. The admonition was repeated and the command to separate from enemies confirmed, to strengthen the prohibition and end every excuse. The heading above carries its finding. The friendship was warned against over and above other oppositional acts because it involves a preference for something other than the object of adoration. Preferring another to the beloved is the gravest of sins in the precepts of love. When the heart becomes engaged with others in the place reserved for the Real, the outcome cannot but be bad, and the punishment promised is to be left to one's own devices and to what was chosen in siding with the disbelievers. What a wretched substitution. It is the same with all who remain apart from the Real: He leaves them with created beings, doubling the affliction by their remaining apart from the Real and remaining with created beings, and both are severe punishments.

### In short

- Alliance, advice, intimacy and exposed secrets are all inside the prohibition.
- The Sultan given is a proof, and by it the torment is warranted.
- The friendship is graver than other opposition, for it sets another beloved in the place of the Beloved, and the punishment is to be left with created beings.

145.text:
The depth: "Surely the hypocrites will be in the lowest depths of the Fire" (4:145). The sentence of the wavering is pronounced.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Surely the hypocrites will be in the lowest depths of the Fire"** sentences ʿAbdullāh ibn Ubayy and his followers, with every hypocrite after them, for their evil, betrayal and scheming against the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions. Ad-darak al-asfal, the lowest depth, means the bottom of the Fire, as Ibn ʿAbbās said. Other scholars held that the Fire has ever lower depths, just as Paradise has ever higher grades, the placing to occur on the Day of Resurrection, due to their tremendous kufr.

**"you will never find for them any helper"** names the abandonment. Ibn Jarīr recorded from ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd that they will be inside coffins of Fire that surround them, closed and sealed. Asked about the hypocrites, Ibn Masʿūd said that they will be placed in coffins made of fire and shut into them at the Fire's lowest depth, with no helper found to save them from the misery and the painful torment.

The inward reading reads the depth downward into the heart. The hypocrite is not one sincerely seeking protective trust, for īmān, being true to the trust, is what brings protection, and the one who holds true to it is saved by it from the Fire. That which causes the falling to the lowest level cannot be called faith. It is verified, it is said, by the words that Allah is the best of schemers (3:54), said again in the other place (8:30), His scheming above all scheming. Once the hypocrites' scheming with the believers stood exposed, their punishment ran more severe than that of the open disbelievers. Of the tradition that each meets Allah in the state he kept, it is said that He transfers them from the present state to one like it: lowest in being cut off today, lowest in the Fire tomorrow. The depth of their cutting off now is the name of īmān they bear while holding not even a sliver from Allah, the greatest of afflictions. Of the reason for the level, one saying is the company they kept here with the greatest name of Allah without respect, and another, the presence without propriety in what they said, and by this they were driven far away.

### In short

- The lowest depth is the bottom, and the coffins of fire are closed and sealed on their occupants.
- What saves from the Fire is the trust held true, and the name of faith without a sliver of it is the greatest affliction.
- Company with the greatest name, kept without respect or propriety, ends in the farthest removal.

146.text:
The door out: "except those who repent, mend their ways, hold fast to Allah, and are sincere in their devotion to Allah; they will be with the believers" (4:146). After the sentence comes the exemption, for the sense of fear generated by an impending punishment usually becomes the reason for early repentance in a good-natured person.

### Phrase by phrase

**"except those who repent"** opens the exemption. Whoever among the hypocrites repents in this life finds the repentance and the sorrow accepted, if it is sincere and followed by righteous deeds, all the while depending on the Lord. The showing off is replaced with sincerity, so that the good deeds benefit, even if they were minute.

**"they will be with the believers"** places them, on the Day of Resurrection, among the company they once feigned, and **"Allah will grant the believers a great reward"** crowns the company.

The statement about making the faith pure for Allah carries the meaning of sincerity. A deed acceptable to Allah must be free of hypocrisy and exclusively for His sake and pleasure, and the jurists have given the meaning of the mukhlis, the sincere one, in one line:

> A sincere person is one who acts for Allah alone and does not like that people praise him for it. One rendering hears the holding fast as the holding of the belief in Allah's divine Oneness inwardly, and the purity as the purifying of that belief for Him alone.

### The preposition of accompaniment

The inward reading counts the conditions. Not all of them are ordinarily required to repent of a sin. For hypocrites renouncing hypocrisy they are necessary, because of the stubborn nature of their disbelief. For those who meet the conditions He said "with the believers," the preposition of accompaniment rather than of belonging. The allusion is to an imperfection of rank, even after the sincere amendment of the past. Regarding its meaning they have recited: apologies are easy, and what a difference between apologies and thankfulness. The repentance here means renouncing the hypocrisy, amending in the sincerity of faith, and holding fast to Allah by absolving the self of its own power and strength, bearing witness to the blessing of God in the guidance and the deliverance. The religion is made purely God's when the deliverance is regarded as His grace, not the earning of the newfound faith nor the credit of the renounced past.

### In short

- The exemption stands open in this life: repentance, amendment, reliance and purity replace the showing off with sincerity.
- The sincere one acts for Allah alone and dislikes the praise of people for it.
- The preposition of accompaniment keeps the rank imperfect, and the deliverance is grace, not earning.

147.text:
The question that clears the account: "Why should Allah punish you if you are grateful and faithful? Allah is ever Appreciative, All-Knowing" (4:147). The verse stands among those that evoke hope.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Why should Allah punish you if you are grateful and faithful?"** is a denial in the form of a question. Allah is too Rich to need anyone, and He only punishes the servants for their sins. He would not punish the thankful who correct their actions and believe inwardly in His divine Oneness, in Him and His Messenger.

**"Allah is ever Appreciative, All-Knowing"** gives the reason twice over. He appreciates those who appreciate Him, has knowledge of those whose hearts believe in Him, and gives them perfect reward.

### The two tokens

The inward reading unfolds the two tokens. He has appointed two things as protection from punishment, thankfulness, shukr, and belief, īmān, and they are simple and light qualities. Thankfulness is an assertion, a word said, and belief is a state. When the words and the state both please Him, He makes the way easy for the servant. Praise is sound only from one who is faithful, for it is an act of willing obedience, and the obedience of those without faith is not genuine. The belief meant is the belief of the end, for salvation belongs to those who at the end of the day believe, so that the meaning is: no abiding chastisement for the thankful in their present state who believe in the end. It is said that the thankful believer attests one thing above all: salvation comes through God, not through the thankfulness or the belief. Thankfulness, it is said, is the witnessing of the blessing from God, and belief the seeing of God within it, as if He said that whoever knows the blessing as from God should not let its witness cut him off from the Giver. The word rendered Appreciative, All-Knowing reads in the other form, Allāh shākirun ʿalīmun, and the rendering of the first reads shākiran ʿalīman. His thankfulness means the commending of the servant and the bearing of witness to him in what he does. The true sense of thankfulness is praise of the beautiful actor, the muḥsin, by the mention of his beautiful action, the iḥsān. The servant gives thanks to God by praising Him for His beautiful action toward him, which is His blessing, and the Lord gives thanks to the servant by praising him for his beautiful action, which is his willing obedience.

### In short

- Punishment answers sin alone, and gratitude with faith closes the account.
- Thankfulness is a word, belief a state, and both together make the way easy.
- Thankfulness sees the blessing, belief sees the Giver in it, and the Appreciative commends the beautiful act of the obedient.

148.text:
The exception of the wronged: "Allah does not like negative thoughts to be voiced" (4:148), "except by those who have been wronged. Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing". The verse permits one voice and discourages the rest.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Allah does not like negative thoughts to be voiced"** means, in the explanation of Ibn ʿAbbās, that no one should invoke Allah against anyone else unless wronged, in which case the invocation against the wrongdoer is allowed, though patience is better.

**"except by those who have been wronged"** draws the permission's line. Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī commented that one should not invoke curses against whoever wronged him, but rather make the supplication:

> O Allah! Help me against him and take my right from him.

In another narration he allowed the wronged one to invoke without transgressing the limits. ʿAbdul-Karīm ibn Mālik al-Jazarī drew the line of retaliation: a curse may be answered with a curse, but a lie may not be answered with a lie, for "whoever takes revenge after he has suffered wrong, for such there is no way of blame against them" (42:40). Abū Dāwūd recorded from Abū Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> Whatever words are uttered by those who curse each other, then he who started it will carry the burden thereof, unless the one who was wronged transgresses the limit.

The occasions set the verse in life. One record ties it to Abū Bakr, who was verbally abused by a man, and another to a man who sought hospitality with some people and, receiving no proper hospitality from them, complained, whereupon the verse came down giving him dispensation to complain. The permission granted here is bounded in the very next breath, for the following verse, 149, opens the higher door beyond it.

### The etiquette of correction

The teaching beneath sets the etiquette of correction. In life one comes to know one's shortcomings and faults through the people around one, but Allah disapproves of public criticism that defames the person. Everyone has the right to give counsel with the motive of reform, but the counselling should be done in private, not in public, and if something must be said publicly to check a vice from spreading, the wrongdoer should not be named, the reference kept in general terms. Day in and day out Allah overlooks people's crimes, and His servants too should follow that divine principle. The oppressed may tell of the wrong, yet patience and forgiveness remain better. The victim thereby shows he cares for the loss of the Hereafter above any loss here, the thought of the greater loss rendering the small one insignificant.

The inward reading deepens the etiquette. What the wronged one says about his wronger is not evil in the true sense, by the permission of God, yet letting the matter drop is the good thing, for the requital of an evil is an evil like it, and whoever pardons and reconciles has his reward with God (42:40). Whoever knows his Protector hears grows ashamed of free voice for the urgings of the lower self. The evil out loud, it is said, is what a person hears within himself when he thinks ill of others, and the elect take responsibility in their inward thoughts for what, heard from ordinary people, might be held against them. On the exception the readings divide: some say not even the wronged one, and others that the wronged one has the right to mention who intentionally wronged him. Those who do not prefer the praise of the Real over defaming fellow creatures are cheated of the present moment, and those who look at created beings with the eye of connection to the Real see servants of God and speak no ill of them.
