One man said to his companion that out of respect he would bear him the lowliest service, beyond what he would bear for his own son, and when such commitment stands between human beings, the servant's regard for refined behaviour toward his Protector is worthier still. Among ordinary people, the utterance of evil out loud is their description of Allah in ways for which they have no permission or divine sanction.

### In short

- The wronged may raise the voice, by supplication, complaint or equal retaliation, and never with a lie.
- The beginner of the cursing carries the burden, and patience remains better than all permission.
- Abū Bakr's abuse and the refused guest set the verse in life.
- Counsel goes private, public correction stays unnamed, and the elect answer even for thoughts.

149.text:
The higher door: "Whether you reveal or conceal a good or pardon an evil" (4:149), "surely Allah is Ever-Pardoning, Most Capable". The two verses together give a law to eradicate injustice and oppression from the world.

### The law of the two verses

This is no dictatory formulation of the usual worldly kind. It is a law of persuasion and awe. The victim of injustice may protest against the perpetrator or go to a court of law to seek redress, the basic demand of justice and a source of the eradication of crimes. Alongside the option stands the restriction of sūrat an-Naḥl: if a person inflicts injustice on you, you may retaliate for it, on condition that the retaliation not exceed the unjust aggression, for else it is you who turn unjust (16:126). An injustice, in short, is never returned by another injustice, and the retaliation to injustice, where made, runs through justice alone. With this course comes the instruction that revenge, though permissible, is not the better part, for observing ṣabr, patience, and forgiving is better.

The verse also teaches that the oppressed person who goes about complaining of his injustice is not counted under backbiting, ghibah, which is ḥarām, for the oppressor himself gave the victim the opening to complain. On the one hand, then, the Holy Qur'ān allows the option of even retaliation, and on the other, by teaching the oppressed high morals, forgiveness and forgetting, and by setting the great gain of the life-to-come before him, it persuades the sacrifice of a little of the legitimate right. To do good openly or keep it secret, or to overlook an evil deed, is better, for Allah is All-Forgiving, All-Powerful. Primarily the verse concerns the forgiving of injustice, but by mentioning the doing of good, openly or secretly, the hint is given that the overlooking is great, and whoever elects it becomes deserving of the mercy and forgiveness of Almighty Allah.

The ending carries its own lesson. Allah is powerful in the absolute sense, able to punish whomsoever He wills, yet He is All-Forgiving. A human being, who does not have much power or choice, may simply lack the capability of taking revenge, and for such a person overlooking and forgiving are far more desirable. The principle of the Qur'ān thus upholds justice by permitting equal retaliation and exhorts the aggrieved to forgive and forgo, and the result is described in the Book: "Good and evil are not equal. Repel evil with what is better, and your enemy will become like a close friend" (41:34). Court decisions and revenge do play a role in checking injustice, but the parties to a dispute are usually left saddled with long-term grievances and abhorrence that breed future disputes. The lesson in morality of the Qur'ān patches up the quarrelling parties instead, till even old enmities change into close and lasting friendships. From here the passage moves to verses 150, 151 and 152, where the verdict is given that whoever believes in Allah but not in His messengers, or believes in some and disbelieves in others, is no believer but an open disbeliever, with no road to salvation in the Hereafter.

### The praise of the Throne and the pardon

Among the attributes of Allah stands this one, that His servants are forgiven and pardoned by Him though He is able to punish, and the word of the heavens matches. It was reported that some of the angels who carry the Throne praise Him in the words:

> All praise is due to You for Your forbearing, even though You have perfect knowledge.

Others supplicate:

> All praise is due to You for Your forgiving, even though You have perfect ability to punish. An authentic hadith states:

> No charity shall ever decrease wealth, and Allah will only increase the honour of a servant who pardons, and he who is humble for Allah's sake, then Allah will elevate his grade.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Whether you reveal or conceal a good"** reads two ways in the inward record. To show good is to take on the good manners found in the law, the ādāb of the sharīʿa, and to conceal it is to recognize the truth in the precepts of the deeper reality.

**"or pardon an evil"** is to adopt from Allah what He has entrusted, in the most beautiful ways of behaving.

**"surely Allah is Ever-Pardoning, Most Capable"** means He is Pardoning of your defects and Powerful in causing you to attain what you love and to recognize the true nature of what you seek. It is said that whoever shows good becomes an example for humankind in what he practises and proposes, from which others may be guided. It is said that whoever conceals it, content with only His knowing it, safeguards himself from the evils of affectation and trusts that whoever acts for Him will be seen and known by Him. Whoever pardons abandons what the lower self calls to, and Allah grants His pardon for what he does, holding also the power to afflict with what the oppressor is afflicted. This warns against heedlessness in witnessing the favour, and alerts to the seeking of refuge from the loss of protection, ʿiṣma, and from abandonment into discord and trial. The final counsel runs in threes. Well-doers are shown good outwardly. Those who spare you their evil receive loyalty and inward prayer. The badly-doing are pardoned with generosity and graciousness. The pardon found from Allah will match what you yourself do, for your sins are the more numerous. He has the power to give you in favour and blessings what vengeance can never attain.

### In short

- Protest and court are permitted, retaliation is hemmed by equality, and patience with forgiveness stands above both.
- The complaint of the oppressed is not backbiting, for the oppressor himself opened the door.
- The pardoner is honoured, the humble elevated, and the angels of the Throne praise the forbearing knowledge and the able forgiveness.
- Repelling evil with what is better turns an enemy into a close friend, and the old enmities of the pardoning become friendships that last.

150.text:
The divided faith: "Surely those who deny Allah and His messengers and wish to make a distinction between Allah and His messengers, saying, “We believe in some and disbelieve in others,” desiring to forge a compromise" (4:150). The verse gives the verdict on the pickers and choosers among the believers of old.

### Phrase by phrase

**"those who deny Allah and His messengers"** names the Jews and the Christians, who differentiate between Allah and His messengers regarding faith, believing in some prophets and rejecting others. The Jews believe in the prophets except ʿĪsā (Jesus) and Muḥammad ﷺ. The Christians accept the line of prophets yet reject its Final and Seal, the most honoured among them. The Samirah, the Samaritans, believe in no prophet after Yūshaʿ (Joshua), the successor of Mūsā (Moses) ibn ʿImrān. The Majūs are said to believe only in a prophet called Zoroaster, though they do not believe in the law he brought, casting it behind them. One gloss names Kaʿb and his followers for the words, and the Makkans too belong in the pattern, for they believed in the prophethood of Ibrāhīm (Abraham) yet would not acknowledge the Prophet of their own time.

**"and wish to make a distinction between Allah and His messengers"** means in faith, in prophethood and in surrender to Allah, dividing between Him and them by believing in Him but not in them.

**"saying, “We believe in some and disbelieve in others”"** exposes the method. They follow their desires, lusts and the practices of their forefathers, for they have no proof for the distinction, and there is none. Whoever rejects a single prophet out of envy, bias and personal whim has disbelieved in all of them, since mankind is required to believe in every prophet Allah sent to the people of the earth, and the rejection of one only demonstrates that the professed faith in the others is not valid, but an act of following desire and whim.

**"desiring to forge a compromise"** means seeking a way in between, a religion between disbelief and faith. All such attempts amount to a middle course between truth-worship and self-worship, so that Paradise is secured without any sacrifice of self-interest. The prophets of the past were all faced in their times with the same hostile reactions now faced by the Arab prophet, yet the past prophethood, once time has done its work, is absorbed into the thinking of a person from birth, while the prophet of the day appears an ordinary human being and a controversial figure. Believing in him requires a complete change of mindset, a new intellectual journey, a finding of Allah again at the level of awareness. Belief in a past prophet continues the forefathers' ways, a faith by birth and not by choice, and what matters in the eyes of Allah is the faith adopted by choice.

### Salvation depends on Islam

The verdict exposes the rudderless and crooked ways of those who, to appear tolerant in their dealings with other faiths, would present their religion and religious beliefs as gifts on a platter, telling people of other faiths, contrary to the clear injunctions of the Qur'ān and Sunnah, that Muslims do not think salvation depends on Islam alone, that a Jew could keep his creed and a Christian hers and both look forward to salvation. Islam stands unmatched in justice, fairness, sympathy, goodwill and tolerance toward non-Muslims. But favours are made within the limits of one's rights and possessions, and religious principles and articles of faith are not property to donate. Islam is generous in tolerance and equally firm in the defence of its frontiers, absolving itself decisively from all forms of disbelief while providing full protection to the national hallmarks of others. Had Islam believed in salvation through every religion, it would have had no right to stress the spreading of its message to the limit of staking property and life. The coming of the noble Prophet ﷺ with the glorious Qur'ān would be rendered redundant, and the entire jihād carried out by him and the rightly-guided caliphs would become nothing but the lust for more land.

Some have fallen into doubt by misreading verse 62 of sūrat al-Baqarah, which says that those who believed, and those who were Jews and Christians and Sabeans, whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day and does good deeds, has a reward with the Lord. That verse gives no full detail of what constitutes faith, and its incomplete study misled readers into thinking belief in the prophets no condition of salvation. The Qur'ān has its own terminology, in which belief in Allah, to be acceptable, must stand in conjunction with belief in the Prophet, for even the Satan admits that there is a God and that He is One. The clarification is the Book's own: "So, if they believe in the like of what you believe in, they have certainly found the right path" (2:137). The faith is valid only as the faith of the Muslims, the belief in the Prophet indispensably joined to the belief in Allah. Whoever turns away is in antagonism, with Allah sufficient against them. The verse under discussion has already declared that whoever rejects even one of the prophets of Allah is an avowed disbeliever, a kāfir, and a recipient of the punishment of Hell.

The inward reading hears the watch behind the sentence. To the shamefulness of their disbelief they added the blameworthy actions enumerated here, and the chastisement is doubled as requital for the sin, "that you will know that He is ever on the watch" (89:14) over those who act in corrupt and harmful ways.

### In short

- Jews, Christians, Samaritans and Majūs each hold a list of prophets and cut it short, and the rejection of one prophet is the disbelief of them all.
- The compromise sought is a way between faith and disbelief, securing Paradise without the sacrifice of self-interest.
- Salvation depends on Islam, and the faith of the forefathers by birth does not equal the faith of choice.
- Verse 62 of al-Baqarah speaks in the Book's own terminology, where belief in Allah includes the Prophet, and the doubters were answered by 2:137.

151.text:
The verdict: "they are indeed the true disbelievers. And We have prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment" (4:151). The verse closes the case of the divided faith with its name and its sentence.

### Phrase by phrase

**"they are indeed the true disbelievers"** means that their disbelief in the very prophet they claim to believe in is clear, for the claimed faith in a certain messenger is not true. Had they truly believed in him, they would have believed in the other messengers, especially when the other messenger has a stronger proof of his truthfulness, or at least they would have striven hard to acquire knowledge of his truth. Disbelieving in some of the messengers is like disbelief in Allah and all His messengers, and the verdict names the whole company, the Jews and the other disbelievers, each an avowed kāfir.

**"And We have prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment"** is the just requital for belittling the prophets they disbelieved in, ignoring what the prophets brought to them from Allah, out of interest in the insignificant possessions of this world. Or their behaviour followed their disbelief in the Prophet after full awareness of his truth, as the Jewish rabbis did in the time of Muḥammad, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Envy of the great prophethood Allah gave him drove them to denial, defiance, enmity and war. Allah sent humiliation upon them in this life, to be followed by disgrace in the Hereafter: "And they were covered with humiliation and misery, and they drew on themselves the wrath of Allah" (2:61), in this life and the next. The punishment abases its bearers, and one reading adds that it is severe.

### The pattern of the rabbis

Their behaviour, in one reading, followed the disbelief of the rabbis who knew his truth. That is the gravest form of the pattern, for the belittling was not of ignorance but against knowledge, and the humiliation sent upon them in this life answers it measure for measure.

### In short

- The divided faith is kufr outright, and the claimed belief in a listed prophet is no belief at all.
- The humiliation answers the belittling, and the rabbis who envied and fought the Prophet ﷺ carry it in both worlds, as sūrat al-Baqarah has said.

152.text:
The undivided faith: "As for those who believe in Allah and His messengers—accepting all; rejecting none—He will surely give them their rewards. And Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful" (4:152). The verdict on the dividers is matched by the verdict on the whole-hearted.

### Phrase by phrase

**"those who believe in Allah and His messengers—accepting all; rejecting none"** refers to the ummah of Muḥammad ﷺ, who believe in every Book Allah has revealed and every prophet Allah has sent, declaring His Oneness, associating no partner with Him, and making no distinction between any of the messengers as the disbelievers do. One gloss names ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām and his followers. The Book draws their portrait: "The Messenger believes in what has been revealed to him from his Lord, and so do the believers. Each believes in Allah, His angels, His Books and His Messengers. We make no distinction between any of His Messengers" (2:285).

**"He will surely give them their rewards"** means the great rewards, the tremendous favour and the handsome bounty prepared for them, because of their faith in Allah and His messengers.

**"And Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful"** extends to their sin, if they have any, Forgiving toward His friends, Merciful toward those who obey Him, forgiving of anyone of them who dies, Merciful toward whoever dies in a state of repentance.

The reading of the whole passage is sealed by the rule of the Book itself. The concluding verse, printed with the reference 15:22 in the record, reaffirms that the Hereafter belongs to those who believe in Him and in all His prophets, and the Prophet ﷺ said that one part of the Qur'ān explains the other, so no one may explain the Qur'ān in any way contrary to the explanation the Qur'ān itself gives.

### The covenant at full width

The inward reading sets the condition at full width. Belief in all the messengers, with confirmation of everything commanded, earned the acceptance and the beautiful recompense. Letting go of one's faith in some individuals is letting go of the faith of whole time periods. Allah accepts no faith that omits the messages that came before, and none that omits what the faith demands, for He made that the condition of its actualization and its perfection. The allusion is that whoever does not wholeheartedly enter the covenant holds not so much as a sliver of the reality of communion. The Prophet ﷺ said:

> The pilgrimage is the day of ʿArafa. Anyone who traverses the distance, even if he comes from a deep ravine, but then holds back even a little from ʿArafāt, has not experienced the pilgrimage.

And he said:

> The servant who has contracted with his master to be freed is still a servant to the last dirham.

### In short

- The ummah of the Prophet ﷺ believes in every Book and every prophet, and the reward prepared is great, the bounty handsome.
- One part of the Qur'ān explains the other, and the concluding verse, as the record numbers it, seals the rule.
- The covenant must be entered whole, for the pilgrim who holds back a little of ʿArafāt has no pilgrimage, and the faith that omits a message or a duty has no acceptance.

153.text:
The impossible demand: "The People of the Book demand that you ˹O Prophet˺ bring down for them a revelation in writing from heaven" (4:153). The verse sets the demands of the Jews beside the demands their fathers made of Mūsā, and the comparison is not in their favour.

### Phrase by phrase

**"The People of the Book demand that you ˹O Prophet˺ bring down for them a revelation in writing from heaven"** records what the Jewish chiefs asked of the Holy Prophet ﷺ: a book sent down from heaven, all written there, like the Torah that came to Mūsā, and then they would believe him. Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Quraẓī, as-Suddī and Qatādah say they wanted a heavenly book lowered to them in the manner of the Tawrah given to Mūsā. Ibn Jurayj adds that they wanted books sent down bearing the names of persons among them and attesting that he was truly a messenger. One report names Kaʿb and his followers, and another says they asked for a book containing all that was good for them and all that was bad, their rewards and their punishments. The occasion is reported plainly: they said to the Prophet ﷺ that if he was truly a prophet, he should bring them an actual book from heaven as Mūsā did, and the verse was revealed about them. The demand was a device to drag and stall, born of stubbornness, defiance, rejection and disbelief, for their chronic urge to take an opposite stand made them offer one excuse after another. By revealing the verse, Allah let His Prophet ﷺ see the real state of affairs, giving him comfort and peace of mind against a people used to harassing the prophets of Allah. The disbelievers of Quraysh asked for similar things, as Sūrat al-Isrāʾ relates: "And they say: We shall not believe in this Qur'ān" (17:90).

**"They demanded what is even greater than this from Moses, saying, “Make Allah visible to us!”"** reaches back to the fathers who went further still. Their forefathers said, "O Mūsā! We shall never believe in you until we see Allah plainly" (2:55), demanding with their own eyes a sight of Him, and a thunderbolt from heaven destroyed them for their wickedness, their rejection of Mūsā and their audacity toward Allah. The event is explained in Sūrat al-Baqarah: they were struck by the bolt while they looked, then raised up after their death so that they might be grateful. The asking itself was blameworthy, for they impudently demanded the vision, and there was no excuse for it after the miracles had come to them. Their seeking of the vision carried no wish for instruction, no wish to confirm a faith, and no intensity of longing drove them to it. It showed a lack of manners. Even if the system of nature were altered to show them the realities, the display would last only a time, and the freedom that led them to rebelliousness would go on misusing itself as before.

**"So a thunderbolt struck them for their wrongdoing"** means the Fire that burnt them, death seizing them as punishment when they harassed Mūsā with the demand.

**"Then they took the calf for worship after receiving clear signs"** refers to the al-Bayyināt, the tremendous miracles and unequivocal proofs they saw at the hand of Mūsā in Egypt. They had also watched their enemy Firʿawn and his soldiers drown, every soldier of them, in the sea. Yet soon after, passing a people who worshipped idols, they said to Mūsā, "Make for us a god as they have gods" (7:138). The story of the calf is told in Sūrat al-Aʿrāf (7) and Sūrat Ṭā Hā (20) after Mūsā went to meet his Lord, and when he returned, Allah decreed that those who had not worshipped the calf should kill those who had, for their repentance to be accepted. They complied, and Allah resurrected them afterwards. Though fully cognizant of clear proofs of Allah's Oneness, and that no partner shares His Divinity, the Israelites stooped lowest of the low. They took a calf as their object of worship, passing by their own genuine Creator.

**"Still We forgave them for that ˹after their repentance˺"** means He left them and did not exterminate them, for Allah remained forbearing when the occasion demanded that they be eliminated.

**"and gave Moses compelling proof"** means authority and power, the staff and the white hand, an evident command over them, shown when he bade them slay themselves in repentance and they obeyed. The unjust, however, always finds an explanation of Allah's signs by which to refute them and continue a life of transgression far from His ways. A prophet is a man among human beings, appearing before the people as a common man, and it is in his utterances that he gives clear arguments proving his status as Allah's messenger. Man's trial demands that he believe without seeing and discover the inner realities, so believing after seeing makes no sense.

### The inward reading of the clear authority

The verse holds two unseemly acts: the demand to be shown Allah, and the worship of the calf after clear signs were manifest. There is an allusion to those content with the calf as their object of worship. A self bent low before such a thing has no witness left to give of the Real. The innermost selves of those people were untouched by deeper knowledge, so they clung with their intellects to a limited thing and let it be their object of worship. The clear authority given to Mūsā is proof made manifest, yes, and a light besides, guarding him from likening God to anything and from stripping Him of His attributes through taʿṭīl. It is actualization and declaring God incomparable, neither stripping Him of His attributes nor comparing Him to His creation. It is said to be the power to hear the divine speech without intermediary, and it is said to belong to this community in the future, when they abide in the state of meeting God. In the tradition of the vision, the Prophet ﷺ said:

> You will not be gathered together in one group in seeing Him.

### In short

- The demand for a book from heaven was a stalling device, answered by the record of the fathers who demanded to see Allah plainly and were struck by the thunderbolt.
- The calf was worshipped after clear signs in Egypt and the drowning of Firʿawn, yet Allah forgave after their repentance and gave Mūsā compelling proof.
- Sight is not the door of faith, for the trial of man asks for belief without seeing.

154.text:
The terms of the covenant: "We raised the Mount over them ˹as a warning˺ for ˹breaking˞ their covenant and said, “Enter the gate ˹of Jerusalem˺ with humility.” We also warned them, “Do not break the Sabbath,” and took from them a firm covenant" (4:154). The verse lists the binding commands and the standing pledge.

### Phrase by phrase

**"We raised the Mount over them ˹as a warning˺ for ˹breaking˞ their covenant"** tells of the people who flatly refused to acknowledge the canonical law of the Torah, refraining from implementing its rulings and refusing what Mūsā brought them from Allah. So Allah uprooted the Mount of Ṭūr and fixed it above their heads, suspended over them, and they were ordered to prostrate, which they did, even looking above while prostrating for fear that the mountain might fall on them. The Book recalls it: "When We raised the mountain over them as if it had been a canopy, and they thought that it was going to fall on them. We said: Hold firmly to what We have given you" (7:171). God fashioned that extraordinary scene at Mount Ṭūr so that the Jews would be bound by a solemn covenant there.

**"and said, “Enter the gate ˹of Jerusalem˺ with humility”"** names the gate of the city, of Jericho. They were to pass into Bayt al-Quds bowed down, saying Ḥiṭṭah, that is: O Allah, take from us our sin of abandoning jihād. In word and action alike they defied it, wriggling into the House on their behinds and muttering shaʿrah, the hair, ḥinṭah, a wheat grain. For that, forty years of wandering in the desert of Tīh was laid upon them.

**"We also warned them, “Do not break the Sabbath”"** is the command to keep the day holy and keep what Allah had barred on it, and one reading of the warning says only: act not unjustly. A variant reading of the prohibition is lā taʿaddū, the original tāʾ assimilated with the dāl, close in meaning to lā taʿtadū. The transgression was fishing during it, catching fish on the day of Sabbath, a command from Him that was not to be transgressed.

**"and took from them a firm covenant"** means a strong covenant, regarding Muḥammad ﷺ as one gloss has it. Rebellion carried them on, and by deceit and trickery they did the very things Allah had barred, as Sūrat al-Aʿrāf relates in asking about the town that was by the sea. One command after another they set aside, and the solemn pledge with Allah they broke, who had enjoined them to enter their synagogue with humility, pray to God in all humbleness and submissiveness, and keep their struggle for livelihood strictly within the bounds He set. So disgrace was their portion in the life of this world, and in the Hereafter the worst punishment awaits them. The same pattern had already run through the earlier verse, from the miracles in Egypt to the calf, from Firʿawn drowned in the sea to the demands of Quraysh in Sūrat al-Isrāʾ, yet the People of the Book had the al-Bayyināt before their eyes and broke every term.

### The signs that did not avail

Each sign added outwardly only deepened the denial and rejection in their hearts. More communications did them no good, for the eyes of those hearts stayed shut to witnessing what came to them. God most high said:

> But signs and warners do not avail a folk who will not believe. (10:101)

This is the case with all the prophets, and the history of the Israelites furnishes ample proof of it.

### In short

- The Mount was raised over a people refusing the Torah's rulings, and the shadow of it hovered until they accepted the covenant.
- The gate was to be entered bowing with Ḥiṭṭah, but they crawled and mocked, and forty years of wandering followed.
- The Sabbath was broken by fishing, the firm covenant broken by deceit, and signs did not avail hearts that would not see.

155.text:
The record of the crimes: "˹They were condemned˺ for breaking their covenant, rejecting Allah’s signs, killing the prophets unjustly, and for saying, “Our hearts are unreceptive!”—it is Allah Who has sealed their hearts for their disbelief, so they do not believe except for a few—" (4:155). The verse opens the charge sheet that runs to the end of the passage.

### Phrase by phrase

**"for breaking their covenant"** names the first crime. The Jews broke the promises and vows Allah took from them, and history recorded one consequence of it: their disbelief in Muḥammad ﷺ and the Qur'ān ended with the capitation tax laid upon them.

**"rejecting Allah's signs"** means His āyāt, His signs and proofs and the miracles they witnessed at the hands of their own prophets.

**"killing the prophets unjustly"** tallies the long record of offenses against the prophets of Allah. Many of them they killed, may Allah's peace be upon them all, and never with any right.

**"and for saying, “Our hearts are unreceptive!”"** records their excuse. Their word "Ghulf" means wrapped with covering, as Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, ʿIkrimah, as-Suddī and Qatādah explained. They claimed their hearts could absorb any kind of knowledge yet could not grasp what the Prophet ﷺ said, as if the hearts were wrapped and the message simply could not enter. The idolaters had said the like before them: "And they say: Our hearts are under coverings from that to which you invite us" (41:5). The Jews would say it ironically, showing not inability but conviction that whatever their misconduct, their salvation stood safe.

**"it is Allah Who has sealed their hearts for their disbelief"** overturns the excuse. It is not as they say. Allah set the seal upon their hearts because of their disbelief, as explained before in sūrat al-Baqarah, and so they cannot heed any admonition.

**"so they do not believe except for a few"** means hearts grown used to kufr, transgression and weak faith. The little faith left to them will be of no use. The few are ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām and his companions and followers, who did believe.

### The birthright they presumed

Revelation had asked of the Jews a surrender to the will of God in this world, holding out Paradise in the next. The first half of that bargain they dropped, the second they treated as a birthright. Rot spread through the community, and their trust that salvation came by lineage alone grew so firm that acknowledging the new Prophet seemed simply unnecessary. Their hearts were not sealed by nature. The seal answered the misconduct.

The inward reading traces the descent step by step. Because they committed these prohibited acts, and were marked by acts that deserve punishment, they were made to alight at the dwellings of disgrace, and punishments of every kind were sent down upon them. The misfortune of their oppositional acts gathered force as it went. Leave the disobedient to himself and he drifts into acts still more prohibited. The covenant they violated without repentance, and so were pulled toward disbelief in the signs. That misfortune in turn set them loose upon the prophets, whom they slew wrongfully. Then came the audacity to claim a keen ability to comprehend, saying their hearts were vessels for every kind of knowledge. The reply came that Allah sealed them, hiding from them the place of deeper knowledge, ʿirfān, and they wandered on in their errors.

### In short

- Covenant broken, signs rejected, prophets killed: the three crimes stand recorded, and the jizyah followed in history.
- The claim of wrapped hearts was an ironic excuse, answered by the seal their disbelief earned.
- The few who believed, like ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām, show the door was never closed by anything but their own doing.

156.text:
The calumny: "and for their denial and outrageous accusation against Mary" (4:156). The charge sheet turns from the community's crimes to the slander of a woman.

### Phrase by phrase

**"for their denial"** is a second disbelief, in ʿĪsā (Jesus) and the Gospel, added to all that came before.

**"and outrageous accusation against Mary"** brings the report of Ibn ʿAbbās, given by ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah, that the Jews accused Maryam of fornication. As-Suddī, Juwaybir, Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq and several others said the same. It is apparent in the verse itself, for they accused Maryam and her son of grave charges, claiming he was an illegitimate son. Some of them even claimed she was menstruating while fornicating. One report adds that the calumny was the cause of their being turned into swine.

### The two errors

Error has two directions. A person may run past the limit or fall short of the truth, and both miss. Some slandered Maryam with the charge of fornication. Others ran past the limit differently, naming her son the son of God. Each group erred in its own way. Maryam, it is said, was a friend of God at whose hands two parties met ruin: the party of excess and the party of shortfall. So stands the rule for all His friends. Disrespect ruins the rejecters, and adulation beyond what may be said of anyone ruins the overpraisers. This is something most of the great ones have had to endure.

### In short

- The denial was doubled: the messenger rejected and his mother slandered.
- Slander from one side and excess from the other both miss the truth about Maryam and her son.

157.text:
The boast answered: "and for boasting, “We killed the Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary, the messenger of Allah.” But they neither killed nor crucified him—it was only made to appear so. Even those who argue for this ˹crucifixion˺ are in doubt. They have no knowledge whatsoever—only making assumptions. They certainly did not kill him" (4:157). The verse gives the truth of the most famous false claim in their history.

### Phrase by phrase

**"and for boasting, “We killed the Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary, the messenger of Allah.”"** records words uttered only in jest and mockery, saying in effect: we killed the man who styled himself the messenger of Allah. The polytheists had mocked in the same tone: "O you to whom the Dhikr has been sent down! Verily, you are a mad man!" (15:6).

**"But they neither killed nor crucified him—it was only made to appear so"** refers to the person whom the Jews thought was ʿĪsā. The one slain and crucified was an associate of theirs, and Allah cast the likeness of ʿĪsā over him, so they thought it was him. In sūrat Āl ʿImrān, five promises had already been given about foiling the Jewish plans against ʿĪsā and shielding him from their hostile intentions: "O ʿĪsā! I will take you and raise you to Myself" (3:55). Among them was the pledge that the Jewish design on his life would come to nothing. The present verse makes it explicit: they did not kill him nor crucify him. What actually happened was that they were deluded by resemblance.

**"Even those who argue for this ˹crucifixion˺ are in doubt"** — those who differ therein are full of doubts, the Jews who claimed to kill him and the ignorant Christians who believed them out of ignorance and lack of reason. When some of them saw the slain man, some said the face is that of ʿĪsā but the body is not his, so it cannot be he. Others answered: no, it is he. They are all in confusion, misguidance and bewilderment.

**"They have no knowledge whatsoever—only making assumptions"** — they follow nothing but conjecture. They have no certitude based on any true knowledge. The diverse claims they advanced only landed them in mutual differences.

**"They certainly did not kill him"** closes the verse on their own uncertainty. Which man died they never knew for sure, and doubt and confusion covered the whole matter.

### How they were deluded by resemblance

Ad-Daḥḥāk tells it this way. When the Jews resolved to kill ʿĪsā, his disciples assembled at a given place and ʿĪsā joined them there. Iblīs it was who pointed the execution squad to the house, and four thousand men closed around the place. ʿĪsā said to his disciples that one of them could go out and be killed and then be with him in Paradise. One of them offered, and ʿĪsā gave him his shirt and head-cover. The likeness of ʿĪsā settled on him, and the moment he stepped outside the Jews, sure they had their man, seized and crucified him. ʿĪsā meanwhile was lifted away.

Another report runs differently. The Jews had sent a man known to the Arabs as Teetlanoos to kill ʿĪsā. He found no one, for ʿĪsā had already been lifted by Allah toward Himself. Coming back out, the man found himself wearing the looks of ʿĪsā. To the Jews he was ʿĪsā, and so they carried off and killed one of their own.

There is room for whichever of the situations came to pass, for the Holy Qur'ān has not determined any particular situation. Allah alone knows what really happened. Seen with the other reports, however, the verse yields one common factor: a compelling delusion was cast over Jews and Christians alike. What actually took shape stayed hidden from them, though conjecture bred claim after claim. Reports add that when some stirred to what had happened, they said that they seemed to have killed their own man, for the one put to death resembled the Messiah in face only, not in the rest of the body. If this man is the Messiah, they asked, where is our own man? And if this is our man, where is the Messiah?

### The story behind the boast

When Allah sent ʿĪsā with proofs and guidance, the Jews envied him for his prophethood and his obvious miracles: curing the blind and the leprous, bringing the dead back to life by Allah's leave, shaping a bird from clay, breathing into it so that it became a bird by Allah's leave and flew. He performed other miracles besides, yet they defied and belied him and tried their best to harm him. He could not live long in any one city and had to travel often with his mother, peace upon them both. The Jews remained unsatisfied. They carried their complaint to the king of Damascus, in those days a Greek polytheist who worshipped the stars, telling him that a man in Jerusalem, in Bayt al-Maqdis, was misleading the people, splitting them and stirring unrest among the king's subjects. Angered, the king wrote to his deputy in the city: arrest this rebel leader, put a stop to him, crucify him, and set a crown of thorns upon his head. On a Friday evening the deputy went with some Jews to the house where ʿĪsā stayed with twelve, thirteen or seventeen of his companions. They surrounded it, and when ʿĪsā sensed that they would soon enter, he asked who would volunteer to be made to look like him and be his companion in Paradise. A young man volunteered, was judged too young, kept volunteering, and at last heard: well then, you will be that man. Over the young man settled the exact likeness of ʿĪsā. A hole opened in the roof, and ʿĪsā, made to sleep, rose through it to heaven. When those in the house came out, the watchers took the man who looked like him, crucified him at night and crowned him with thorns. The Jews boasted of a killing, and some Christians accepted the false claim. Those in the house had witnessed the ascension, while the rest thought the crucified man was ʿĪsā. They even told of Maryam sitting under the corpse weeping, and of the dead man speaking to her. All of it stood as a test from Allah, wise in its design, for His servants.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim recorded a longer account from Ibn ʿAbbās. Just before the raising, ʿĪsā came to his companions, twelve inside the house, his hair dripping water, and told them that some among them would disbelieve in him twelve times after having believed. Then he asked who would volunteer that his image appear as his own and be killed in his place, and be with him in Paradise. The youngest kept volunteering until ʿĪsā said: you will be that man. The resemblance was cast upon him, and ʿĪsā ascended through a hole in the house while the Jews took the young man and crucified him. The followers then divided into three groups. One, the Yaʿqūbiyyah, said: Allah stayed among us as long as He willed, then rose to heaven. Another, the Nasṭūriyyah, said: Allah's son stayed among us as long as he willed, then Allah took him. The third, the Muslims, said: Allah's servant and messenger stayed among us as long as Allah willed, and then Allah took him to Himself. The two disbelieving groups joined hands against the Muslim group and killed them, and Islam was then veiled until Allah sent Muḥammad ﷺ. Its chain of narration up to Ibn ʿAbbās is authentic, and an-Nasāʾī carries it as well, through Abū Kurayb reporting from Abū Muʿāwiyah. Many among the Salaf likewise stated that ʿĪsā asked for a volunteer to carry his appearance and be killed in his stead, and to be his companion in Paradise.

### The inward reading

One report of the inward school has the slanderer himself, the betrayer, clothed in that likeness and killed upon the cross in the other's place. A proverb of the age already knew the pattern: who digs a grave for his brother falls into it. It is also said that ʿĪsā said whoever agreed to have his resemblance cast upon him, so that he would be killed in his place, would have the Garden, and one of his companions agreed. Because that man patiently bore the injury, he was not deprived of the recompense from Allah, for "Indeed We do not leave the reward of those of good deeds to go to waste" (18:30).

False conviction emboldens every crime. The covenant sits light on such people, clear arguments bounce off them, and against whoever calls them to truth they stop at no aggression, not even calumny to dishonour the caller. Yet every plot of theirs must fail. Allah's power and His immutable system of nature stand behind His envoys, and through all plots and all opposition arrives every kind of divine succour, right up to the mission's completion.

### In short

- The boast was mockery, and the truth is the reverse: they killed neither the messenger nor anyone certain, only a likeness they mistook for him.
- The reports differ in detail, the common factor is the delusion, and the Qur'ān fixes only that.
- The volunteer who took the likeness chose the Garden, and the reward of his good deed was not left to waste.

158.text:
The raising: "Rather, Allah raised him up to Himself. And Allah is Almighty, All-Wise" (4:158). Where the plot failed, the divine promise prevailed, as verses 157 and 158 together declare.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Rather, Allah raised him up to Himself"** means into heaven, in body and spirit together, saved whole from their plot. The planning of the Jews to kill him proved insignificant against the power of Allah, who had taken it upon Himself to protect him, lifting him toward Himself as the promise of sūrat Āl ʿImrān had said.

**"And Allah is Almighty"** names the One never weak, whose will nothing resists. Might and mastery are His domain, and His vengeance reaches His enemies.

**"All-Wise"** covers all He decides and ordains for His creatures, His actions wise, His triumph granted to His friends, every deed of His fitted by wisdom to its end. Should the materialists, boxed into a single track, find the lifting beyond their understanding, the limit is theirs, not the deed's.

### The return before the end

The raised one comes back. Al-Bukhārī recorded that Abū Hurayrah said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> By Him in Whose Hands my soul is, the son of Maryam will shortly descend among you as a just ruler. He will break the cross, kill the pig and abolish the jizyah. Then wealth will abound and no one will accept charitable gifts any more. At that time one prostration will be better for them than this life and all that is in it.

From Abū Hurayrah, Imām Aḥmad transmits the call of Ihlāl that ʿĪsā will raise on the mountain highway of ar-Rawḥāʾ, for ḥajj, for ʿumrah, or for both, and Muslim transmits it as well. Then there is the question al-Bukhārī records from the Prophet ﷺ: what will your state be when al-Masīḥ, son of Maryam, comes down among you, and your imam is one of yourselves? Aḥmad and Muslim record that one too. The power that raised him is the power that guards the mission until it is complete.

### The rank of the ransomed one

The inward reading does not forget the volunteer. Because that companion of ʿĪsā was without any imperfection in his lower self, his nafs, he became his friend in spirit, in rūḥ. When ʿĪsā went up to the place of intimacy, maḥall al-zulfa, the spirit of him who ransomed ʿĪsā with his own lower self went up to the place of nearness, maḥall al-qurba. The one who was killed in the likeness received the recompense of his good deed, for Allah does not let that reward go to waste.

### In short

- The raising was body and spirit, the failure of the plot and the keeping of the promise.
- Almighty answers their plotting, All-Wise answers every question raised against the manner of it.
- The one who wore the likeness was not forgotten: his spirit was raised to nearness as ʿĪsā was raised to intimacy.

159.text:
The finale of the passage: "Every one of the People of the Book will definitely believe in him before his death. And on the Day of Judgment Jesus will be a witness against them" (4:159). The verse answers the boast of the killing with two certainties: a universal belief still to come, and a testimony that will stand against them.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Every one of the People of the Book"** gathers the Jews and the Christians, every last one of them, into a single verdict.

**"will definitely believe in him"** means a belief in ʿĪsā as he truly is: not a sorcerer, as the Jews said, and not Allah, nor His son, nor His partner, as the Christians said. Blinded at present by malice and envy, these people cannot see reality as it is. The Jews reject him as a prophet and call him a liar and an impostor. Some Christians, in ignorance like the Jews, accepted that he was crucified and killed. Others, in an excess of belief, went past every limit and took him for God and son of God. Yet the verse promises a time when their eyes will open and they will know that all their notions about ʿĪsā, and about Muḥammad al-Muṣṭafā ﷺ, were false.

**"before his death"** carries two readings, and both are recorded. In one, the pronoun of "his death" returns to the Person of the Book. At the moment of death, when the angels come and the veil of the barzakh lifts before the dying man's eyes, he will believe, but that belief will not profit him, just as the belief of Pharaoh did not profit him while he drowned. The other reading, adopted by a large number of Companions and their Successors and supported by authentic hadith, returns the pronoun to ʿĪsā himself: before the death of ʿĪsā, after he descends at the approach of the Hour. Abū Mālik commented that this occurs after ʿĪsā returns and before he dies, when all of the People of the Scripture will believe in him. So the People of the Book of that time, Jews and Christians, will believe in him genuinely. The Christians of that day will enter Islam with beliefs held true. Of the Jews, the hostile will be killed and the remainder will submit. Then kufr will be banished from the world with all its forms, and Islam will finally reign supreme on the earth. And he will die afterwards on this very earth, after every last Jew of that time has passed.

**"And on the Day of Judgment Jesus will be a witness against them"** means, as Qatādah said, that he will testify before them: the message from Allah he truly delivered, and a servant of Allah he truly was. His witness will stand against their conduct when he was sent to them, against actions that agreed with the sacred law or not. The like of it stands at the end of sūrat al-Māʾidah: "O ʿĪsā, son of Maryam! Did you say unto men" (5:116), a passage that runs until "Almighty, the All-Wise" (5:118).

### The report that fixes the reading

The reading that ties the verse to the descent rests on strong ground. From Abū Hurairah it is reported that the Holy Prophet ﷺ said:

> The son of Maryam shall definitely reappear as a just ruler. He will kill the Anti-Christ and the swine. He will break the Cross, and worship shall be for Allah alone, the one Lord of all the worlds.

Abū Hurairah then said to read, if one wished, the verse of the Qur'ān, verse 159, with its mention of none being left of the People of the Book who has not believed in ʿĪsā before the stated death, and he said with stress, before the death of ʿĪsā, three times over. The report comes from a highly venerated Companion on the added strength of a sound chain of narrators, and it determines that the verse relates to the coming of ʿĪsā close to the qiyāmah.

Support comes from sūrat az-Zukhruf: "he is a sign of the Hour" (43:61). A larger number of the early authorities said the pronoun there returns to ʿĪsā, so that he himself is the sign. Another reading of the word, la-ʿalamun with the vowel opened, makes it plainer still, for ʿalam in that form means a sign or symbol. Ibn ʿAbbās gave this added support, reporting that the verse refers to ʿĪsā, who will come before the qiyāmah.

Taken together, the statement "before his death" and the authentic hadith of Abū Hurairah prove conclusively that ʿĪsā is alive, that he will reappear close to the Day of Doom, and that the Jews will be overcome. The tidings of his coming as a just ruler have been conveyed through an uninterrupted succession of narrations, more than a hundred of them, collected by the teacher Anwar Shāh al-Kashmīrī, a great servant of Islam. The collection was compiled in Arabic and published long ago, and more recently the major Syrian scholar al-ʿAllāmah ʿAbd al-Fattah Abū Ghuddah published from Beirut a fine edition of the work, enlarged with explanations and notes. Absolute and unanimous among the Muslims is the belief in the coming of ʿĪsā toward the later times, and whoever denies it goes out of the pale of Islam.

The inward reading draws its own lesson from the dying-hour belief. Because He determined that no amān, no protection, will be granted to them at the time of despair, their īmān at that time will not benefit them. What is taken into consideration comes from the protection granted by the Real, not from the servant's faith.

### The descent and the work he will do

Al-Bukhārī recorded, in the chapter about the prophets under the descent of ʿĪsā son of Maryam, that Abū Hurayrah said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> By Him in Whose Hands my soul is, the son of Maryam will shortly descend among you as a just ruler. He will break the cross, kill the pig and abolish the jizyah. Then there will be an abundance of wealth and nobody will accept charitable gifts any more. At that time one prostration will be better for them than this life and all that is in it.

Imām Aḥmad recorded from Abū Hurayrah that ʿĪsā will call the Ihlāl from the mountain highway of ar-Rawḥāʾ, for ḥajj, ʿumrah or both, and Muslim recorded it too. Aḥmad recorded another hadith of the same cast: he descends, slays the pig, smashes the cross, leads the congregation in prayer, showers wealth until none will take it, ends the jizyah, and makes for ar-Rawḥāʾ to perform ḥajj or ʿumrah, or both together. Ḥanzalah noted that Abū Hurayrah added, reciting the verse, that they will believe in ʿĪsā before ʿĪsā dies, though he could not say whether that belonged to the Prophet's hadith or was Abū Hurayrah's own word. Ibn Abī Ḥātim also recorded it. Al-Bukhārī recorded the question the Prophet ﷺ put: what will your state be when al-Masīḥ, son of Maryam, comes down among you, and the imam leading you is one of you? Imām Aḥmad and Muslim recorded it too.

Imām Aḥmad recorded the fuller description:

> The Prophets are paternal brothers. Their mothers are different, but their religion is one. I, more than any of mankind, have the right to ʿĪsā, son of Maryam, for there was no prophet between him and me. He will descend, and if you see him, know him. He is a well-built man, the color of his skin between red and white. He will descend wearing two long, light yellow garments. His head appears to be dripping water even though no moisture touched it. He will break the cross, kill the pig, banish the jizyah and call the people to Islam. Allah will destroy all religions except Islam, and Allah will destroy al-Masīḥ ad-Dajjāl, the False Messiah. Safety will fill the earth, so much so that lions will mingle with camels, tigers with cattle and wolves with sheep, and children will play with snakes, which will not harm them. ʿĪsā will remain for forty years and then die, and the Muslims will offer the funeral prayer for him.

Abū Dāwud also recorded it.

### The great confrontation

In his Ṣaḥīḥ, Muslim recorded from Abū Hurayrah, on the authority of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, that the Romans must first occupy al-Aʿmāq or Dābiq before the Hour can start. An army of the best people on earth at that time will come from al-Madīnah and challenge them. Camped face to face, the Romans will ask to fight those who captured some of their men, and the Muslims will refuse to abandon their brothers. A third of the army will flee, and those are the ones Allah will never forgive. Another third will be killed, the best martyrs before Allah. The last third will be victorious, never stricken with fitnah, and they will capture Constantinople. While dividing the spoils, swords hung on olive trees, Shayṭān will shout that al-Masīḥ, meaning ad-Dajjāl, has cornered their people. They will set out for ash-Shām, and there ad-Dajjāl will appear. As the Muslims arrange their lines and the prayer is called, ʿĪsā, son of Maryam, will descend and lead them in prayer. At the sight of him the enemy of Allah will dissolve just as salt dissolves in water, and Allah will kill him by the hand of ʿĪsā, showing the Muslims his blood on the spear.

Muslim recorded that ʿAbdullāh bin ʿAmr said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> You will fight the Jews and will kill them, until the stone says: O Muslim, there is a Jew here, so come and kill him.

And Muslim recorded from Abū Hurayrah that the Hour will not start until the Muslims fight the Jews and kill them. The Jew will take cover behind stone or tree, and the tree will cry out: O Muslim, O servant of Allah, a Jew hides behind me, come and slay him. All but al-Gharqad, for that one is a tree of the Jews.

### The hadith of an-Nawwās bin Sāmʿān

In his Ṣaḥīḥ, Muslim bin al-Ḥajjāj has the account of an-Nawwās bin Sāmʿān: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ mentioned ad-Dajjāl one day, belittling him, blind as he is yet claiming to be Allah, and speaking of him in grave terms, until the hearers thought he was hiding in the date gardens of al-Madīnah. Sensing their anxiety, he asked what was the matter, and on being told, he said:

> I fear other than ad-Dajjāl for you. If he appears while I am still among you, I will be his adversary on your behalf. If he appears while I am not among you, each one will depend on himself, and Allah will be the Helper of every Muslim after me. He is young, with very curly hair, and his eye is smashed. I thought that he looked like ʿAbd al-ʿUzza bin Qaṭan. Whoever lives long and meets him, let him recite the beginnings of sūrat al-Kahf. He will appear on a pass between ash-Shām and al-ʿIrāq, and will wreak havoc to the right and the left. O servants of Allah, hold fast.

Asked how long he would stay, he said forty days: one day like a year, one like a month, one like a week, and the rest like ordinary days. Asked whether the prayers of one day would suffice for the year-long day, he said no, but to count for their due measure. His speed on earth will be like a storm driven by the wind. He will come to a people, call them, and be believed, ordering the sky to rain and the land to grow, so their cattle return with the longest hair, the fullest udders and the fattest stomachs. He will come to another people and be rejected, leaving them to wake destitute, stripped of every possession. He will pass a deserted land and tell it to bring out its treasures, and they will follow him like swarms of bees. He will summon a man in his youth, strike him once with the sword and cut him in two, then call the dead man, who will come back radiant with pleasure and laughter. While all this is happening, Allah will send down al-Masīḥ, ʿĪsā, son of Maryam. His descent will be by the white minaret east of Damascus, dressed in garments lightly touched with saffron, both hands resting on the wings of two angels. Droplets scatter as his head dips. When he lifts it, precious stones like pearls scatter. No disbeliever can survive his breath, which reaches as far as his sight. Ad-Dajjāl he will pursue to the gates of Ludd in Palestine, and there he will kill him. A people who resisted and survived will pass by him, and he will anoint their faces and tell them their grades in Paradise.

While this happens with ʿĪsā, Allah will reveal to him that He has raised a people of His creation that no one can fight, and that he should gather His servants at at-Ṭūr, the mountain of Mūsā in Sinai. Then Gog and Magog will be raised, swarming swiftly from every mound, their front forces drinking all of Lake Tabariyyah, the last of them saying as they pass that the lake once had water. ʿĪsā and his companions will be cornered until the head of a bull is more precious to them than a hundred dinars today. Their supplication will go up, and Allah will loosen an-Naghaf, a worm, upon the necks of Gog and Magog, so that morning finds every one of them dead, like the death of a single soul. Coming down from at-Ṭūr, ʿĪsā and his companions will find no hand-span of earth free of their fat and rot, and they will supplicate again. Allah will send birds as large as the necks of camels to carry the corpses away wherever He wills, then a rain from which no house of mud or animal hair is spared, cleansing the earth until it is as clean as a mirror. Commanded to produce its fruits and regain its blessing, the earth will feed the group from a pomegranate whose skin shelters them, and the milk of one camel will suffice a large group. Then a pure wind will take the soul of every believer, and only the evildoers will remain, indulging in shameless public vice, and on them the Hour will begin.

Imām Aḥmad and the collectors of the Sunan also recorded this hadith, which explains the verse of sūrat al-Anbiyāʾ: "Until, when Yaʾjūj and Maʾjūj are let loose from their barrier" (21:96). In the year seven hundred and forty-one, a white minaret of stone was built in the Umayyad mosque of Damascus in place of one destroyed by a fire the Christians were suspected of starting, and there is a strong feeling that this is the minaret of the descent.

### The account of ʿAbdullāh bin ʿAmr

In his Ṣaḥīḥ, Muslim transmits through Yaʿqūb bin ʿĀṣim bin ʿUrwah bin Masʿūd ath-Thaqafī that ʿAbdullāh bin ʿAmr once answered a man asking about a hadith that dated the Hour. He declared the glory of Allah at the very idea, saying only that tremendous incidents would soon be witnessed, the House, the Kaʿbah, destroyed by fire, and other things besides. Then he related that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that ad-Dajjāl would appear in his nation and remain for forty, the narrator doubting whether days, months or years. Then Allah would send down ʿĪsā, son of Maryam, looking just like ʿUrwah bin Masʿūd, who would seek ad-Dajjāl and kill him. People would remain seven years with no enmity between any two. Then a cool wind from ash-Shām would take the soul of every person with even an atom's weight of good or faith, finding him even in the middle of a mountain. The evildoers left behind would be light as birds with the comprehension of beasts, knowing neither righteousness nor evil. Shayṭān would appear to them and command the worship of idols, while provision came to them in abundance and life was good. Then the Trumpet would be blown, and everyone who hears it will tilt his head to catch the distant sound. The first to hear it will be a man busy at the water pool for his camels, and he and all the people will swoon. Heavy rain will follow, and with it the bodies of the people swell and grow. The Trumpet will sound again and the people will be resurrected, staring about. It will be said: O people, come to your Lord, "but stop them, verily, they are to be questioned" (37:24). The share of the Fire will be brought forth, from every thousand nine hundred and ninety-nine. That is the day when "the children will turn grey-headed" (73:17), the day "when the Shin shall be laid bare" (68:42).

### His form described

From ʿAbdur-Raḥmān bin Adam it is narrated, on the authority of Abū Hurayrah, that the Prophet ﷺ described him for his people: whoever sees ʿĪsā should know him. a well-built man, his skin between red and white, descending in light yellow garments, his head looking as if dripping water no moisture touched. Al-Bukhārī and Muslim recorded from Abū Hurayrah the account of the night of Ascension: the Prophet ﷺ met Mūsā, tall, with hair like one of the men of the tribe of Shanuʾah, and he met ʿĪsā, of moderate height and red-faced as if he had just come out of a bath, and he saw Ibrāhīm, whom he resembled more than any of the prophet's own children did. Then al-Bukhārī has, through Mujāhid, the report of Ibn ʿUmar that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> I saw Mūsā, ʿĪsā and Ibrāhīm. ʿĪsā was of red complexion, with curly hair and a broad chest. Mūsā was of brown complexion, with straight hair and a tall stature, as if he was from the people of az-Zutt.

Al-Bukhārī and Muslim recorded that Ibrāhīm said that ʿAbdullāh bin ʿUmar related that the Prophet ﷺ once mentioned the False Messiah before the people, saying that Allah is not blind in His eye, but al-Masīḥ ad-Dajjāl is blind in his right eye, his eye like a protruding grape. Muslim recorded the dream at the Kaʿbah: a light-colored man of beautiful color, hair combed to his shoulders and dripping water, circling the House leaning on two men, and he was told: this is al-Masīḥ, son of Maryam. Behind him, a man with very curly hair, blind in the right eye, looking exactly like Ibn Qaṭan, and he was told: he is al-Masīḥ ad-Dajjāl. Al-Bukhārī recorded that Sālim reported his father as swearing that the Prophet ﷺ never called ʿĪsā red. What he related was a dream of circling the Kaʿbah: a brown man, ample-haired, pacing between two others, water dripping from his head, and he was told this was the son of Maryam. Looking behind, he saw a fat man, red in complexion, hair curled hard, the right eye blind and bulging like a grape, and was told this was ad-Dajjāl, the closest likeness being Ibn Qaṭan. Ibn Qaṭan, az-Zuhrī noted, belonged to the tribe of Khuzaʿah and had died in the days of Jāhiliyyah. So runs the wording of al-Bukhārī.

### In short

- Every soul of the People of the Book will believe in ʿĪsā as he is, whether at the useless hour of death or, as the strong reading holds, before his own death after the descent.
- The descent is fixed by an uninterrupted succession of reports: he comes as a just ruler, breaks the cross, kills the pig and ad-Dajjāl, abolishes the jizyah, and dies after forty years.
- The end-time sequence, the Romans at al-Aʿmāq, the wars with the Jews, ad-Dajjāl, Gog and Magog and the Trumpet, is mapped in the hadiths of Abū Hurayrah, ʿAbdullāh bin ʿAmr and an-Nawwās bin Sāmʿān.
- On the Day of Judgment he is a witness, not an accused: he delivered the message, and he is but a servant of Allah.

160.text:
The foods withdrawn: "We forbade the Jews certain foods that had been lawful to them for their wrongdoing, and for hindering many from the Way of Allah" (4:160). The passage turns from belief to dinner table, and the punishment fits a people who bent the law itself.

### Phrase by phrase

**"We forbade the Jews certain foods that had been lawful to them"** declares that the Jews' injustice and transgression, shown forth in major sins, moved Allah to prohibit a portion of the pure, lawful things once allowed them. Their wrongdoing, in the Arabic, is of some of those of Jewry, not all. Two readings of the prohibition are given. It could be one of decree only, meaning that Allah let the Jews falsely interpret their Book, changing and altering the information about what was allowed, so that out of exaggeration and extremism in religion they prohibited some things for themselves. Or it could mean that in the Tawrah itself, Allah prohibited things allowed before, for all food had been lawful to the Children of Israel before the Tawrah was revealed: "except what Isrāʾīl made unlawful for himself before the Tawrah was revealed" (3:93), namely the meat and milk of the camel. Later, many things were prohibited in the Tawrah, as sūrat al-Anʿām (6) recounts: to those who are Jews every beast with undivided hoof was barred them, and the fat of ox and sheep likewise, saving what clings to their backs or entrails or is mingled with bone. Thus were they recompensed for their rebellion.

**"for their wrongdoing"** explains a difference. The good things forbidden carried no physical or spiritual harm in themselves. In the Sharīʿah brought by Muḥammad al-Muṣṭafā ﷺ, what is known as ḥarām is forbidden for one or the other harm it brings. With the Jews it was the reverse: pure things were taken from them as punishment for transgression and disobedience.

**"and for hindering many from the Way of Allah"** names a double obstruction: themselves and others were alike turned from the truth, a behavior carried from the past into the present. Obstructing good became a standing feature of theirs. Enemies of the messengers they were and remained, killing many of the prophets, denying Muḥammad ﷺ and ʿĪsā (Jesus), peace upon them, and barring the very mention of Allah's religion. One mark of a self-styled religion is the self-styled sign: a group that invents its own rules of lawful and unlawful, observes the outward forms with great care, and takes worldly benefit from ways God forbade, while putting obstacles in the path of the divine caller. Such people are bracketed with the patently irreligious, however religious the forms they keep.

### The inward measure

Embarking on prohibited things necessitates the forbidding of licit things. When gentleness and generosity reach a servant, the cause is his keeping of the Sharīʿah's outward and his reverence for it in spirit and heart, through which he attains rest in whispered prayer and the soft favors that union brings. If harshness and severity appear instead, it is because he looked with denial on the sanctuary of the Sharīʿah and put the religion's prohibited things to work in following the commanding soul. Whoever holds back from the outward of the Sharīʿah finds the beauty of the Ḥaqīqah veiling its face from him. Were the Sharīʿah taken away, the turning wheel would halt. Were the religion taken away, the Twins would leave the sky.

### In short

- Pure foods were withdrawn as punishment, not for any harm in the foods, whether by the Tawrah's ruling or by their own tampering hands.
- The camel of Isrāʾīl and the hoof and fat of sūrat al-Anʿām mark the span of the prohibition.
- Hindering others from the way runs in the family history, and self-styled law-making is its signature.

161.text:
The crooked gain: "taking interest despite its prohibition, and consuming people's wealth unjustly. We have prepared for the disbelievers among them a painful punishment" (4:161). The charge sheet adds the money crimes.

### Phrase by phrase

**"taking interest despite its prohibition"** recalls a ban already given: Allah had forbidden them ribā, and the prohibition stood written in the Torah. Yet they took it, making usury lawful for themselves through various kinds of tricks, ploys and cons.

**"and consuming people's wealth unjustly"** means devouring men's substance by false pretences, through transgression and bribery, through bribes offered in adjudication, taking wealth without any legitimate right.

**"We have prepared for the disbelievers among them a painful punishment"** singles out the disbelievers among the Jews, and the pain of what is prepared will reach their very hearts.

The inward reading keeps the measure proportional: forbidden acts breed the loss of what was allowed. Let a man trespass with his outward self and the permitted states he once enjoyed grow closed to him, while the subtle kindnesses once received in his innermost self are quietly taken back.

### In short

- Ribā was forbidden in their own Book, and clever devices do not launder it.
- Bribery and false pretences devour wealth, and the punishment prepared for it is felt in the heart.
- Wrongdoing closes the doors that obedience had opened, outward and inward alike.

162.text:
The exception: "But those of them well-grounded in knowledge, the faithful ˹who˺ believe in what has been revealed to you ˹O Prophet˺ and what was revealed before you—˹especially˺ those who establish prayer—and those who pay alms-tax and believe in Allah and the Last Day, to these ˹people˺ We will grant a great reward" (4:162). After the censure, the door.

### Phrase by phrase

**"those of them well-grounded in knowledge"** describes people firm in the religion and full of beneficial knowledge, established in knowledge, a subject treated before in sūrat Āl-'Imrān (3). The verse, said Ibn ʿAbbās, came down about ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām and about Thaʿlabah bin Saʿyah, Zayd bin Saʿyah and Asad bin ʿUbayd, men who entered Islam and held true to what Allah sent Muḥammad ﷺ with. They were of the People of the Book who, when the Holy Prophet ﷺ came, found in him fully and unmistakably all the qualities their scriptures had prophesied of the Last among prophets, and believed, like ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām, Usayd and Thaʿlabah. In one reading the knowledge meant is knowledge of the Torah, and the believers meant are all the believers, the Emigrants and the Helpers.

**"the faithful ˹who˺ believe in what has been revealed to you ˹O Prophet˺ and what was revealed before you"** marks them out: the Qur'ān and every scripture before it they believe, the Torah and the Gospel among them, even though the Jews around them refused to believe.

**"˹especially˺ those who establish prayer"** means the diligent, those who perfect their five daily prayers. The Arabic phrase wa'l-muqīmīna l-ṣalāta stands in the accusative as a laudative, and it is also read in the nominative.

**"and those who pay alms-tax"** reads as the zakah due on wealth and property, or as those who purify themselves, or as both together. Allah knows best.

**"and believe in Allah and in the Last Day"** joins belief that no deity deserves worship except Allah to belief in resurrection after death, with reward or punishment for good and evil deeds.

**"to these ˹people˺ We will grant a great reward"** names Paradise, an immense and abundant reward. One reading of the verb is We shall surely give, another He shall surely give.

### What salvation turns on

The great reward is promised for faith and righteous deeds together. As for salvation as such, it depends on the correction of the essentials of doctrine, subject to one condition: that one's life ends with the blessing of īmān. Not every Jew stood outside this door. Those not caught up in human interpolations, who discovered the original divine religion, who rose above prejudice, the blind imitation of their community's ways and opportunism, found no obstacle to recognizing the truth and surrendering to it. They could see the truth despite every kind of mental block, and these are the people ushered into the Paradise God prepared for them.

### The three knowledges

The inward reading hears the phrase "well-grounded" as a ladder. The firmly rooted in knowledge are those who have gathered its varieties, the knowledge belonging to the Sharīʿah, to the Ṭarīqah, and to the Ḥaqīqah. The Sharīʿah's knowledge is gained by learning. The Ṭarīqah's by practice. The Ḥaqīqah's is simply found, arriving as a gift. Concerning knowledge of the Sharīʿah, He says: "Ask the folk of the remembrance" (16:43). Concerning knowledge of the Ṭarīqah, He says: "Seek the means of approach to Him" (5:35). Concerning knowledge of the Ḥaqīqah, He says: "We taught him knowledge from Us" (18:65). He turned knowledge of the Sharīʿah over to a teacher, knowledge of the Ṭarīqah over to a guide, and knowledge of the Ḥaqīqah He kept to Himself. Whoever fancies he has no need of a teacher for the Sharīʿah is a heretic. Whoever claims the Ṭarīqah is possible without a guide is a tempter. Whoever names any teacher of the Ḥaqīqah besides the Real is deluded. It has been said that the firmly rooted learn the Sharīʿah and put it into practice through self-purification until they perceive the Ḥaqīqah in their secret core. Thus Muṣṭafā said:

> When someone acts on what he knows, God will bequeath him knowledge of what he does not know.

Knowledge not practiced is wasted and becomes an argument against its holder. Knowledge practiced becomes an argument to his benefit, and the knowledge of the Ḥaqīqah reaches him as a gift.

### In short

- ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām and his fellows, named by Ibn ʿAbbās, stand inside the door the censure closed.
- Prayer, zakah, and belief in Allah and the Last Day are the entry lines, and the reward is Paradise.
- The firmly rooted climb by three knowledges, the learned law, the practiced path, and the gift found in the secret core.

163.text:
The equal sending: "Indeed, We have sent revelation to you ˹O Prophet˺ as We sent revelation to Noah and the prophets after him. We also sent revelation to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and his descendants, ˹as well as˺ Jesus, Job, Jonah, Aaron, and Solomon. And to David We gave the Psalms" (4:163). Verse 163 answers the demand for a written book from heaven by putting the Prophet ﷺ in the company of every name the demanders themselves accept.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Indeed, We have sent revelation to you ˹O Prophet˺ as We sent revelation to Noah and the prophets after him"** was revealed as a rebuttal. Sukayn and ʿAdī bin Zayd said to the Prophet ﷺ that they did not know that Allah had sent down anything to any human after Mūsā. The answer came down: revelation reached Muḥammad ﷺ exactly as it reached Nūḥ and the prophets after him. Wahy is a command of Allah, unique and inimitable, His message sent to prophets, and whoever believed in the revelation given to the past prophets must believe in this one too. Whoever rejects it becomes, so to say, a rejecter of all those revelations.

**"We also sent revelation to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and his descendants"** continues the line: Ibrāhīm and his two sons Ismāʿīl and Isḥāq, then Yaʿqūb the son of Isḥāq, and the al-Asbāṭ, the offspring of the twelve sons of Yaʿqūb, the prophets of the twelve tribes of the Israelites. To each of these, the tradition notes, Gabriel was sent as he was sent to Ibrāhīm.

**"˹as well as˺ Jesus, Job, Jonah, Aaron, and Solomon"** continues the register, and **"And to David We gave the Psalms"** closes it. The Zabūr is the name of the Book revealed to Dāwūd, known in earlier scripture as the Psalms. One reading of the Arabic word would make it the name of the revealed Book, another a verbal noun meaning inscribed.

### The demand answered

The question the People of the Book had asked, that the Prophet ﷺ bring them a book all written up from the heavens, was first answered in the mode of reproach. Here it is proved false differently. The great prophets named in the verse are prophets these demanders themselves accept, and they accept them on the basis of their miracles, without any book lowered from the sky before their eyes. Let them keep to that line of argument, then, for Sayyidnā Muḥammad al-Muṣṭafā ﷺ has his miracles as well, and there is no reason they cannot step forward and believe in him too. The truth of the matter is that the demand is no quest for truth. It is rooted in prejudice and hostility.

Why the likeness to Nūḥ in particular? In the days of Ādam the wahy stood at its beginnings, attaining perfection only with the prophethood of Nūḥ. The first state was one of educational initiation, and by Nūḥ's time it had reached the stage of testing: reward held out to draw the obedient, punishment held over the disobedient. From Nūḥ the chain of great prophets began, and from his time the first punishment descended on those who transgressed against divine revelation. Before that, people were considered excusable and allowed to learn through good counsel. Once religious education was widespread and no hidden reason for avoidance remained, punishment did descend, the Great Flood in the days of Nūḥ, then different punishments in the days of Ṣāliḥ, Shuʿayb and many others, peace on them all. The likeness thus serves full warning on the People of the Book and the disbelievers of Makkah: whoever will not believe in the revelation of the Last of the Prophets ﷺ will deserve the greatest punishment.

The personal presence of Nūḥ was itself a miracle. He was blessed with nine hundred and fifty years, lost none of his teeth, had no streak of white in his hair, and faced no deficiency in his strength, yet he spent his whole lifetime braving the pain his people inflicted on him with matching patience and fortitude.

### The inward reading

Prophethood's exaltedness is the foundation on which both worlds rest, and the fruit of prophethood is the Sharīʿah's beauty. Right the path of the Sharīʿah is, and the prophets are its marks. Until the leader sees the road, he does not lead: "I invite to God upon insight, I and whosoever follows me" (12:108). The Exalted Lord sent the prophets to make apparent the road of obedience, so that servants might reach generous bestowal and reward, and to make apparent the road of disobedience and warn against it, so that servants might avoid it and not be deemed worthy of punishment. That is infinite bounty and endless generosity. Had He left the servants in place, sent no Messenger and held no lamp of guidance in their road, they would have stayed wrapped in createdness, darkened by their own opinions, eating everything that is their poison and doing everything that is their destruction. The prophets are mercy and leaders for the world's folk, the best of creatures, the callers at the top of the street of friendship, the cupbearers at the lip of the water of life. The Sharīʿah's title-page they are, and the Ḥaqīqah's proof. To him who was given the Qur'ān it was said: "I was given the Qur'ān and the like of it along with it," and he said elsewhere: "I have a moment with God embraced by no proximate angel, nor any sent prophet."

### In short

- Revelation to Muḥammad ﷺ is of one kind with revelation to Nūḥ, Ibrāhīm, the tribes, and the rest, and rejecting it rejects them all.
- The written-book demand collapses on the demanders' own acceptance of miracle-bearing prophets.
- From Nūḥ onward the excuse ran out: education completed, punishment began, and the warning now stands for Makkah and the People of the Book alike.

164.text:
The unnamed and the spoken-to: "There are messengers whose stories We have told you already and others We have not. And to Moses Allah spoke directly" (4:164). Verse 164 opens the register that no register can close.

### Phrase by phrase

**"There are messengers whose stories We have told you already"** points to the names Allah named in the Qur'ān.
