Set down before the revelation of this verse, they are: Ādam, Idrīs, Nūḥ, Hūd, Ṣāliḥ, Ibrāhīm, Lūṭ, Ismāʿīl, Isḥāq, Yaʿqūb, Yūsuf, Ayyūb, Shuʿayb, Mūsā, Hārūn, Yūnus, Dāwūd, Sulaymān, Ilyās, al-Yasāʿ, Zakariyyā, Yaḥyā and ʿĪsā, and their leader, Muḥammad ﷺ. Several scholars also listed Dhūl-Kifl among the prophets.

**"and others We have not"** means there are other prophets whom Allah did not mention in the Qur'ān, messengers not told of by name. As reported by Sayyidnā Abū Dharr al-Ghifārī, the Holy Prophet ﷺ said that Almighty Allah had sent one hundred and twenty-four thousand prophets, of whom three hundred and thirteen were Sharīʿah-bearing messengers. Another count relates eight thousand prophets in all, four thousand of them from the Children of Israel and four thousand from other peoples, as stated by Shaykh Jalāl al-Dīn al-Mahallī in his commentary on sūrat Ghāfir. The modes of wahy differ: sometimes an angel with a message, sometimes a written Book, sometimes Almighty Allah speaking directly to His Messenger. When wahy comes, in whatever mode, acting in accordance with it becomes obligatory. The Jewish saying that they would believe only if a written Book like the Torah came to them is, to say the least, short on sense and tall on disbelief.

**"And to Moses Allah spoke directly"** confers Mūsā's honor, whence his name Kalīm, the one Allah addressed directly, without intermediary, in a manner befitting Him. Al-Ḥāfiẓ Ibn Marduwyah recorded that ʿAbdul-Jabbār bin ʿAbdullāh said that a man came to Abū Bakr bin ʿAyyash and said he had heard someone recite the verse as "and to Allah, Mūsā spoke directly." Abū Bakr answered that only a disbeliever would recite it so. Al-Aʿmash recited it with Yaḥyā bin Wathāb, then to Abū ʿAbdur-Raḥmān as-Sulamī, then to ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭālib, and so to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "and to Mūsā Allah spoke directly." Abū Bakr bin Abī ʿAyyash was angry with the man because he altered the words and their meanings, for he was of the Muʿtazilah, who denied that Allah spoke to Mūsā or speaks to any of His creation. One teacher of that school who recited it so was told: what then would he do with Allah's word, "And when Mūsā came at the time and place appointed by Us, and his Lord spoke to him" (7:143)? The later verse cannot be altered or changed.

### The inward reading

God's way with His friends is to veil some and make others known, and so it is with the prophets: He proclaims the names of some and refers to others generally. All the prophets, taken whole or one by one, are owed belief, just as all the friends, whole or single, are owed respect. With the servants too He veils some states and makes others apparent, asking purity and sincerity for what He shows, and jealously protecting their hearts from treating what He veils as an entitlement. That Allah spoke directly to Mūsā tells of His selecting him to hear His speech without intermediary.

### In short

- The told and the untold both stand under one obligation of belief, by name or in general.
- The counts differ, 124,000 with 313 law-bearing, or 8,000 split between the Children of Israel and others, and the register stays open.
- The direct speech to Mūsā is an honor guarded by the reciters, for whoever reverses it recites disbelief.

165.text:
The purpose of them all: "˹All were˺ messengers delivering good news and warnings so humanity should have no excuse before Allah after ˹the coming of˺ the messengers. And Allah is Almighty, All-Wise" (4:165). The verse states the reason for the whole institution.

### Phrase by phrase

**"messengers delivering good news and warnings"** means good news of Paradise for those who believe and obey, and practice the good things that please Allah, and warning of His punishment and torment for those who defy His commandments and disbelieve.

**"so humanity should have no excuse before Allah"** states the arrangement: books sent down, messengers sent with good news and warnings, and what He likes and is pleased with, and what earns His displeasure, all explained. With that, no excuse survives for anyone before Allah on the Day of Judgement. He had already said that if He had destroyed them with a torment before this, they would have said: "Our Lord! If only You had sent us a Messenger, we should certainly have followed Your signs, before we were humiliated and disgraced." The messengers were sent to pre-empt that plea, the plea of the person who never heard, who might say: our Lord, why no messenger to us, that we might follow Your signs and join the believers?

**"after ˹the coming of˺ the messengers"** marks the cutoff: now that messengers have come with miracles and pointed out the straight path of truth, no one may be excused from accepting the true faith on any pretext. Such is the nature of divine revelation: an absolute argument, final, conclusive and disarming, before which all arguments lie surrendered. This is the wisdom of Allah and His way of working.

**"And Allah is Almighty, All-Wise"** reads as Mighty in His kingdom and in vengeance upon those who disbelieve in His messenger, Wise in His actions and in His decree that they believe in the messengers.

The Two Ṣaḥīḥs carry the report of Ibn Masʿūd from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ:

> No one is more jealous than Allah. That is why He prohibited all types of sin, committed in public or in secret. No one likes praise more than Allah, and that is why He has praised Himself. No one likes to give excuse more than Allah, and that is why He sent the prophets as bearers of good news and as warners.

In another narration the Prophet ﷺ added that this is why He sent His messengers and revealed His Books.

### The plan the messengers serve

God created man, and then He created Paradise and Hell, and man was settled on the earth with freedom to do as he wishes. The freedom is temporary, meant for his trial, so that good and bad may be distinguished. Both kinds of people have been mixed in this world, with equal opportunity to gain from the blessings of God, and after the appointed time of trial the groups will be separated, one lodged in the Gardens of Paradise forever, the other consigned to Hell for all eternity. The plan set man in an extraordinarily delicate spot: the outcome of his brief stay would arrive as one of two extremes, comfort without end or chastisement without end. Hence, alongside the natural arrangements for divine guidance, God sent His messengers and His scriptures, that none stay unaware of the reality of life, and none excuse his misconduct by pleading ignorance of the divine plan. When all human beings without exception are weighed in the divine scale, their test papers cannot differ from one another, and so every prophet brought the same message: everyone stands at a perilous watershed, Paradise on one side and Hell on the other.

The inward reading adds the measure of worth. God informed created beings of the messengers' worth, that reward is gathered from them alone and punishment avoided by what they warn against, for no other road leads created beings to the comfort they seek or away from the hurt they dread, now or at the end. How could one who has need of God have an argument against God? Yet God addressed them in accordance with their understandings.

### In short

- Good news and warning together exhaust the messenger's task, and after them the excuse is dead.
- The Two Ṣaḥīḥs carry the reason in the Prophet's ﷺ own words: none likes to give excuse more than Allah.
- One scale, one message, one watershed: the messengers made the trial fair.

166.text:
The testimony: "Yet ˹if you are denied, O Prophet,˺ Allah bears witness to what He has sent down to you—He has sent it with His knowledge. The angels too bear witness. And Allah ˹alone˺ is sufficient as a Witness" (4:166). The verse turns from the deniers to the Witness whose word closes the file.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Allah bears witness to what He has sent down to you"** holds whatever they do. Denial, defiance, disbelief in you, O Muḥammad, none of it changes the testimony: you are His Messenger, the Glorious Qur'ān, which Gabriel brought you, the Book in which falsehood cannot come to it from before it or behind it, sent down by the All-Wise, Worthy of all praise. Ibn ʿAbbās relates the scene: a deputation of Jews reached the Holy Prophet ﷺ, who said to them: surely you know that I am a true messenger of Allah? They refused, and the verse came down. Al-Kalbī's report names the leaders of Makkah instead: they went to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said they had asked the Jews about him and the Jews claimed not to know him, so let him produce a witness that Allah had sent him, and thereupon the verse came down. The Book was revealed with full realization that he deserved it.

**"He has sent it with His knowledge"** means such of His knowledge as He willed His servants to reach: the clear signs of guidance and truth, what draws Allah's pleasure and what draws His displeasure, and the Unseen, past and future together. It includes His honorable attributes, unknowable even to a sent messenger or an illustrious angel save by Allah's leave: "And they will never compass anything of His knowledge except that which He wills" (2:255).

**"The angels too bear witness"** to the truth of what he came with and what was revealed to him, along with Allah's own testimony.

**"And Allah ˹alone˺ is sufficient as a Witness"** closes the matter: with no other testimony, His suffices. By naming His knowledge of the Prophet's sincerity, God comforted him against the lies told by created beings.

### Whose validation counts

Different prophets received different kinds of succour from God, according to the requirements of the age, and so it is still, that those who come forward to spread His message receive special divine succour fitted to their circumstances. In the Prophet's time, the Jews enjoyed the status of representatives of the divine religion. They supposed themselves the chosen people, the sole custodians, occupying all the religious positions of honor, unwilling to acknowledge any other's greatness, and so they refused to believe that the Arab prophet had been sent by God. They thought religion was their monopoly, that without their testimony a person claimed to be God's representative would lack all credibility. They had forgotten that this is God's universe, its system tended by God's obedient angels. The real validation comes from God, supported by the entire system of the universe. It is God, with His entire universe, who supports His messenger, not anyone's self-styled suppositions. Such, too, is the sordid conduct of those who conceal his character traits and the circumstantial indicators of his appearance present in the Torah, and keep others from the true faith by producing things that are not there or jumbling together what distorts the truth.

### In short

- Allah's own testimony, with the angels', stands behind the revelation, and it needs no commission from the Jews of Madīnah or the leaders of Makkah.
- The Book came down carrying knowledge of guidance, of the Unseen, and of attributes no angel can compass.
- Validation belongs to God and the universe He runs, not to self-appointed custodians of religion.

167.text:
The far straying: "Those who disbelieve and hinder ˹others˺ from the Way of Allah have certainly strayed far away" (4:167). The verse names the double crime and its direction.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Those who disbelieve"** in Muḥammad ﷺ and the Qur'ān follow no truth themselves.

**"and hinder ˹others˺ from the Way of Allah"** adds the active crime: they labor to keep people from Allah's path, His religion and His obedience, concealing the descriptions of Muḥammad ﷺ, and these concealers are the Jews.

**"have certainly strayed far away"** is the verdict: they defied the truth, deviated, and went far astray from guidance. There is no greater foolishness than theirs: their words are refuted by the whole universe, and their stand opposes a plan backed by the universe's Lord.

### In short

- Unbelief joined to obstruction doubles the straying.
- Concealing the descriptions of the Prophet ﷺ is the obstruction named.
- Speaking against the universe's own Lord is a losing position.

168.text:
The sealed verdict: "Those who disbelieve and wrong themselves—surely Allah will neither forgive them nor guide them to any path" (4:168). The verse carries the judgment against the wrongers.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Those who disbelieve"** in Allah's signs, Book and Messenger.

**"and wrong themselves"** by their disbelief and by hindering others from His path, committing sins and violating His prohibitions. One reading identifies the wrongers as those who ascribe partners to Allah, another as those who wronged the Prophet ﷺ by concealing his descriptions.

**"surely Allah will neither forgive them"** as long as they remain thus.

**"nor guide them to any path"** of good, of salvation from His punishment.

The inward reading sets the weight. God set their blocking of believers from the truth on a level with disbelief in Him, weighing the rights of His friends no lighter than His own right. He made their wrongdoing, ẓulm, the same as their kufr, and attached to both the justly deserved abiding punishment. Wrongdoing may not equal disbelief in earning endless stay, yet its misfortune runs deeper: God may let the wrongdoer go until disbelief swallows him. Such perverse behavior leads them, day by day, further from the truth, until they fall into the pit of eternal damnation.

### In short

- Disbelief plus hindrance plus sin: the self-wronging is complete, and forgiveness waits on change that never comes.
- The right of God's friends weighs like His own right, and barring from truth equals unbelief.
- Abandonment is the quiet road from wrongdoing to disbelief.

169.text:
The one path left: "except that of Hell, to stay there for ever and ever. And that is easy for Allah" (4:169). The exception removes every other destination.

### Phrase by phrase

**"except that of Hell"** is the exception to every withheld guidance: the path that leads to Hellfire is the one path still open to them.

**"to stay there for ever and ever"** is decreed for them to abide therein once they enter, never to die in it and never to be taken out.

**"And that is easy for Allah"** counts with Him a light matter, and nothing can hinder His decision.

### In short

- Guidance withheld leaves one direction, and it does not circle back.
- Abiding without end is decreed, and the decree costs Allah nothing.

170.text:
The call to everyone: "O humanity! The Messenger has certainly come to you with the truth from your Lord, so believe for your own good. But if you disbelieve, then ˹know that˺ to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise" (4:170). With the objections answered, the address swings open to all human beings, for they are the direct addressees here.

### Phrase by phrase

**"O humanity!"** addresses the people of Makkah first, and beyond them every people, for once the prophethood of Sayyidnā Muḥammad al-Muṣṭafā ﷺ stands confirmed, the Qur'ān carries Allah's message out to all human beings wherever they are.

**"The Messenger has certainly come to you with the truth from your Lord"** lists what he brought: guidance, the religion of truth and clear proof from Allah, with the declaration of Allah's divine Oneness and the Qur'ān.

**"so believe for your own good"** urges belief in what he has brought and follow him, for it is better for you in this world and the Afterlife than what you are presently seeking. The essence of the message is that salvation lies nowhere but in belief in the prophethood of Muḥammad ﷺ, so believe and prosper.

**"But if you disbelieve, then ˹know that˺ to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth"** counts all of it His possessions, creatures and servants. Allah is too rich to need your faith, and your disbelief could never reach Him with harm. He said it through Mūsā: "If you disbelieve, you and all on earth together, then verily, Allah is Rich, Owner of all praise." The disbelievers lose everything while Allah loses nothing, and with His limitless domain and power, who could conceive of bringing loss or harm to Him? Let them not be put on the wrong foot by the delay or decrease of punishment in this world, for He does what His wisdom allows to prevail.

**"And Allah is All-Knowing"** covers those who deserve to be guided and makes it easy for them, and He knows those who do not deserve it and makes them blind to it, leading them to deviation.

**"All-Wise"** spans His statements, His actions, His legislation and all that He decrees.

### The threshold of Lordhood

The verse alludes to this: Lordhood's threshold and Unity's majesty need no obedience from the obedient, and the worship of creatures in heaven and earth leaves Him untouched. Were all creation to fold back into the concealment of nonexistence, spheres, heavens, existing things and things coming to nothing alike, His purity and lordhood would lose nothing. His Unity's beauty is His eternity, and His eternity's majesty is His solitariness. From Abū Dharr al-Ghifārī comes a sound hadith, from God's Messenger, from God:

> O My servants, I have forbidden Myself to do wrong, and all of it is forbidden to you. So do not wrong each other! Surely you are the ones who err by night and day, and I am the one who forgives sins and does not care. So ask forgiveness of Me, and I will forgive you. O My servants, if the first of you and the last of you and the men of you and the jinn of you had the heart of the most godwary man among you, that would add nothing to My kingdom. O My servants, if the first of you and the last of you and the men of you and the jinn of you had the heart of the most depraved man among you, that would diminish nothing from My kingdom. O My servants, if the first of you and the last of you and the men of you and the jinn of you were to ask from Me and I were to give every man among them what he asked for, that would diminish nothing from Me, except as the ocean is diminished when a needle is dipped into it once.

And the verse says more: even if all creatures put aside the activity of servants and loosened the belt of obedience, they could not go outside of servanthood, nor lift from themselves the bonds of slavehood in respect of creation. The denial of the call of God is in truth the denial of oneself, so clearly is the call made that no one need fail to understand it. With the windows of the heart kept open, the divine call arrives as an exact answer to one's own quest, the truth veiled in human interpretations brought to him pure and original by God's own arrangement, an expression of God's own wisdom and knowledge rather than the personal ambition of a human being.

### In short

- The Messenger ﷺ came with truth, and believing in him profits the believer, not the Lord.
- To Allah belongs everything in the heavens and the earth: disbelief diminishes nothing, not even a needle's dip in the ocean.
- He knows who deserves guidance and who deserves deviation, and His wisdom runs through statements, actions and decree.

171.text:
The great correction: "O People of the Book! Do not go to extremes regarding your faith; say nothing about Allah except the truth. The Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary, was no more than a messenger of Allah and the fulfilment of His Word through Mary and a spirit ˹created by a command˺ from Him. So believe in Allah and His messengers and do not say, “Trinity.” Stop!—for your own good. Allah is only One God. Glory be to Him! He is far above having a son! To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. And Allah is sufficient as a Trustee of Affairs" (4:171). Having dealt with the Jews, the passage turns to the Christians and corrects, in one verse, the largest doctrinal error ever charged to a prophet's name.

### Phrase by phrase

The opening words of the verse, **"O People of the Book! Do not go to extremes regarding your faith"**, address the Christians, the people of the Gospel, and the Jews with them, for excess is the common factor between them. The Arabic word al-Ghuluww means to cross the limits or transgress, and Imām al-Jaṣṣāṣ said in his Aḥkām al-Qur'ān that excess in faith is crossing the limit set therein. The verse was revealed about certain Christian denominations who claimed that Jesus is the son of Allah, and about the Nestorian Christians of Najrān who claimed that Jesus and the Lord are partners. Over ʿĪsā the Christians went so far past the grade Allah gave him that prophethood was left behind and a god emerged, worshipped as Allah is worshipped.

**"say nothing about Allah except the truth"** means: no lying claim that Allah has a wife or a son. Glorified, praised and honored is He in might, grandeur and greatness, and no deity deserves worship, no Lord exists, but Him.

**"The Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary, was no more than a messenger of Allah"** counts him one of Allah's servants, one of His creatures. To him Allah said Be, and he was, and as a messenger he was sent. Before him passed many messengers, and his mother was a Siddīqah, and the two of them ate food, as the Book states: "They both ate food" (5:75).

**"and the fulfilment of His Word through Mary"** names a word from Allah bestowed on Maryam: He created him with the word Be, carried by Jibrīl to Maryam. By Allah's leave Jibrīl breathed ʿĪsā's life into her, and so he came to be, in place of the ordinary conception of man and woman.

**"and a spirit ˹created by a command˺ from Him"** means created by Allah's command, for he had no father to conceive him. He came to existence through the word that Allah uttered and the life that Allah sent with Jibrīl.

**"So believe in Allah and His messengers"** asks belief that Allah is One and Alone, without son or wife, and know with certainty that ʿĪsā is the servant and messenger of Allah, believing in all the messengers without making a distinction between them.

**"and do not say, “Trinity.”"** forbids elevating ʿĪsā and his mother to be gods with Allah. The three in their saying were a son, a father and a wife, God, Jesus and his mother.

**"Stop!—for your own good"** orders cessation and repentance, for it is better in this world and the Afterlife, and what is better to say is the profession of His Oneness.

**"Allah is only One God. Glory be to Him! He is far above having a son!"** rises above every such claim.

**"To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth"** gathers all as creatures, property and servants under His control and disposal.

**"And Allah is sufficient as a Trustee of Affairs"** names the Disposer of affairs, the Guardian and Witness over what is said about ʿĪsā, sufficient as Defender and Lord of all created beings.

### The excess forbidden

Human weakness it is: spot an outstanding aspect in a thing, and exaggerated views of it follow. Polytheism and personality cults alike are the fruit of that excess. The Christians committed excess in believing and honoring ʿĪsā when they went to the extreme of taking him to be God, son of God, or the third of three. The Jews committed the excess of the opposite direction: they did not accept him even as a prophet, and they were audacious enough to impute a false accusation to his revered mother and cast a slur on her parentage. The truth between the two: a human being born to Maryam, Masīḥ is nonetheless a true messenger of God. Beyond that all is false and ineffectual, whether it slight him or inflate him.

The excess did not stop at the prophets. Once used to it, both groups extended the attitude to the apostles, followers and deputies of their prophets. Having assigned godhood to a prophet, the Christians invested the prophet's followers with immunity from sin, without even investigating whether such followers genuinely adhered to his teachings or were no more than hereditary religious guides. The result was a leadership astray in itself, adding to the strayings of others. The Qur'ān described this condition exactly: "They took their rabbis and their monks to be their lords besides Allah" (9:31). Having made a prophet a god, they proceeded to worship later-day religious leaders in the name of following the prophet.

Because the deviation was a common scene of the time, the Holy Prophet ﷺ built defences for his own community. In the Musnad of Imām Aḥmad, from a report of Sayyidnā ʿUmar, he said:

> Do not exaggerate in my praise as was done by Christians in the case of ʿĪsā, son of Maryam. Beware, I am only a servant. So call me a servant of Allah and His messenger.

Al-Bukhārī recorded it through Ibn ʿAbbās from ʿUmar, and Ibn al-Madīnī rated it sound and authentically reported. Anas bin Mālik supplies the companion scene: a man hailed the Prophet ﷺ as our master, son of our master, the most righteous of us and son of our most righteous. The reply came:

> O people! Say what you have to say, but do not allow Shayṭān to trick you. I am Muḥammad bin ʿAbdullāh, Allah's servant and Messenger. By Allah, I do not like that you elevate me above the rank that Allah has granted me.

The highest rank he claimed was messengerhood, and raising it higher, to partnership in the attributes of Almighty Allah, is precisely the excess he forbade.

The Christians, having no limit to their disbelief for their ignorance, multiplied creeds that contradict each other: some believe ʿĪsā is Allah, some that he is one in a trinity, some that he is the son of Allah, prompting the wry saying that ten Christians meeting will part as eleven sects. Saʿīd bin Baṭrīq, Patriarch of Alexandria and a noted Christian scholar, recorded around the year four hundred after the Hijrah how a Christian council was convoked under Constantine, the founder of the city bearing his name. There the assembled Christians produced what they named the Great Trust, in reality the Great Treachery. Patriarchs attended by the thousand, two thousand and more, in such disarray that sects multiplied among them, some numbering twenty members, some fifty, some a hundred. Finding upward of three hundred patriarchs agreed on a single notion, the king lent it his backing and made it his creed. Deviant philosopher that he was, Constantine threw his weight behind that party alone: churches rose in its honor, its doctrines were drilled into children at baptism, books multiplied around it, and rival sects felt the king's oppression. Out of another council came the Jacobites, out of a third the Nestorians. All three agreed that ʿĪsā was divine, disputing only how his divinity related to his humanity: unity, or incarnation. Each accuses the others of heresy, while all three stand in disbelief.

### His Word

Three meanings are given for calling ʿĪsā the word of Allah. Imām al-Ghazzālī noted that two factors operate in the birth of a child: the sperm, and the saying of the word Be by Almighty Allah. Since the first factor was out of the question for ʿĪsā, he was called the word of Allah by attribution to the second, coming into existence solely through the word, without material means, the word delivered to Maryam. Others said the expression means the glad tiding of Allah, as when the angels said: "O Maryam, Allah gives you the good news of a word" (3:45). Still others read kalimah in the sense of sign, as elsewhere: "She testified to the word of her Lord as true" (66:12). The likeness is Adam's: "He created him from dust, then said to him: Be, and he was" (3:59). ʿAbdur-Razzāq narrated that Maʿmar said that Qatādah said the verse means He created him with the word Be. Ibn Abī Ḥātim recorded that Aḥmad bin Sinān al-Wāsiṭī heard Shādh bin Yaḥyā say that the word itself ʿĪsā was not. His existence arose from the word, not as the word. Al-Bukhārī recorded that ʿUbādah bin aṣ-Ṣāmit said that the Prophet ﷺ said:

> If anyone testifies that none has the right to be worshipped but Allah alone, who has no partners, and that Muḥammad is His servant and Messenger, and that ʿĪsā is Allah's servant and Messenger and His Word which He bestowed on Maryam and a spirit created by Him, and that Paradise is true and Hell is true, then Allah will admit him into Paradise with the deeds he performed.

Another narration has the entry made through whichever of the eight doors of Paradise he wishes, and Muslim records it too.

### A spirit from Him

Why is ʿĪsā called a spirit, and what does from Him mean? Several readings are reported. Some explain by lexical usage: in recognized usage spirit carries the sense of essence, lending a thing the effect of pristine purity. Born of no father, the outcome of nothing but the will of Allah and the word Be, ʿĪsā was blessed with the most perfect degree of purity, and the attribution to Allah is there to hold him in esteem. It is like attributing mosques to Allah as the mosques of Allah, or the Holy Kaʿbah as the House of Allah, or a worshipfully obedient person as ʿAbd Allāh, the servant of Allah. In the same way the Holy Prophet ﷺ is referred to in sūrat Banī Isrāʾīl: "Glory to Him who carried His servant" (17:1), the attribution reflecting honor. Others said his purpose was to infuse spiritual life into dead hearts, as the spirit is the cause of physical life, and in this sense the word is used of the Qur'ān as well: "thus We have revealed to you a spirit of Our command" (42:52). Others said spirit means secret: being, through his unusual birth, a sign and secret of Allah, he was called the spirit of Allah. Others supply the omitted word: the possessor of a spirit from Him, the distinction being that Allah turned his attribution toward Himself though all rational beings possess a spirit. And yet others read the word as the blowing of breath: Jibrīl, as commanded by Allah, blew upon the collar of Sayyidah Maryam, and that became the conception, as the verse points: "then We blew Our spirit in her" (21:91). None of these readings makes ʿĪsā a part of Allah or a divine person. One that possesses a spirit is compound, and God transcends being compound.

The classic repartee makes the logic plain. Rūḥ al-Maʿānī preserves a scene from the court of the Caliph Hārūn ar-Rashīd. A Christian physician there took on the scholar ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn al-Wāqidī in debate, claiming the Qur'ān itself makes ʿĪsā a part of Allah, and reading this very verse with its words "a spirit from Him". The reply came from the same Book: "He has subjected to you all that is in the heavens and all that is in the earth; it is all from Him" (45:13), where everything is attributed to Allah by the same from Him. If a spirit from Him means part of Him, then everything in the heavens and the earth is a part of Allah. Silenced, the Christian physician chose to become a Muslim. So it is with the she-camel of Allah and the command to "sanctify My House for those who circumambulate it" (22:26): the attribution honors the thing, and an authentic hadith says "I will enter on my Lord in His Home". The honor is real, the partness is not.

### One God, no son

The verse closes the argument with ownership. Everything was created by Him, everything lies under His mastery, everyone is His servant: who then could be His partner, His associate, His son? Almighty Allah is the dispenser of all needs, the sole caretaker of everyone's wants, universally and perennially sufficient, needing nobody. "He is the originator of the heavens and the earth. How can He have children" (6:101), and of those who say the Most Gracious has begotten a son, the Book says they have brought forth a terrible thing, up to His word "Alone" (19:95). Sūrat al-Māʾidah says it at both ends: "Surely, in disbelief are they who say that Allah is the Messiah, son of Maryam" (5:17), and at the Day of Resurrection Allah will ask: "O ʿĪsā, son of Maryam! Did you say unto men: worship me?" (5:116). The Christians of the trinity held three separate principles: one sect that Masīḥ is God himself appearing in the world, one that he is the son of God, one a unity in trinity of father, son and Mary, with a further group substituting the Holy Spirit, the rūḥ al-Quds, for Maryam. All are addressed in the Qur'ān, separately and jointly, and told the one truth. The inward reading adds: they followed their own opinion, describing what they worshipped in the likeness of created beings, and contradicted themselves with one that is three and three that is one. Persistence in the false only deepens the falseness.

### The fences against excess

The Prophet ﷺ set the fences in practice. It appears in hadith that at the ḥajj he asked Sayyidnā ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbbās to go and collect pebbles to throw at the Jamarāt. He returned with average-sized pebbles, which the Prophet ﷺ liked very much, saying twice: like these, like these. Then he said:

> It is your duty to avoid excess in faith, for communities before you were destroyed because of being excessive in their faith.

Three rules come out of this. The sunnah limit for pebbles thrown at the Jamarāt is average size, for big rocks are excess. The legal limit of everything is what the Holy Prophet ﷺ determined by word and deed, and going beyond it is ghulūw. Precisely defined, excess in faith is the crossing of the limit set for doing something.

The same principle governs the material world. Greed for luxury beyond need is blameworthy, but the Prophet ﷺ, while prohibiting worldly greed, set the proper limits by word and deed: he declared marriage his way, explained the blessings of children, prescribed living well with the family and fulfilling everyone's rights, called working for one's family an obligation after the obligation, and stressed business, agriculture, industry and labor. The establishment of an Islamic state and the promotion of a system governed by Islam he declared part of the mandate of prophethood. Engagement in these pursuits within the limits of need is not gross love of the material. The Jews and Christians, not realizing this, involved themselves in monasticism, which the Qur'ān refuted: they took to ways not prescribed for them, seeking Allah's pleasure, "then they failed to fulfill the conditions of what they had themselves imposed" (57:27).

The same principle guards the sunnah against invention. Every bidʿah, every self-promoted innovation in established religion, departs from the limits of moderation he demarcated in worship and in dealings, and he said:

> Every bidʿah is straying, and every straying ends in Jahannam.

Bidʿah is everything assumed to be part of religion that is not in his word and deed, clearly or by hint. Shah Waliyyullāh said Islam condemns it as a serious offense because it opens the doors to alteration in religion, and in his famous book, Hujjatullāh al-Balīghah, he detailed the circumstances under which attempts have been made to inject alterations into Islam, and the concern of the Sharīʿah, which installed defensive mechanisms on every such door. That is what happened to the earlier communities: they added things to what their Book said and their prophet taught, generation after generation, until the true religion could no longer be told apart from the additions.

The disease has two faces among Muslims. One group holds there is no such thing as a religious teacher or shaykh: the Book of Allah is sufficient for us, they are men, so are we. Every ambitious pseudo-intellectual, unlettered in Arabic and unfamiliar with the exegesis given by the Prophet ﷺ and the early scholars, then looks at a translation and is hoisted as a scholar of the Qur'ān. Had a book without a teacher been enough, Allah could have made written copies appear in every home, and no prophet needed teaching. No one becomes a physician by reading translations of medical books, no engineer by browsing engineering texts, no master tailor or chef from books on sewing and cooking. The system needs teaching and learning under a teacher. The other face takes just about anyone as a guide, almost blindly, without checking intellectual achievement, personal behavior, concern for people, or whether the teaching is against the Qur'ān and sunnah. The Sharīʿah marks out the middle course: learn the Book of Allah from the men of Allah, and know the men of Allah by the Book of Allah.

### In short

- Excess in faith destroyed the communities before: the Christians raised a messenger to godhood, the Jews dropped him below his rank, and both extended the error to the followers of their prophets.
- ʿĪsā is a messenger, a word bestowed on Maryam by Be, and a spirit created by command, an honor of attribution and not a part of Allah, as the court of Hārūn ar-Rashīd heard.
- The trinity, in all its sects and councils, is told to cease, for Allah is one God, far above a son, the owner of the heavens and the earth and the sufficient Trustee of Affairs.
- The fences stand: average pebbles at the Jamarāt, limits set by word and deed, no monasticism, no bidʿah, and teachers recognized by the Book they carry.

172.text:
The servant who is not ashamed: "The Messiah would never be too proud to be a servant of Allah, nor would the angels nearest to Allah. Those who are too proud and arrogant to worship Him will be brought before Him all together" (4:172). The opening statement of the verse puts the question of honor where the Christians misplaced it.

### Phrase by phrase

**"The Messiah would never be too proud to be a servant of Allah"** answers a taunt. The Christians told the Prophet ﷺ that what he said of Jesus was shameful. Al-Kalbī preserves the fuller dialogue: the delegation of Najrān said, why do you insult our lord? He asked who their lord was, and they said Jesus. What do I say about him? he asked. You say he is the servant and messenger of Allah, they answered. He told them it was not shameful for Jesus to be the slave of Allah. They insisted it was shameful, and this verse was revealed. Qatādah said the same of it: such servants will never be arrogant. Masīḥ will never scorn his servitude, will never not acknowledge it, for being a servant of Allah, devoted to His worship and obedient to His will, is an honor in itself, a nobility of the highest class. Sayyidnā ʿĪsā and the near angels are the best testifiers to the worth of that blessing. How could they spurn such an honor? His first words, as an infant, were: "I am God's servant" (19:30). How, then, is he taken for a god?

**"nor would the angels nearest to Allah"** names the favored angels, the carriers of the Throne, who never go against Allah's instruction, never disregard being His servants. The mention is a splendid digression, refuting those who claim the angels are gods or daughters of God, just as the Christians' claim was refuted before them. It does not imply the angels are superior to the Messiah. God was addressing them in accordance with their beliefs, for they believed in the superiority of angels over human beings.

**"Those who are too proud and arrogant to worship Him will be brought before Him all together"** warns whoever scorns His service and grows proud. Proud, Ibn ʿAbbās said, means insolent, and all such, believers and unbelievers, will He assemble on the Day of Resurrection, judging between them with a justice that cannot wrong.

### The measure of greatness

The worst disgrace imaginable lies in worshipping someone other than Allah. That is what the Christians did in taking Masīḥ as the son of Allah and the object of worship, and what the disbelievers did in taking angels as daughters of Allah and worshipping them along with their idols. For them there is punishment and disgrace. The inward reading adds: how can they disdain His worship when honor and dignity come through worship? How can they be too proud to humble themselves when ruin comes from pride? Servants become beautiful in their humility toward their masters. Prophets and angels have reached the highest stage of awareness of God's greatness and of their own helplessness, and their realization surpasses that of all others. One who has realized his own helplessness has, in essence, found how he relates to God.

### In short

- Servanthood is the honor, not the shame, and the Messiah said so with his first words in the cradle.
- The near angels own the same servitude, which settles the angels-worshippers as it settles the Christians.
- Insolence gathers all the proud before the Judge on a day none escapes.

173.text:
The two paydays: "As for those who believe and do good, He will reward them in full and increase them out of His grace. But those who are too proud and arrogant, He will subject them to a painful punishment. And besides Allah they will find no protector or helper" (4:173). The verse sorts the assembled crowd into two.

### Phrase by phrase

**"As for those who believe and do good"** joins faith in Muḥammad ﷺ and the Qur'ān to acts of obedience done with sincerity, in agreement with the sacred law.

**"He will reward them in full"** means wages for deeds paid without reduction, reward in Paradise.

**"and increase them out of His grace"** adds bounty upon bounty, kindness, ample mercy and favor: what no eye has seen nor ear heard, what never entered any man's heart to wish.

**"But those who are too proud and arrogant"** describes refusal of worship and obedience out of arrogance, being too proud even to believe.

**"He will subject them to a painful punishment"** means the chastisement of the Fire with degradation, disgrace and dishonor, earned by arrogance and rebellion. As the Book says elsewhere: "Verily! Those who scorn My worship, they will surely enter Hell in humiliation" (40:60).

**"And besides Allah they will find no protector or helper"** removes every recourse: no relative to benefit them, no friend to ward off the punishment, no helper to shield them from it.

### The deepest pain

The inward reading names the deepest pain: communion with the Beloved, never to be attained again by those who once came to know His majesty. Once what they know becomes indisputable, being left behind will be plain to them. Their sorrow on that day, mourning what slipped from their hands, will outburn every other punishment. The aware person has eyes and reaches his destination. The unaware is blind, and wanders astray until he falls into the pit of abomination.

### In short

- Full wages plus increase, beyond what eye, ear and heart have ever known, await faith with good deeds.
- The proud enter Hell in humiliation, with no protector and no helper besides Allah.
- The sharpest pain is the communion forever missed by those who once knew His majesty.

174.text:
The proof and the light: "O humanity! There has come to you conclusive evidence from your Lord. And We have sent down to you a brilliant light" (4:174). After refuting the beliefs that ascribed godhood to Jesus, the passage opens outward with a universal address.

### Phrase by phrase

**"O humanity! There has come to you conclusive evidence from your Lord"** announces a plain, unequivocal proof that eradicates all possibility of excuse and every evil doubt. One reading names the proof itself: a messenger from your Lord, Muḥammad ﷺ, the definitive argument come against the people of Makkah. Ibn ʿAbbās said the Holy Prophet ﷺ was called the burhān, the proof, for his blessed person, his noble morals, his miracles, and his receiving the very revelation of the Book of Allah. Rūḥ al-Maʿānī carries the same reading. Beyond these open proofs no other proof is needed. His person is, in itself, proof personified.

**"And We have sent down to you a brilliant light"** names, as Ibn Jurayj and others said, the Qur'ān, a clear light directing to the Truth, a scripture expounding the lawful and the unlawful, which falsehood cannot touch from any angle, a revelation from the Wise and Praised One. Verse 15 of sūrat al-Mā'idah says the like: "There has come to you from Allah a light and a clear Book." A question arises there, for the conjunction demands dissimilarity and light and Book seem one. The recorded answer: difference in expression is enough, the meanings remaining the same. And if the light is taken as the Holy Prophet ﷺ and the Book as the Qur'ān, that too is correct. It does not make him light in the literal sense, for it goes nothing against his being physically human.

### The call like sunrise

So loud and clear is a divine call to human beings that darkness is wiped out and life's realities lit to their utmost. Its arguments fortify it so well that denial cannot stand against it. Ridicule the deniers may offer, but logic they cannot. When God makes the sun rise, light and darkness separate, and the same divine power runs through the call of truth: after it, truth and untruth stand so clearly parted that no one in his senses finds it hard to understand. To see the sun, though, a man must open his eyes, and to receive guidance from the call, he must pay full attention. One who does not heed it stays deprived even while the call is being made.

The inward reading hears two lamps lit for the servant: one before him, the sunnah's lamp, which is the proof itself, and one within, the heart's lamp of faith and shining light. Happy is the servant who walks between these two lamps. One breath with the Friend is worth the two worlds, and one vision of the Friend is given gratis to a hundred thousand spirits. The grateful soul answers: in gratitude I send my spirit to You, one whiff of union doing what a hundred spirits never could.

### In short

- The proof come from the Lord is either the Prophet ﷺ himself, morals, miracles and revelation in one person, or the book-borne argument he carries.
- The light sent down is the Qur'ān, clear, untouched by falsehood, expounding the lawful and the unlawful.
- Like sunrise, the call parts truth from untruth, but eyes must be opened to see it.

175.text:
The holding and the guiding: "As for those who believe in Allah and hold fast to Him, He will admit them into His mercy and grace and guide them to Himself through the Straight Path" (4:175). The verse maps the whole journey of the believer in one line.

### Phrase by phrase

**"those who believe in Allah and hold fast to Him"** means, in one reading, His worship and reliance on Him for everything at all. Ibn Jurayj said it means they believe in Allah and hold fast to the Qur'ān. Another reading adds Muḥammad ﷺ and the Qur'ān to the object of belief, and reads the holding fast as holding to Allah's divine Oneness.

**"He will admit them into His mercy and grace"** means He grants them His mercy and admits them into Paradise, rewards and ranks increased and multiplied, favor and bounty from Him, honor added.

**"and guide them to Himself through the Straight Path"** opens a clear way with no wickedness in it and no deviation, namely the religion of Islam. It describes the believers in this life and the Hereafter: in this life their footing is straight and safe in creed and in action alike, confirmed in faith, and in the Hereafter they walk the path of Allah that leads to the gardens of Paradise.

### The grip that outlasts the deceiver

Holding on firmly is necessary, because in this world of trial Satan pursues man, deceiving him in many ways and turning him from the truth. Unless a man resolves to support the truth and fight Satan's deceptions, Satan will induce him into his fold. Yet man is not left alone in the trial. Those who wish to tread the path receive divine guidance at every turn, and by God's help they reach their destination. When a man gives all importance to the truth alone, God engenders in him the ability to persevere on the path of pure truth, and so saves him from deviating onto paths that lead astray.

The inward reading divides the labor rightly. The servant contributes faith and the grip of holding fast, as servanthood demands. The Exalted Lord contributes bounty and mercy, in the attribute of loving kindness. Their guidance is to see that every recompense found and every generosity seen flows from His bounty and mercy, never from their own faith or grip. As the Prophet ﷺ said:

> There is none of you who will be saved by his deeds.

They said: not even you, O Messenger of God? He said:

> Not even I, unless God envelops me with His mercy.

### In short

- Belief plus the grip, on Allah, on His Oneness, on the Qur'ān, draws mercy, grace and raised ranks.
- The Straight Path is Islam itself, safe in creed and action now, and the road to the gardens later.
- Deeds do not save anyone by themselves, for the recompense is bounty and mercy from first to last.

176.text:
The closing ruling: "They ask you ˹for a ruling, O Prophet˺. Say, “Allah gives you a ruling regarding those who die without children or parents.” If a man dies childless and leaves behind a sister, she will inherit one-half of his estate, whereas her brother will inherit all of her estate if she dies childless. If this person leaves behind two sisters, they together will inherit two-thirds of the estate. But if the deceased leaves male and female siblings, a male’s share will be equal to that of two females. Allah makes ˹this˺ clear to you so you do not go astray. And Allah has ˹perfect˞ knowledge of all things" (4:176). The sūrah ends where much of it began, with the shares, and the last word on inheritance is also the last word of the whole chapter.

### Phrase by phrase

**"They ask you ˹for a ruling, O Prophet˺"** introduces a question from a Companion. Jābir ibn ʿAbdullāh al-Anṣārī said: I had seven sisters, and I fell so ill that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ came visiting me, found me unconscious, and spat on my face, and I woke. I asked him: O Messenger of Allah, may I bequest two thirds of my wealth to my sister? He said: hold back. I asked: what about half? He said: hold back, and went out and left me. Then he came back and said: O Jābir, you are not going to die of this illness. Allah has revealed verses explaining the share your sisters should have, and He has apportioned two thirds for them. Jābir used to say that this verse was revealed about him.

**"Say, “Allah gives you a ruling regarding those who die without children or parents.”"** names the kalālah. The word, in the Arabs' usage, means the crown that surrounds the head from all sides, and the scholars took it for one who dies leaving behind neither descendants nor ascendants, anyone other than the father and the son. Abū Bakr used to say exactly that, and ʿUmar bin al-Khaṭṭāb felt shy to change a ruling Abū Bakr had issued. His saying carries the majority of the Companions, the followers, and the imams of every age, and it is the ruling the Qur'ān itself indicates.

**"If a man dies childless and leaves behind a sister, she will inherit one-half of his estate"** counts a full sister or a half sister from the father's side, taking her half after the preferential rights are settled, the debts, the wills, the burial expenses. The remaining half goes to the heirs of the aṣbah category, and if none is alive, that half also returns to her. As for a half sister from the mother's side, her share was already fixed in the earlier verse: one sixth if she is alone, and a third shared if there are two or more (4:12). The daughter-and-sister case divided the early authorities. Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn az-Zubayr judged that a man who dies leaving a daughter and a sister leaves the sister nothing, for the verse gives her half only when the deceased leaves no child. The majority disagreed: the daughter takes one half and the sister the other. Muʿādh bin Jabal had so judged in the Prophet's ﷺ own time, as Sulaymān reported from Ibrāhīm, who reported it from al-Aswad. And al-Bukhārī records the fuller case: Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī was asked about a daughter, a grand-daughter and a sister, and ruled the daughter one half and the sister one half, sending the questioners on to Ibn Masʿūd. Ibn Masʿūd answered that he would otherwise have deviated from the rightly guided: the daughter one half, the grand-daughter one sixth, and what remains, a third, to the sister. Confronted with that answer of Abū Mūsā, he said: while this scholar is among you, ask him, not me.

**"whereas her brother will inherit all of her estate if she dies childless"** gives the brother the whole of what his sister leaves if she has no surviving offspring or parent. If a surviving parent exists, he inherits nothing, and where a fixed-share heir stands, such as a husband or a half brother from the mother's side, that share is taken first and the remainder goes to the brother. The rule of the farā'iḍ runs beneath it, as the Prophet ﷺ said in the report of Ibn ʿAbbās: settle the fixed shares on their people first, then whatever remains goes to the nearest male relative.

**"If this person leaves behind two sisters, they together will inherit two-thirds of the estate"** adds that more than two share in the two thirds. From this the scholars took the ruling on two daughters or more, just as the sisters' share had been taken from the verse about the daughters: "if there are only daughters, two or more, their share is two thirds of the inheritance" (4:11).

**"a male's share will be equal to that of two females"** states the agnation principle, applied to sons, grandsons and brothers: the male regularly receives twice the female's share.

**"Allah makes ˹this˺ clear to you so you do not go astray"** means His law and His set limits made clear, so that no one errs in the division after this explanation. Inheritance is not a simple matter, and this is one of the areas where disobeying the divine injunction leads astray from the straight path of guidance.

**"And Allah has ˹perfect˞ knowledge of all things"** declares perfect knowledge of the consequences of everything and of the benefit each matter carries for His servants, and of what each relative deserves, by the degree of relation to the deceased.

### The last verse revealed

Al-Bukhārī recorded that al-Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib said that the last sūrah to be revealed was sūrat Barāʾah, chapter 9, and the last verse to be revealed was this one. The two Shaykhs, Bukhārī and Muslim, report it. Imām Aḥmad recorded the illness behind it from Jābir bin ʿAbdullāh: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ came visiting him when he was so ill he fell unconscious, performed ablution, and poured, or had poured, the remaining water on him. Regaining consciousness, Jābir said he would leave inheritance only through kalālah, and asked what would come of it, and Allah revealed the verse of the farā'iḍ (4:11). The Two Ṣaḥīḥs and the Group recorded it. The chains run from Jābir through the transmitters who carried it, by way of Abu'z-Zubayr and Hisham ibn Abi Abd, from the line of Abū ʿAbd ar-Raḥmān ibn Abī Ḥāmid.

### ʿUmar's three wishes

The meaning and ruling of the kalālah was somewhat confusing even to the Leader of the Faithful. In the Two Ṣaḥīḥs, ʿUmar said that there were three matters he wished the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had explained, so that they could abide by his explanation: the grandfather's share in inheritance, the kalālah, and one particular sort of ribā. Imām Aḥmad recorded that he said he asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about nothing more than the kalālah, until the Prophet ﷺ stabbed him with his finger in the chest and said: the verse at the end of sūrat an-Nisāʾ should suffice for you. Muslim recorded a longer form of it. Ibn Jarīr recorded that Ṭāriq bin Shihāb said that ʿUmar once gathered the Companions and said he would give a ruling on the kalālah so clear that women would discuss it in their bedrooms. At that a snake slid into the house and broke up the gathering, and ʿUmar said: had Allah willed this verdict to happen, it would have happened. Al-Ḥākim Abū ʿAbdullāh an-Naysābūrī recorded that ʿUmar said that had he asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about three things, it would have been better for him than red camels: who should be the khalīfah after him, whether to fight a people who agreed to pay zakah but not to the khalīfah, and the kalālah. Its chain is ṣaḥīḥ, as al-Ḥākim noted, though the two Shaykhs did not record it.

### The two communities compared

The inheritance rulings stand scattered at three places in this sūrah, at the beginning, in the middle, and now at the end. The wisdom may lie in the injustice that prevailed in inheritance before Islam: taken up gradually, the subject would alert the addressees step by step to the need of justice in this area. Around the closing ruling, the comparison of verse 170 and verse 175 completes itself. There, the condition of the disbelievers, to whom belongs what is in the heavens and the earth whether they believe or not, and here, the model of the noble Companions, who believed in Allah and held fast to Him. The People of the Book made the abomination of suggesting a partner and a son in the purest conceivable divinity an article of their faith, and took a blatant position against the revelation. The Companions, without saying much of their fundamentals of faith and their devoted worship, were equally inquisitive about obligations subsidiary and commonplace, those of inheritance and marriage. They waited for wahy, the command of Allah through revelation, and sought the Prophet's ﷺ guidance in everything, though it was easier to do their own bidding under reason or desire. Men and women of faith, they turned to Allah in remembrance and were honored by being addressed by their most exalted Creator, a grace never granted to any other community. What they did not understand, they rechecked with him until satisfied. Two sets of people, and how far apart.

The verse also shows that the Prophet ﷺ gave no decision of his own without the guiding command of revelation. Where no standing guidance existed, he held his decision and waited for wahy to come, and then ruled. In this lies a hint at the wisdom of gradual revelation: had the whole Book come down at one fixed time, as the People of the Book demanded, it would not have carried the benefits of a revelation arriving as needed and when appropriate. This modality accommodated questioners who asked out of necessity and were answered through the recited revelation, al-Wahy al-Matluww. Any verse revealed in favor of a Companion, or answering his question, is treasured as a testament of his virtues, keeping his name and merit alive until the Day of Doom. Thus Jābir b. ʿAbd Allāh is remembered in the Book itself. So sūrat an-Nisāʾ ends, and praise belongs to Allah.

### The inward reading

The ruling cuts disputes short. Humankind desires wealth, and the lower selves incline to greed. Without decisive, fixed amounts, independent judgment, ijtihād, would breed doubts, and the doubts would breed quarrels and mutual attacks. The fixed portions settle the disputants' claims definitively. That inheritance rights were fixed for women, even those with no close relative to defend their cause, shows consideration for their weaker position. The male's larger portion answers the burdens laid on him, providing, seeking income, and supporting.

### In short

- The kalālah is the one who dies leaving neither child nor parent, and the sisters, brothers and combinations receive their measured halves, two thirds, and the two-to-one rule.
- This is the last verse revealed, reported by al-Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib, answered for Jābir and his seven sisters, and it sufficed ʿUmar, who yet wished he had asked three things more.
- The verse displays the Companions' habit of asking and waiting for revelation, and the Book's habit of answering when the need arose.
- Fixed shares cut the greed of the lower selves short, protect the weaker, and weigh the burdens of the stronger.
